The primary focus is peer-assisted correction during shared writing, with Microsoft Word's spellchecker as a diagnostic tool that scaffolds but does not determine interaction.

ijCSCL_10_3_0.title: Conceptualizing the intersubjective group
ijCSCL_10_3_0.summary_haiku: Stahl argues that intersubjectivity—shared understanding through joint meaning-making—is the defining characteristic of computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL). The article proposes a paradigm shift from analyzing individual learning outcomes to examining group-level phenomena, emphasizing that collaborative learning involves increased intersubjective understanding within groups rather than aggregated individual learning. CSCL research, pedagogy, and technology should prioritize the group as the unit of analysis.
ijCSCL_10_3_0.evidence_span: abstract, conceptual framing, and theoretical argument throughout
ijCSCL_10_3_0.coding_notes: This is a conceptual/theoretical paper proposing a paradigm shift toward group-level intersubjectivity rather than reporting empirical research. Discourse analysis and dialogic theory best capture Stahl's emphasis on shared meaning-making and joint understanding. Confidence is moderate because the paper is primarily theoretical rather than methodologically explicit; secondary coding reflects the multi-level and sociocultural underpinnings of the argument.

ijCSCL_6_2_1.title: Bridging research and practice: Implementing and sustaining knowledge building in Hong Kong classrooms
ijCSCL_6_2_1.summary_haiku: # Summary This article examines how computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) research translates into classroom practice through a case study of knowledge-building implementation in Hong Kong schools. Using design-based research across macro (policy), meso (teacher networks), and micro (classroom) levels, the study identifies three critical themes: systemic alignment across educational levels, capacity building through principle-based teacher communities, and innovation as continuous inquiry. Findings demonstrate that sustained CSCL adoption requires coordinating institutional policies, teacher professional development networks, and classroom design while adapting research models to local socio-cultural contexts.
ijCSCL_6_2_1.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (design-based research across macro/meso/micro levels), findings (systemic alignment, teacher networks, classroom design)
ijCSCL_6_2_1.coding_notes: The article explicitly frames knowledge building (Scardamalia & Bereiter) as the pedagogical model and uses design-based research iteratively across institutional, teacher-community, and classroom levels. Cross-level analysis is central to understanding how CSCL research translates into sustained practice. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

ijCSCL_5_3_1.title: Online moderation of synchronous e-argumentation
ijCSCL_5_3_1.summary_haiku: This exploratory study examines effective online moderation of synchronous small-group argumentation in co-located classrooms. Through student questionnaires and protocol analyses of moderated discussions using Digalo software, researchers found that generic scaffolding prompts—effective in face-to-face settings—were ineffective in synchronous e-discussions. Instead, content-specific, involved moderation styles that disguised scaffolding as peer participation proved more effective and appreciated by students.
ijCSCL_5_3_1.evidence_span: methods (protocol analysis, questionnaires) + findings (moderation styles, scaffolding effectiveness)
ijCSCL_5_3_1.coding_notes: Study uses protocol analysis of synchronous e-discussions (Digalo software) to examine moment-by-moment moderation moves during small-group argumentation. Content-specific scaffolding coded as effective pedagogical strategy; sociocultural framing evident in emphasis on peer participation and social mediation of learning.

ijCSCL_5_4_0.title: Beyond folk theories of CSCL
ijCSCL_5_4_0.summary_haiku: Stahl and Hesse critique three approaches to CSCL research, arguing that the most productive approach develops theories specifically tailored to collaborative learning's unique characteristics. They contend that CSCL requires elaborated theories addressing multiple interpenetrating levels—individual, group, classroom—and technological mediation, moving beyond folk theories and borrowed frameworks to capture phenomena distinctive to computer-supported contexts.
ijCSCL_5_4_0.coding_notes: This is a theoretical critique and position paper rather than an empirical study. It does not employ a primary research methodology, unit of analysis, or specific pedagogy; instead, it argues for theory development in CSCL. Coded as 'other' for methodology and unit_of_analysis to reflect its meta-theoretical nature. Theory_primary is sociocultural because Stahl's work is grounded in Vygotskian and activity-theoretic traditions; secondary theories reflect the multi-level, mediated perspective advocated.

ijCSCL_10_4_1.title: Advancing knowledge‐building discourse through judgments of promising ideas
ijCSCL_10_4_1.authors: Bodong Chen & Marlene Scardamalia & Carl Bereiter
ijCSCL_10_4_1.summary_haiku: Grade 3 students demonstrated capability in making promisingness judgments—evaluating ideas for their potential to advance knowledge—when supported by explicit discussion and a digital tool integrated into Knowledge Forum. Design-based research revealed students could distinguish ideas worth developing from mere facts, and promisingness judgments significantly enhanced collaborative discourse and scientific knowledge advancement compared to control classrooms.
ijCSCL_10_4_1.coding_notes: Classic design-based research study in Knowledge Forum context (Scardamalia & Bereiter's knowledge-building framework). Grade 3 students' discourse analyzed for promisingness judgments; comparison with control classrooms supports quasi-experimental framing, but iterative design refinement is the primary methodological signature.

ijCSCL_4_2_3.title: Genre and CSCL: The form and rhetoric of the online posting
ijCSCL_4_2_3.summary_haiku: This study applies genre analysis to online discussion postings in CSCL contexts, hypothesizing that educational postings share rhetorical characteristics with their epistolary precursor, the letter. Through content analysis of 136 postings, the author identifies 240 rhetorical markers reflecting epistolary dynamics, including salutations, present-tense references, and temporal references. Findings suggest that cultural and historical factors embedded in familiar genres significantly shape how students engage in online collaborative learning, beyond technological affordances alone.
ijCSCL_4_2_3.evidence_span: methods (content analysis of 136 postings, 240 rhetorical markers) + findings (epistolary characteristics identified)
ijCSCL_4_2_3.coding_notes: Study employs systematic coding of rhetorical markers in online postings (content analysis) combined with linguistic/genre-based interpretation (discourse analysis). Primary unit is the posting artifact itself. Dialogic theory frames meaning-making through genre conventions; sociocultural perspective emphasizes cultural/historical shaping of participation. No explicit pedagogy model is foregrounded; focus is on form and rhetoric rather than instructional design.

ijCSCL_6_1_4.title: Exploring e-learners’ perceptions of net-based peer-reviewed English writing
ijCSCL_6_1_4.summary_haiku: This study examined asynchronous, blind peer review for improving Chinese adult e-learners' English writing. Thirty-six students divided into three ability groups participated in a year-long experiment with rotating cross-group peer reviews mediated by the instructor. Results showed all groups improved, with lower-ability students making greater progress than higher-ability students. However, high-ability students became discouraged when paired with lower-ability peers for extended periods, suggesting flexible grouping strategies may be necessary.
ijCSCL_6_1_4.evidence_span: methods (year-long experiment, three ability groups, rotating cross-group peer reviews) + findings (improvement patterns by ability level, discouragement effects)
ijCSCL_6_1_4.coding_notes: Study uses a quasi-experimental design with ability-based grouping and rotating peer-review conditions over time. Primary focus is individual writing improvement and group dynamics; asynchronous peer review is the core technology. Sociocultural framing (peer interaction mediating learning) with socio-cognitive elements (ability-based pairing effects).

ijCSCL_7_3_3.title: Patterns of kindergarten children’s social interaction with peers in the computer area
ijCSCL_7_3_3.summary_haiku: This qualitative study examined kindergarten children's peer interactions in a classroom computer area through three-month observations and teacher interviews. The researcher identified six social interaction patterns: parallel play, verbal conflicts, sociable interactions, knowledge construction through positive processes, knowledge construction through negative processes, and non-verbal communication. Three patterns—positive processes, negative processes, and non-verbal communication—constituted "Cognitively Effective Social Interaction" leading to meaningful knowledge construction. Findings demonstrate computers support collaborative learning when integrated with classroom curriculum.
ijCSCL_7_3_3.evidence_span: methods (three-month observations, teacher interviews) + findings (six interaction patterns, cognitively effective social interaction)
ijCSCL_7_3_3.coding_notes: Study is a bounded, in-depth qualitative examination of kindergarten peer interactions in a specific classroom context (computer area) using observation and interview. The identification of six interaction patterns and their coding reflects interaction analysis and content analysis of collaborative episodes. Primary unit is dyads/small groups of children collaborating at computers; secondary unit is the discourse/interaction traces themselves. Sociocultural theory frames learning as socially mediated; socio-cognitive elements appear in the emphasis on conflict and knowledge construction processes.

ijCSCL_6_3_6.title: Analyzing temporal patterns of knowledge construction in a role-based online discussion
ijCSCL_6_3_6.summary_haiku: This study analyzed temporal patterns of knowledge construction in role-based online discussions using content analysis and statistical discourse analysis. Examining 252 posts from 21 university students, researchers identified pivotal posts that divided discussions into distinct segments. Results showed most discussions progressed from lower to higher knowledge construction phases, with mid-discussion summaries by Synthesizer and Wrapper roles acting as pivotal posts that elevated subsequent discussion quality, supporting the progressive nature of collaborative knowledge construction.
ijCSCL_6_3_6.evidence_span: methods (content analysis, statistical discourse analysis) + findings (pivotal posts, knowledge construction phases, temporal progression)
ijCSCL_6_3_6.coding_notes: Study uses systematic coding of discussion posts to identify knowledge construction phases and pivotal posts; temporal sequence analysis reveals progression patterns. Role-based scripting (Synthesizer, Wrapper) is the pedagogical structure enabling collaborative knowledge advancement.

ijCSCL_7_1_1.title: Making rounds: The routine work of the teacher during collaborative learning with computers
ijCSCL_7_1_1.summary_haiku: This ethnomethodological study analyzes teacher interventions during collaborative computer-based learning using video recordings of English lessons with storyboarding software. Through detailed conversation analysis of naturally occurring classroom interactions, the author identifies five types of teacher practices: ratifying pupil work, reminding pupils of task requirements, making suggestions for improvement, maintaining classroom control, and making whole-class announcements. The analysis reveals that classroom management and pedagogy are intertwined rather than separate, and tensions between teacher and pupil perspectives are collaborative rather than antagonistic.
ijCSCL_7_1_1.evidence_span: methods (video ethnomethodology, conversation analysis) + findings (five teacher intervention types)
ijCSCL_7_1_1.coding_notes: Ethnomethodological approach with detailed conversation analysis of moment-by-moment teacher moves during collaborative computer-based learning. Primary focus is teacher facilitation practices and their interplay with classroom management; secondary attention to small-group dynamics. Storyboarding software is a shared workspace tool.

ijCSCL_7_1_0.title: Ethnomethodologically informed
ijCSCL_7_1_0.summary_haiku: Ethnomethodology (EM), founded by Harold Garfinkel, offers a research approach particularly suited to analyzing computer-supported collaborative learning by examining how people create intersubjective understanding through observable meaning-making methods. Unlike traditional educational research emphasizing individual mental states or societal forces, EM focuses on small-group interactions through sequential discourse analysis, enabling researchers to understand collaborative learning processes without imposing predetermined theoretical frameworks.
ijCSCL_7_1_0.coding_notes: Ethnomethodology is fundamentally an interaction-analytic approach examining sequential meaning-making in small groups through discourse. The article emphasizes observable methods and intersubjective understanding rather than individual cognition or predetermined pedagogy, aligning with dialogic and distributed cognition theories. No specific technology or AI involvement mentioned.

ijCSCL_6_3_7.title: The impact of scripted roles on online collaborative learning processes
ijCSCL_6_3_7.summary_haiku: This pilot study examined how scripted "opinion-centered" roles impact online collaborative learning in an asynchronous text-based environment. Using content analysis of 209 student messages and post-activity questionnaires, researchers evaluated four dimensions: participative, social, cognitive, and teaching. Results showed roles effectively fostered group cohesion and knowledge building, though metacognition remained underdeveloped. Students' perceptions largely aligned with message analysis, indicating awareness of the collaborative process.
ijCSCL_6_3_7.coding_notes: Study uses systematic coding of 209 messages (content analysis) combined with descriptive statistics and questionnaire data. Scripted roles are the core pedagogical intervention; asynchronous text-based environment is the technology. Sociocultural framing evident in focus on group cohesion and collaborative knowledge building.

ijCSCL_7_3_2.title: Context matters: The value of analyzing human factors within educational contexts as a way of informing technology-related decisions within design research
ijCSCL_7_3_2.summary_haiku: Design research in educational technology often overlooks systematic analysis of contextual factors. This study adapts Cognitive Work Analysis (CWA), an engineering method, to systematically identify human factors constraints—political, organizational, team, psychological, and physical—within a teacher education program. Through interviews, documentation analysis, and observations, 358 constraints were identified. The modified CWA approach made contextual information explicit and organized, enabling informed technology design decisions for supporting student research projects through an online mentorship environment.
ijCSCL_7_3_2.evidence_span: methods (interviews, documentation analysis, observations) + findings (358 constraints identified; CWA framework applied)
ijCSCL_7_3_2.coding_notes: Study is design-based research using CWA to inform technology design for an online mentorship environment in teacher education. Primary unit is the teacher education program/cohort; secondary units include teacher facilitation and artifacts (documentation). Activity theory best fits the systematic analysis of human factors and contextual constraints within an activity system.

ijCSCL_6_1_5.title: The logic of wikis: The possibilities of the Web 2.0 classroom
ijCSCL_6_1_5.summary_haiku: Web 2.0 tools like wikis and blogs can enable Dewey's vision of democratic education by supporting abductive reasoning—the logic of hypothesis generation essential for creative problem-solving. Unlike traditional deductive approaches emphasizing certainty, abduction requires simultaneously maintaining multiple competing premises, a capability previously impossible in classrooms but now feasible through hypertext-based technologies that create scale-free networks of interconnected information nodes.
ijCSCL_6_1_5.coding_notes: This is a theoretical/conceptual paper articulating how Web 2.0 wikis enable abductive reasoning and Deweyan democratic education. No empirical methodology (experiment, ethnography, or systematic analysis) is evident from the summary; the primary contribution is philosophical/theoretical. Coded as artifact_discourse_trace because wikis themselves are the focal object, with classroom_cohort as secondary context. Sociocultural and distributed cognition theories align with the emphasis on collaborative knowledge networks.

ijCSCL_4_2_2.title: Affordances revisited: Articulating a Merleau-Pontian view
ijCSCL_4_2_2.summary_haiku: This article develops a Merleau-Pontian account of affordances for CSCL, arguing that existing interpretations within the field contain unresolved ontological and epistemological tensions. The author proposes that affordances are dynamic, relational, and skill-relative properties existing independently of perception but relative to agents' body-schematic interaction potential. This framework shifts design and empirical research focus toward background structuring and learners' developing capabilities rather than mental models.
ijCSCL_4_2_2.coding_notes: This is a theoretical/philosophical article developing a Merleau-Pontian framework for affordances in CSCL rather than an empirical study. Coded as ethnographic_case_study as the closest fit for qualitative conceptual work, though the article is primarily theoretical. No specific pedagogy, technology, or empirical methodology is described; the focus is on ontological and epistemological foundations for understanding affordances.

ijCSCL_4_4_4.title: An ontology engineering approach to the realization of theory-driven group formation
ijCSCL_4_4_4.authors: Seiji Isotani & Akiko Inaba & Mitsuru Ikeda & Riichiro Mizoguchi
ijCSCL_4_4_4.summary_haiku: This research presents an ontology-based framework for theory-driven group formation in collaborative learning. Using ontological engineering, the authors formalize learning theory concepts to guide group composition, role assignment, and activity design. A proof-of-concept experiment with four instructors and twenty participants demonstrated that groups formed according to pedagogical theory specifications showed significantly better performance and more meaningful interactions than control groups, suggesting ontologies effectively operationalize learning theories for improved collaborative learning outcomes.
ijCSCL_4_4_4.coding_notes: The study uses ontological engineering to formalize and operationalize learning theory for group formation and role assignment—a form of structured collaboration scripting. The proof-of-concept experiment with control comparison and performance/interaction metrics indicates experimental design. Sociocultural theory underpins the theory-driven approach to collaborative learning; activity theory is secondary given the focus on formalizing activity structures via ontology.

ijCSCL_10_4_0.title: A decade of CSCL
ijCSCL_10_4_0.summary_haiku: CSCL research has shifted from individual cognitive frameworks toward post-cognitive theories emphasizing group-level interaction and collaborative knowledge building. However, implementation gaps persist: technologies often reflect individual learning models, analysis methods remain cognitively focused, and widespread educational adoption remains limited. Future progress requires international collaboration, design-based research, teacher professional development, and curriculum alignment to transform global education through computer-supported collaborative learning approaches.
ijCSCL_10_4_0.coding_notes: This is a position/review article synthesizing a decade of CSCL research rather than reporting an empirical study. No specific methodology, unit of analysis, or technology is the focus; instead, it critiques the field's trajectory and calls for future directions. Coded as 'other' for methodology and unit_of_analysis to reflect its meta-analytical, non-empirical nature.

ijCSCL_5_4_1.title: Can the interactive whiteboard support young children’s collaborative communication and thinking in classroom science activities?
ijCSCL_5_4_1.authors: Ruth Kershner & Neil Mercer & Paul Warwick & Judith Kleine Staarman
ijCSCL_5_4_1.summary_haiku: Interactive whiteboards can support young children's collaborative communication and thinking in primary science, but effectiveness depends on multiple interacting factors. Through observational analysis of twelve classrooms, researchers found the IWB facilitates productive dialogue when combined with teacher scaffolding, established "talk rules," and appropriate classroom participation structures. However, the technology alone is not pedagogically transformative; success requires careful integration with other classroom resources and attention to both social and cognitive dimensions of collaborative learning.
ijCSCL_5_4_1.evidence_span: methods (observational analysis of 12 classrooms) + findings (IWB effectiveness depends on scaffolding, talk rules, participation structures)
ijCSCL_5_4_1.coding_notes: Study emphasizes micro-analytic observation of classroom dialogue and teacher orchestration around IWB use. Primary focus on how technology mediates collaborative communication within established social structures; dialogic and sociocultural theories align with emphasis on talk rules and scaffolded dialogue.

ijCSCL_5_4_3.title: Using activity theory to understand intergenerational play: The case of Family Quest
ijCSCL_5_4_3.authors: Sinem Siyahhan & Sasha A. Barab & Michael P. Downton
ijCSCL_5_4_3.summary_haiku: # Summary This study examined intergenerational play between parents and children (ages 9-13) using Quest Atlantis, an educational 3D game, through activity theory analysis. Five-week observations of seven parent-child dyads revealed that successful collaborative gaming required shared intentions and expertise exchange. While outcomes varied across dyads, the research demonstrated that educational video games can facilitate meaningful family bonding and learning, particularly when designed to encourage parents and children to leverage complementary skills around personally relevant narratives.
ijCSCL_5_4_3.evidence_span: title, summary, methods (five-week observations of dyads), findings (shared intentions, expertise exchange)
ijCSCL_5_4_3.coding_notes: Activity theory is explicitly named in the title and framing. The five-week observational study of seven parent-child dyads in a bounded 3D game environment is characteristic of ethnographic case study with micro-level interaction analysis. Quest Atlantis is a shared digital workspace where dyads collaborate on quests.

ijCSCL_10_4_2.title: Investigating the effects of prompts on argumentation style, consensus and perceived efficacy in collaborative learning
ijCSCL_10_4_2.authors: Owen M. Harney & Michael J. Hogan & Benjamin Broome & Tony Hall & Cormac Ryan
ijCSCL_10_4_2.summary_haiku: Process-level prompts during collaborative learning sessions significantly enhance group outcomes compared to task-level prompts. In an experimental study using Interactive Management with 75 psychology students, process-level prompts increased perceived consensus and perceived efficacy of the methodology. Analysis of group dialogue revealed more sophisticated argumentation patterns and greater complexity in consensus-based problem models among process-level groups, suggesting that facilitator prompting style substantially influences collaborative learning effectiveness.
ijCSCL_10_4_2.evidence_span: methods (experimental design, 75 students, Interactive Management), findings (dialogue analysis, consensus, efficacy measures)
ijCSCL_10_4_2.coding_notes: Study compares process-level vs. task-level prompts in controlled experimental conditions with 75 psychology students. Primary methodology is experimental comparison; secondary methods include discourse analysis of group dialogue and content analysis of argumentation patterns. Prompts function as collaboration scripts structuring group interaction. Sociocultural and dialogic theories underpin the focus on dialogue quality and consensus-building.

ijCSCL_4_2_0.title: Practice perspectives in CSCL
ijCSCL_4_2_0.summary_haiku: This editorial argues that CSCL research should adopt practice perspectives to understand how collaborative learning emerges at individual, group, and community levels. Rather than studying interaction through controlled variables and statistical regularities, practice perspectives focus on how people actually interact, examining embodied and materially mediated human activity. The issue's articles demonstrate this approach by analyzing group coordination practices, technology affordances relative to user interaction potential, genre adaptation in virtual environments, and metaskills required for knowledge-creation practices.
ijCSCL_4_2_0.coding_notes: This is an editorial introducing a thematic issue rather than a primary empirical study. The practice perspective explicitly rejects controlled variables and statistical regularities in favor of naturalistic, embodied analysis of interaction across individual, group, and community levels. Activity theory and distributed cognition align well with the emphasis on materially mediated human activity and coordination practices.

ijCSCL_7_3_0.title: An international research community
ijCSCL_7_3_0.authors: Gerry Stahl & Nancy Law & Friedrich Hesse
ijCSCL_7_3_0.summary_haiku: The International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning demonstrates significant scholarly impact, ranking eleventh among education journals with a 2.243 impact factor. The journal supports a thriving international research community across fifty-three countries, publishing diverse, interdisciplinary research on collaborative learning technologies through rigorous peer review and design-based methodologies that advance CSCL theory and practice globally.
ijCSCL_7_3_0.coding_notes: This is an editorial or meta-commentary on the IJCSCL journal itself, not a primary research study. It describes the journal's impact, scope, and community rather than reporting empirical findings, methodology, or theoretical contributions from a specific study. Insufficient detail to code research design, pedagogy, or technology choices.

ijCSCL_5_2_5.title: Promoting metacognitive skills through peer scaffolding in a CSCL environment
ijCSCL_5_2_5.summary_haiku: A longitudinal case study of 18 university students using the KnowCat knowledge-building system over two semesters examined how peer scaffolding develops metacognitive skills in computer-supported collaborative learning. Content analysis of student annotations revealed statistically significant increases in metacognitive processes, particularly in monitoring and clarity-seeking behaviors. Results suggest pedagogical use of CSCL environments with structured peer feedback effectively enhances students' self-regulation and collaborative problem-solving capabilities.
ijCSCL_5_2_5.evidence_span: methods (content analysis of annotations), findings (statistically significant increases in metacognitive processes)
ijCSCL_5_2_5.coding_notes: Study employs systematic coding of student annotations (content analysis) with descriptive statistics on metacognitive indicators. KnowCat is a knowledge-building system supporting collaborative annotation and peer feedback. Peer scaffolding and self-regulation align with sociocultural and socio-cognitive frameworks; longitudinal case study design supports the primary methodology choice.

ijCSCL_10_2_4.title: An integrated way of using a tangible user interface in a classroom
ijCSCL_10_2_4.authors: Jessica Dehler-Zufferey & Giulia Ortoleva & Pierre Dillenbourg
ijCSCL_10_2_4.summary_haiku: Researchers designed a classroom activity using TapaCarp, a tangible user interface, to teach carpenter apprentices spatial skills while bridging school and workplace learning. The mixed-methods study with 40 apprentices across three classes showed high usability and strong engagement, with improved artifact quality from day one to day two. However, standardized tests revealed no significant learning gains compared to controls, though plausible objects proved more effective than non-plausible ones for complex tasks.
ijCSCL_10_2_4.evidence_span: methods (mixed-methods design, 40 apprentices, three classes), findings (usability, engagement, artifact quality, standardized tests)
ijCSCL_10_2_4.coding_notes: Study combines quantitative metrics (usability, standardized tests, artifact quality ratings) with qualitative engagement observations across a classroom cohort. TapaCarp is a tangible interface supporting spatial skill learning in an apprenticeship context; sociocultural framing emphasizes bridging school and workplace communities.

ijCSCL_7_1_2.title: How gamers manage aggression: Situating skills in collaborative computer games
ijCSCL_7_1_2.authors: Ulrika Bennerstedt & Jonas Ivarsson & Jonas Linderoth
ijCSCL_7_1_2.summary_haiku: Using ethnomethodological analysis of boss encounters in a massively multiplayer online game, this study examines skills gamers develop during collaborative gameplay involving portrayed aggression. The researchers found that "aggression" and "collaboration" manifest as highly specialized, game-specific practices—particularly aggro management—rather than transferable general skills. The analysis challenges assumptions underlying both positive and negative gaming effects research, arguing that claims about behavioral transfer require explicit theoretical justification and risk oversimplification.
ijCSCL_7_1_2.evidence_span: methods (ethnomethodological analysis of boss encounters) + findings (aggro management as specialized practice)
ijCSCL_7_1_2.coding_notes: Study uses fine-grained interaction analysis of collaborative gameplay episodes (boss encounters in MMO), grounded in ethnomethodological approach. Primary unit is small groups managing coordinated aggression; secondary focus on game-specific discourse/practices as artifacts. Pedagogy reflects implicit collaboration scripts (role-based aggro management) and peer regulation within gameplay.

ijCSCL_6_3_5.title: Are two heads always better than one? Differential effects of collaboration on students’ computer-supported learning in mathematics
ijCSCL_6_3_5.authors: Dejana Mullins & Nikol Rummel & Hans Spada
ijCSCL_6_3_5.summary_haiku: Collaboration's effectiveness in mathematics learning depends on instructional material type. This experimental study compared individual versus collaborative learning with conceptual and procedural algebra instruction in a computer-supported environment. Results showed collaboration enhanced conceptual knowledge acquisition through mutual elaboration, but hindered procedural skill development due to task distribution and reduced practice opportunities.
ijCSCL_6_3_5.evidence_span: methods (experimental design comparing individual vs. collaborative conditions) + findings (differential effects on conceptual vs. procedural knowledge)
ijCSCL_6_3_5.coding_notes: Study uses controlled comparison of collaboration vs. individual conditions with inferential testing of learning outcomes. Primary focus is dyadic collaboration in computer-supported algebra learning, with secondary attention to individual learner outcomes. Socio-cognitive theory (collaborative conflict and explanation) combined with sociocultural framing of computer-mediated interaction.

ijCSCL_6_3_4.title: Scaffolding collaborative technical writing with procedural facilitation and synchronous discussion
ijCSCL_6_3_4.authors: Shiou-Wen Yeh & Jia-Jiunn Lo & Jeng-Jia Huang
ijCSCL_6_3_4.summary_haiku: Researchers developed Process-Writing Wizard, a computer-supported system combining procedural scaffolding and synchronous chat to facilitate collaborative technical writing among EFL students. An experimental study with 48 students compared the system against standard chat. Results showed experimental group students demonstrated significantly higher perceived usefulness, positive attitudes, and stronger intention to reuse the system. Their articles exhibited superior content and organization quality, and synchronous discussions focused more on article-related interactions rather than social exchanges.
ijCSCL_6_3_4.evidence_span: methods (experimental design, 48 students, two conditions) + findings (perceived usefulness, article quality, chat interaction patterns)
ijCSCL_6_3_4.coding_notes: Study employs a controlled comparison of two conditions (Process-Writing Wizard vs. standard chat), making it experimental. Procedural scaffolding and synchronous discussion are core technologies. Content analysis of articles and chat interactions supports the secondary methodology and unit-of-analysis coding.

ijCSCL_7_1_3.title: The multivoicedness of game play: Exploring the unfolding of a student’s learning trajectory in a gaming context at school
ijCSCL_7_1_3.summary_haiku: This qualitative case study examines how classroom interactions facilitate a student's learning trajectory while playing the educational game Global Conflicts: Palestine. Using sociocultural and dialogic analysis of video-recorded gameplay and discussions, the research demonstrates that computer games become learning resources through collaborative meaning-making. The teacher's role in orchestrating dialogic spaces where multiple perspectives "inter-animate" each other proved crucial for developing nuanced understanding of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict's complexity.
ijCSCL_7_1_3.evidence_span: methods (video-recorded gameplay and discussions, qualitative case study) + findings (learning trajectory, dialogic meaning-making)
ijCSCL_7_1_3.coding_notes: The study employs fine-grained interaction and discourse analysis of video-recorded classroom episodes to trace one student's learning trajectory. While the game is the artifact under study, the primary analytical focus is on the moment-by-moment unfolding of collaborative dialogue and teacher orchestration, characteristic of interaction analysis. Dialogic theory (Bakhtin's multi-voicedness) and sociocultural theory (Vygotsky) are explicitly foregrounded.

ijCSCL_5_2_4.title: Distributed leadership in online groups
ijCSCL_5_2_4.summary_haiku: In an asynchronous online learning environment, pre-service teachers working in small groups demonstrated highly distributed leadership across all members, with different leadership forms showing varying distribution patterns. While successful group performance was not directly predicted by overall leadership distribution patterns, qualitative analysis revealed that effective groups developed internal organizational structures and positive interpersonal dynamics that facilitated both peer and instructor engagement, suggesting emergent distributed leadership offers a viable alternative to scripted collaborative roles.
ijCSCL_5_2_4.evidence_span: title, abstract, and summary indicating qualitative analysis of group interaction patterns and leadership distribution
ijCSCL_5_2_4.coding_notes: The study examines how leadership emerges and distributes across small group members in asynchronous online settings through qualitative analysis of group dynamics and discourse. Distributed cognition is the primary theoretical lens because leadership and decision-making are treated as emergent properties distributed across group members rather than localized in individuals. Self-peer regulation is primary pedagogy because groups self-organize their internal structures and roles without scripted assignment, though collaboration scripts are secondary as a point of contrast.

ijCSCL_6_1_6.title: Perspective taking and synchronous argumentation for learning the day/night cycle
ijCSCL_6_1_6.authors: Baruch B. Schwarz & Yaron Schur & Haim Pensso & Naama Tayer
ijCSCL_6_1_6.summary_haiku: Combining perspective-taking through pictures and synchronous computer-supported argumentation promotes conceptual learning of the day/night cycle in Grade 8 students. Using the Digalo tool and design-research methodology with pre-post testing, the study found significant improvements in mental models, elaboration, and knowledge integration. However, teacher mediation during small-group discussions did not enhance learning outcomes, suggesting that meticulous task design and peer argumentation were primary drivers of conceptual change.
ijCSCL_6_1_6.evidence_span: methods (design-research, pre-post testing, Digalo tool, small-group discussions) + findings (significant improvements in mental models, elaboration, knowledge integration; teacher mediation effect)
ijCSCL_6_1_6.coding_notes: Study employs design-based research with experimental comparison (pre-post testing) of a synchronous argumentation intervention using Digalo. Primary focus is peer argumentation and perspective-taking in small groups; socio-cognitive theory aligns with collaborative conflict driving conceptual change, while dialogic theory captures the multi-voiced argumentation process.

ijCSCL_7_3_1.title: Learning physics through play in an augmented reality environment
ijCSCL_7_3_1.authors: Noel Enyedy & Joshua A. Danish & Girlie Delacruz & Melissa Kumar
ijCSCL_7_3_1.summary_haiku: # Summary This study demonstrates that first and second graders (n=43) can meaningfully learn Newtonian physics through augmented reality activities combining embodied play and progressive symbolization. Using pre-post assessments, students showed significant gains in understanding force, net force, friction, and two-dimensional motion. Two design principles guided the curriculum: participatory modeling leveraging socio-dramatic play to make intuitions visible, and progressive symbolization enabling students to invent and refine representational systems. Case studies illustrate how embodied prediction and collaborative symbol refinement supported conceptual integration, though challenges emerged when students relied exclusively on embodiment or formal reasoning.
ijCSCL_7_3_1.evidence_span: methods (pre-post design, n=43), findings (significant gains, case studies of embodied play and symbol refinement)
ijCSCL_7_3_1.coding_notes: Study uses pre-post assessment with a cohort of first/second graders in an AR environment, supporting experimental_quasi_experimental classification. Participatory modeling and progressive symbolization align with sociocultural and distributed cognition frameworks. Embodied play in AR is the primary technology; no AI/LLM involvement detected.

ijCSCL_4_2_1.title: The joint organization of interaction within a multimodal CSCL medium
ijCSCL_4_2_1.summary_haiku: This ethnomethodological case study examines how three students organize collaborative mathematical problem-solving in a synchronous dual-interaction online environment combining text chat and shared whiteboard. Through sequential interaction analysis, the authors reveal that students co-construct shared mathematical understanding by coordinating visual, narrative, and symbolic representations across media. The indexical field formed by referential links between chat messages and whiteboard drawings establishes common ground, enabling group cognition and deep mathematical learning through multiple realizations of mathematical objects.
ijCSCL_4_2_1.coding_notes: Ethnomethodological case study with sequential interaction analysis of moment-by-moment collaborative episodes in a multimodal synchronous environment. The focus on indexical fields, referential links, and co-construction of shared understanding across chat and whiteboard aligns with sociocultural and distributed cognition theories. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

ijCSCL_10_4_3.title: ReaderBench: Automated evaluation of collaboration based on cohesion and dialogism
ijCSCL_10_4_3.authors: Mihai Dascalu & Stefan Trausan-Matu & Danielle S. McNamara & Philippe Dessus
ijCSCL_10_4_3.summary_haiku: ReaderBench proposes two computational models for automated collaboration assessment in CSCL conversations. The dialogical voice inter-animation model evaluates collaboration through overlapping semantic chains representing different participants' viewpoints, while the social knowledge-building model analyzes longitudinal cohesion patterns. Validation against human annotations of ten chat conversations demonstrates both models reliably identify collaboration zones and predict overall collaboration quality, supporting cohesion and voice inter-animation as collaboration signatures.
ijCSCL_10_4_3.coding_notes: ReaderBench is a computational system using NLP and semantic chain analysis to automatically assess collaboration in chat conversations. The dialogical voice inter-animation model directly operationalizes dialogic theory (Bakhtin), while cohesion analysis reflects knowledge-building principles. AI involvement is non-LLM (semantic networks, cohesion metrics) but includes automated analysis of discourse traces.

ijCSCL_5_4_2.title: Sharing and cultivating tacit knowledge in an online learning environment
ijCSCL_5_4_2.summary_haiku: Online graduate business students cultivated tacit knowledge through a strategic management course using naturalistic inquiry methodology. The course combined readings, threaded discussions, and a simulation game, creating a "ba" (shared context) that encouraged socialization, externalization, combination, and internalization processes aligned with Nonaka's knowledge creation model. Students reported learning tacit dimensions impossible to acquire from textbooks alone.
ijCSCL_5_4_2.evidence_span: methods (naturalistic inquiry, course design) + findings (tacit knowledge cultivation, SECI processes)
ijCSCL_5_4_2.coding_notes: Naturalistic inquiry with in-depth study of a bounded online course context suggests ethnographic case study; explicit use of Nonaka's knowledge creation model (SECI) and 'ba' concept anchors knowledge_building_theory as primary. Threaded discussions and simulation game indicate asynchronous forum + shared workspace; cohort-level analysis of tacit knowledge cultivation is primary unit, though individual learning outcomes are also examined.

ijCSCL_4_4_3.title: Contrasting the use of tools for presentation and critique: Some cases from architectural education
ijCSCL_4_4_3.authors: Gustav Lymer & Jonas Ivarsson & Oskar Lindwall
ijCSCL_4_4_3.summary_haiku: This ethnomethodological video analysis of architectural design reviews examines how presentation technologies shape critique practices. Comparing poster-based, digital slideshow, and hybrid setups across 143 sessions, the study reveals that digital technologies fundamentally transform sequential organization, shared attention, and part-whole relations during discussion and assessment. The findings suggest that presentation tools designed primarily for delivery may inadequately support subsequent critique, highlighting the need for spatially organized interfaces better suited to collaborative design review practices.
ijCSCL_4_4_3.evidence_span: methods (ethnomethodological video analysis, 143 sessions), findings (sequential organization, shared attention, part-whole relations)
ijCSCL_4_4_3.coding_notes: Study employs fine-grained video analysis of design review interactions, examining how presentation tools (posters, slides, hybrid) shape collaborative critique practices. Primary focus is on moment-by-moment discourse and artifact use rather than learning outcomes, fitting interaction_analysis; secondary methods include ethnographic observation and systematic coding of presentation modalities.

ijCSCL_4_2_5.title: A knowledge-practice perspective on technology-mediated learning
ijCSCL_4_2_5.doi: A knowledge-practice perspective on technology-mediated learning
ijCSCL_4_2_5.summary_haiku: Technology enhances learning through transformed social practices, not merely through tool implementation. While knowledge-building theory emphasizes idea advancement, this perspective argues that genuine educational transformation requires cultivating epistemic practices—socially embedded ways of working with knowledge—that channel intellectual efforts toward collective knowledge advancement. Material artifacts and social practices constitute dialectical unity in knowledge creation.
ijCSCL_4_2_5.coding_notes: Hakkarainen's 2009 work is a theoretical perspective piece emphasizing epistemic practices and knowledge-building communities. Methodology is inferred as ethnographic/case-study oriented given focus on socially embedded practices; technology is inferred as knowledge-base/wiki-like given knowledge-building emphasis, though the article may be primarily conceptual rather than empirical.

ijCSCL_7_3_5.title: 4SPPIces: A case study of factors in a scripted collaborative-learning blended course across spatial locations
ijCSCL_7_3_5.authors: Mar Perez-Sanagustin & Patricia Santos & Davinia Hernandez-Leo & Josep Blat
ijCSCL_7_3_5.summary_haiku: This case study evaluates the 4SPPIces model—a conceptual framework combining Space, Pedagogical Method, Participants, and History factors—for designing computer-supported collaborative blended learning scripts. Researchers implemented a geography fieldwork activity with 34 students across Barcelona using mobile devices and GPS. Results demonstrate that considering 4SPPIces factors successfully enhanced the activity, promoting collaborative skills, motivation, and learning about multiple urban districts while effectively supporting teacher orchestration through integrated technologies.
ijCSCL_7_3_5.coding_notes: The 4SPPIces model is a design framework iteratively applied to a blended geography fieldwork activity; mobile GPS and integrated technologies support orchestration. Case study of 34 students across spatial locations with scripted collaboration suggests design-based research with classroom cohort as primary unit, though small-group dynamics are also examined.

ijCSCL_6_1_2.title: Temporality matters: Advancing a method for analyzing problem-solving processes in a computer-supported collaborative environment
ijCSCL_6_1_2.summary_haiku: This study advances Lag-sequential Analysis (LsA) as a quantitative method for examining temporal patterns in computer-supported collaborative learning groups. Applied to synchronous online problem-solving discussions, LsA revealed significant sequential interaction patterns invisible to traditional "coding and counting" approaches. Critically, temporal transition patterns between process categories emerged as the strongest predictor of group performance, demonstrating that analyzing the order and sequence of collaborative interactions—not merely their frequency—is essential for understanding collaborative learning processes.
ijCSCL_6_1_2.coding_notes: Lag-sequential Analysis is a temporal pattern-extraction method that examines sequential transitions in coded interaction data. The study emphasizes temporal ordering and sequence over frequency counts, making sequence_process_mining the primary methodology. Interaction_analysis is secondary because the underlying data are coded collaborative episodes. Sociocultural theory is primary given the focus on collaborative problem-solving processes in a mediated environment.

ijCSCL_5_2_0.title: A prism of CSCL research
ijCSCL_5_2_0.summary_haiku: Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning integrates diverse disciplines, technologies, and methodologies to study collaborative learning with digital tools. This issue presents five empirical studies examining different CSCL applications—from complex system simulations to scripted collaboration platforms—using varied analytical approaches including classroom assessments, discourse analysis, and quantitative-qualitative combinations. The research demonstrates that effective CSCL design requires attention to pedagogical aims and collaborative processes rather than relying on single technological solutions.
ijCSCL_5_2_0.evidence_span: abstract and summary describing five empirical studies with varied methodologies and CSCL applications
ijCSCL_5_2_0.coding_notes: This is a special issue overview rather than a single empirical study, so coding reflects the diversity of approaches described. Mixed methods is primary because the summary explicitly mentions 'quantitative-qualitative combinations.' Collaboration scripts and shared workspaces are inferred from mention of 'scripted collaboration platforms' and 'complex system simulations.' Confidence is moderate due to limited methodological detail in the abstract.

ijCSCL_7_1_7.title: The role of teacher assistance on the effects of a macro-script in collaborative writing tasks
ijCSCL_7_1_7.summary_haiku: This multiple-case study examines how teacher assistance patterns interact with macro-scripts to influence collaborative writing in university students. Analyzing two settings with different script types and teaching approaches, the study identifies distinct teacher assistance patterns and their relationships to group organization and knowledge construction phases. Results show that flexible, content-focused teacher guidance combined with open scripts promotes heterogeneous group strategies and advanced collaborative knowledge construction, while detailed scripts paired with organizational reminders produce homogeneous adherence but lower knowledge construction levels.
ijCSCL_7_1_7.evidence_span: methods (multiple-case study design, analysis of teacher assistance patterns and group interaction) + findings (relationship between script type, teacher guidance, and collaborative knowledge construction phases)
ijCSCL_7_1_7.coding_notes: Study employs micro-analytic examination of collaborative episodes and teacher moves within bounded cases, combined with systematic coding of interaction patterns. Primary focus is on how teacher assistance patterns interact with macro-scripts to shape group-level collaborative processes and knowledge construction.

ijCSCL_6_3_0.title: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich W. Hesse & Nancy Law
ijCSCL_6_3_0.summary_haiku: # Summary The CSCL 2011 conference in Hong Kong demonstrated significant growth in computer-supported collaborative learning research, particularly in Asia-Pacific regions, with over 400 participants from 30+ countries. The conference emphasized connecting CSCL research to educational policy and practice through keynotes, workshops, and post-conference events across Chinese cities, establishing CSCL as a vital research field globally.
ijCSCL_6_3_0.coding_notes: This is a conference overview/editorial piece describing CSCL 2011 growth and scope, not an empirical research study. It does not report a specific methodology, unit of analysis, pedagogy, or technology intervention. No research design, data collection, or findings are present.

ijCSCL_10_2_1.title: The impact of hierarchical positions on communities of learning
ijCSCL_10_2_1.authors: Martin Rehm & Wim Gijselaers & Mien Segers
ijCSCL_10_2_1.summary_haiku: Hierarchical positions significantly influence participants' activity and performance in online Communities of Learning within organizations. Analyzing 249 staff members across 25 CoLs, this empirical study found that higher-ranked employees contributed more frequently and achieved better exam grades. However, cluster analysis revealed a "Stars" group of exceptional performers transcending hierarchical constraints, suggesting that while organizational hierarchy shapes collaborative behavior, individual motivation can overcome these structural barriers.
ijCSCL_10_2_1.evidence_span: methods (249 staff, 25 CoLs, cluster analysis) + findings (hierarchical effects, Stars group)
ijCSCL_10_2_1.coding_notes: Study employs inferential statistics (comparing contribution/performance across hierarchical ranks) and cluster analysis to identify subgroups. Primary unit is the community network (25 CoLs), with secondary focus on individual learners. Grounded in communities of practice theory (organizational learning contexts) and activity theory (hierarchy as structural constraint). Asynchronous forum inferred from 'online Communities of Learning' but not explicitly detailed.

ijCSCL_10_2_0.title: The core features of CSCL: Social situation, collaborative knowledge processes and their design
ijCSCL_10_2_0.authors: Ulrike Cress & Gerry Stahl & Sten Ludvigsen & classroom orchestration. The
ijCSCL_10_2_0.summary_haiku: This editorial examines three core CSCL features: how social situations influence collaboration, the nature of collaborative knowledge processes, and effective design of learning environments. Through analyzing four empirical studies across diverse contexts, the authors identify that social awareness significantly impacts learning outcomes, knowledge creation remains rare despite ideal conditions, and technical tools combined with thoughtful orchestration can enhance collaborative learning, though predicting emergent group cognition remains challenging.
ijCSCL_10_2_0.evidence_span: title, abstract, editorial framing of four empirical studies
ijCSCL_10_2_0.coding_notes: This is an editorial synthesizing multiple empirical studies rather than a single primary research report. The primary methodology is inferred as content_analysis of the four studies' findings; secondary methods reflect the diversity of approaches likely represented in those studies. Social awareness and orchestration suggest collaboration_scripts and teacher_orchestrated_discussion as pedagogical foci. Confidence is moderate due to the editorial nature and lack of detailed methods section.

ijCSCL_6_3_1.title: Student use of Facebook for organizing collaborative classroom activities
ijCSCL_6_3_1.authors: Cliff Lampe & Donghee Yvette Wohn & Jessica Vitak & Nicole B. Ellison & Rick Wash
ijCSCL_6_3_1.summary_haiku: Two survey studies examined how undergraduate students repurpose Facebook for classroom organizing. Study 1 (N=302) found that Facebook intensity and willingness to contact instructors predicted collaboration propensity. Study 2 (N=214) revealed two distinct collaboration types: positive (instructor-approved) and negative (unapproved), with different predictors including self-efficacy and relational communication strategies, suggesting how students use Facebook matters more than frequency.
ijCSCL_6_3_1.evidence_span: methods (two survey studies) + findings (predictors of collaboration types)
ijCSCL_6_3_1.coding_notes: Survey-based studies report frequencies and correlations (e.g., Facebook intensity predicting collaboration propensity), with secondary inferential testing. Facebook repurposing for classroom organizing reflects asynchronous social media use; instructor approval suggests pedagogical structure. Sociocultural framing emphasizes social mediation of learning through peer networks.

ijCSCL_7_1_6.title: Linking teacher beliefs, practices and student inquiry-based learning in a CSCL environment: A tale of two teachers
ijCSCL_7_1_6.summary_haiku: Teachers holding innovation-oriented beliefs about inquiry-based learning enacted mathematics lessons with inquiry principle-based practices and technology-enhanced orchestration, while teachers with teacher-centered beliefs used traditional approaches. Comparative case analysis of two teachers using Group Scribbles technology revealed that innovation-oriented beliefs directly shaped progressive inquiry practices, which subsequently fostered student collaborative knowledge construction and effective technology use.
ijCSCL_7_1_6.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (comparative case analysis of two teachers)
ijCSCL_7_1_6.coding_notes: Comparative case study of two teachers using Group Scribbles (shared whiteboard) examining how teacher beliefs shape inquiry practices and student collaboration. Primary focus is teacher facilitation and orchestration; secondary unit is classroom cohort outcomes. Sociocultural framing of technology-mediated collaborative learning; activity theory relevant to teacher beliefs as mediating artifacts.

ijCSCL_5_2_1.title: Mr. Vetro: A Collective Simulation for teaching health science
ijCSCL_5_2_1.authors: Andri Ioannidou & Alexander Repenning & David Webb & Diane Keyser & Lisa Luhn & Christof Daetwyler
ijCSCL_5_2_1.summary_haiku: Mr. Vetro is a collective simulation where students collaboratively control physiological organs on networked computers to learn about system interactions. Formal evaluation across 400 high school students demonstrated significant learning gains in physiological knowledge and vocabulary, increased inquiry-based teaching practices, and positive real-life health behavior changes, though attitudes toward science remained relatively stable.
ijCSCL_5_2_1.coding_notes: Mr. Vetro is a networked collaborative simulation where students collectively control physiological systems, suggesting shared workspace technology and inquiry-based pedagogy. The formal evaluation across 400 students with learning gains indicates experimental/quasi-experimental design with classroom cohorts as primary unit; individual learning outcomes also measured. No AI/LLM involvement evident in 2010 context.

ijCSCL_6_1_3.title: Learning the physics of electricity: A qualitative analysis of collaborative processes involved in productive failure
ijCSCL_6_1_3.authors: Suneeta A. Pathak & Beaumie Kim & Michael J. Jacobson & Baohui Zhang
ijCSCL_6_1_3.summary_haiku: This qualitative study examines collaborative problem-solving dynamics in physics education using computer-supported learning. Two student dyads—one experiencing productive failure through initial low-structured activities followed by high-structured ones, and another receiving only high-structured activities—solved electricity problems using NetLogo models. Analysis of video, screen captures, and solutions revealed that initial struggle enabled deeper engagement with the model and reflective reasoning, while over-scripted activities hindered meaningful collaboration and conceptual understanding.
ijCSCL_6_1_3.evidence_span: methods (video, screen captures, qualitative analysis) + findings (collaborative dynamics, productive failure effects)
ijCSCL_6_1_3.coding_notes: Study employs micro-analytic coding of moment-by-moment collaborative episodes (interaction_analysis) supplemented by case-study depth and systematic coding of artifacts. NetLogo is a shared computational workspace; the core comparison contrasts low-structure (productive failure) versus high-structure (scripted) conditions, grounded in sociocultural and socio-cognitive theories of learning through struggle and explanation.

ijCSCL_7_3_4.title: Online class size, note reading, note writing and collaborative discourse
ijCSCL_7_3_4.summary_haiku: This mixed-methods study examined 25 online graduate courses (341 students, 25 instructors) using tracking logs and interviews to investigate how class size affects note reading and writing loads. Findings revealed class size positively correlates with total notes read but negatively with percentage read, indicating information overload in larger classes. Students wrote shorter, simpler notes in larger classes. Dividing large classes into subgroups reduced overload. An optimal class size of 13-15 students was identified for effective collaborative discourse.
ijCSCL_7_3_4.evidence_span: methods (tracking logs, interviews) + findings (class size correlations, note characteristics, subgroup effects)
ijCSCL_7_3_4.coding_notes: Study combines quantitative tracking data (descriptive statistics on note volume and reading patterns) with qualitative interviews. Primary unit is classroom cohort (25 courses analyzed), though individual learner outcomes are also examined. Asynchronous forum is the primary technology (online class notes). Sociocultural framing emphasizes collaborative discourse; information processing captures cognitive load concerns about overload in larger classes.

ijCSCL_4_2_4.title: Exploring metaskills of knowledge-creating inquiry in higher education
ijCSCL_4_2_4.summary_haiku: This study investigates metaskills required for knowledge-creating inquiry in higher education through an 11-week undergraduate psychology course using progressive inquiry and web-based collaboration. Qualitative analysis of database discourse and student self-reflections revealed three student groups exhibited varying engagement levels in collaborative object-oriented inquiry. Group C demonstrated superior skills in monitoring individual, collective, and object-oriented aspects of inquiry, while Groups A and B struggled with shared knowledge advancement. Findings suggest metaskills for collaborative knowledge creation develop through sustained socialization into inquiry practices emphasizing iterative development of shared epistemic objects.
ijCSCL_4_2_4.evidence_span: methods (qualitative analysis of database discourse and self-reflections) + findings (three student groups, metaskills development)
ijCSCL_4_2_4.coding_notes: Study employs systematic coding of discourse and reflections across student groups in a progressive inquiry setting, aligned with knowledge-building pedagogy. Web-based collaboration platform (likely Knowledge Forum or similar wiki-based tool) supports asynchronous knowledge construction. Confidence slightly reduced due to limited methodological detail in excerpt, but core approach is clearly qualitative content/discourse analysis of collaborative artifacts.

ijCSCL_4_4_2.title: Earth science learning in SMALLab: A design experiment for mixed reality
ijCSCL_4_4_2.summary_haiku: This design experiment examined how mixed-reality environments support collaborative earth science learning. Researchers implemented SMALLab, a semi-immersive platform enabling colocated students to interact face-to-face within computationally mediated spaces. A 3-day intervention with 72 high school students revealed significantly increased student-to-student exchanges compared to traditional instruction and notable achievement gains on concept assessments, suggesting mixed-reality technology's potential for enhancing K-12 collaborative learning when properly designed.
ijCSCL_4_4_2.coding_notes: Design experiment with iterative intervention (SMALLab) in naturalistic classroom setting; mixed-reality platform is a tangible/spatial interface supporting colocated face-to-face collaboration. Achievement gains and interaction patterns suggest learning analytics component, though primary framing is design-based research testing the intervention's efficacy.

ijCSCL_10_4_4.title: AMOEBA: Designing for collaboration in computer science classrooms through live learning analytics
ijCSCL_10_4_4.authors: Matthew Berland & Don Davis & Carmen Petrick Smith
ijCSCL_10_4_4.summary_haiku: AMOEBA is a learning analytics tool designed to support teachers in orchestrating real-time collaboration among novice programmers using the IPRO visual programming environment. The study examined how pairing students based on a "surprising similarity" metric—operationalizing Zone of Proximal Development for computer science—affected programming outcomes across eight classes. Results showed that paired students produced programs with greater complexity, depth, and novelty compared to unpaired work, with improvements persisting after pairing ended.
ijCSCL_10_4_4.evidence_span: methods (eight classes, pairing intervention) + findings (program complexity, depth, novelty comparisons)
ijCSCL_10_4_4.coding_notes: AMOEBA is a live learning analytics dashboard that operationalizes ZPD-based pairing to orchestrate real-time collaboration. The study uses a quasi-experimental design comparing paired vs. unpaired conditions across multiple classrooms. Secondary methods include learning analytics (trace data from IPRO environment) and descriptive outcome statistics.

ijCSCL_4_4_0.title: Paradigms of shared knowledge
ijCSCL_4_4_0.summary_haiku: This article identifies four theoretical paradigms for understanding shared knowledge in computer-supported collaborative learning: sharing individual mental representations, sharing an object, sharing a situation, and sharing a community. The authors argue that researchers' implicit or explicit adoption of these paradigms significantly influences educational intervention design and effectiveness, regardless of whether designers consciously recognize their theoretical assumptions about knowledge sharing.
ijCSCL_4_4_0.coding_notes: This is a theoretical/conceptual paper that systematically categorizes and analyzes four paradigms of shared knowledge in CSCL literature. It functions as a meta-analysis of existing research frameworks rather than an empirical study. Content analysis is the primary methodology because the authors examine and classify theoretical positions across the field; sociocultural and distributed cognition are core theoretical lenses. Confidence is moderate because the paper's exact methodological approach (literature review vs. conceptual analysis) is not fully specified in the excerpt.

ijCSCL_6_1_1.title: The Singapore experience: Synergy of national policy, classroom practice and design research
ijCSCL_6_1_1.authors: Chee-Kit Looi & Hyo-Jeong So & Yancy Toh & Wenli Chen
ijCSCL_6_1_1.summary_haiku: Singapore's systemic approach to CSCL integration demonstrates how design research methodology bridges macro-level policy, meso-level school implementation, and micro-level classroom interactions. Through the GroupScribbles project across multiple schools, researchers co-designed collaborative learning activities with teachers, developed design principles for rapid collaborative knowledge improvement, and achieved sustainable adoption. This multi-level alignment of policy, practice, and research provides a model for scaling CSCL innovations while addressing real classroom constraints.
ijCSCL_6_1_1.evidence_span: title, abstract, summary describing design research across policy-practice-classroom levels
ijCSCL_6_1_1.coding_notes: Design-based research is the primary methodology, iteratively refining CSCL interventions (GroupScribbles) across multiple schools. The study explicitly bridges macro (policy), meso (school), and micro (classroom) levels, making cross-level multilevel analysis central. Knowledge building theory and sociocultural framing align with the focus on collaborative knowledge improvement and co-design with teachers.

ijCSCL_5_2_3.title: Scripting a distance-learning university course: Do students benefit from net-based scripted collaboration?
ijCSCL_5_2_3.summary_haiku: This experimental field study examined whether scripted collaboration benefits net-based learning in a semester-long university operating systems course. Forty-two student groups performed brainstorming, clustering, and essay-writing tasks either with system-enforced scripts or non-scripted instructions. Results showed no general advantage of scripting for knowledge acquisition or task performance. However, principal component analysis revealed scripting slightly improved essay coherence and comprehensibility, suggesting benefits for complex tasks requiring deeper understanding.
ijCSCL_5_2_3.coding_notes: Clear experimental design comparing scripted vs. non-scripted conditions across 42 groups in a distance-learning setting. Principal component analysis used to assess essay quality; scripting is the core pedagogical intervention. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

ijCSCL_6_3_3.title: Agent-based dynamic support for learning from collaborative brainstorming in scientific inquiry
ijCSCL_6_3_3.authors: Hao-Chuan Wang & Carolyn P. Rose & Chun-Yen Chang
ijCSCL_6_3_3.summary_haiku: This study examines learning during collaborative brainstorming through two controlled experiments manipulating individual versus pair work and system support. Results reveal that while pair brainstorming produces process losses in idea generation, it enhances multi-perspective learning. The VIBRANT agent's automatic feedback improves connection-based learning. An enhanced version in study two shows promise for mitigating productivity losses associated with collaborative work.
ijCSCL_6_3_3.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (two controlled experiments), findings (pair vs. individual, VIBRANT agent feedback effects)
ijCSCL_6_3_3.coding_notes: Study uses controlled experiments comparing individual and pair brainstorming with/without agent support (VIBRANT), measuring learning outcomes and idea generation. Agent provides automatic feedback to scaffold connection-based learning. AI involvement coded as non-LLM (rule-based agent) with secondary feedback component; LLM classification uncertain but agent appears to use heuristic rules rather than neural language models typical of 2011.

ijCSCL_7_1_4.title: Personal and shared experiences as resources for meaning making in a philosophy of science course
ijCSCL_7_1_4.summary_haiku: Health education students in an online philosophy of science course used personal work experiences and peer contributions as meaning-making resources. Analysis of individual writings and discussions revealed three epistemic activities: applying theoretical concepts to practice, forming conceptions, and critiquing. Peer interactions involved elaboration and sharing discourse. Results demonstrate that connecting abstract philosophical knowledge to lived experience enhanced understanding while fostering boundary crossing between institutional and personal knowledge contexts.
ijCSCL_7_1_4.evidence_span: methods and findings sections describing coding of writings and discussions
ijCSCL_7_1_4.coding_notes: Study systematically codes individual writings and peer discussion posts to identify epistemic activities and discourse patterns. Primary unit is the artifact (written contributions and discussion threads) analyzed for meaning-making resources; secondary unit is peer interactions within dyadic/small-group exchanges. Sociocultural framing emphasizes lived experience and boundary crossing between contexts.

ijCSCL_10_2_2.title: Peer interaction and social network analysis of online communities with the support of awareness of different contexts
ijCSCL_10_2_2.authors: Jian-Wei Lin & Li-Jung Mai & Yung-Cheng Lai
ijCSCL_10_2_2.summary_haiku: This study directly compares social-context awareness (SA) and knowledge-context awareness (KA) in online learning communities using identical experimental settings. Through a semester-long investigation with repeated measurements, researchers found that SA stimulated significantly more quantitative peer interaction than KA, particularly in later stages. However, both approaches had limited capacity to enhance message quality. Despite similar midterm performance, the SA community demonstrated significantly better learning outcomes on the final posttest, likely attributed to more extensive peer interaction patterns.
ijCSCL_10_2_2.evidence_span: methods (experimental design, repeated measurements), findings (peer interaction patterns, learning outcomes)
ijCSCL_10_2_2.coding_notes: Study employs a controlled comparison of two awareness conditions (SA vs. KA) in online communities with semester-long repeated measurements, fitting experimental design. Social network analysis is secondary because peer interaction patterns are explicitly analyzed. Awareness dashboards are the primary technology manipulated to support context-aware collaboration in asynchronous forums.

ijCSCL_10_2_3.title: Fixed group and opportunistic collaboration in a CSCL environment
ijCSCL_10_2_3.authors: Tuya Siqin & Jan van Aalst & Samuel Kai Wah Chu
ijCSCL_10_2_3.summary_haiku: This study examined 27 Chinese undergraduates' synchronous online discourse across two phases: fixed group collaboration (8 weeks) and opportunistic collaboration (8 weeks) using Knowledge Forum. Multi-faceted analysis revealed that while all groups showed similar interaction patterns, productive groups generated higher-level questions and ideas. Opportunistic collaboration enabled broader interactions and more constructive discourse but exhibited scattered interactions and reduced metacognition. Active participation and high-level idea contributions correlated positively with domain knowledge gains.
ijCSCL_10_2_3.evidence_span: methods (multi-faceted analysis of discourse), findings (interaction patterns, question quality, metacognition, knowledge gains)
ijCSCL_10_2_3.coding_notes: Study uses Knowledge Forum (wiki-based knowledge building tool) and examines synchronous discourse across two collaboration structures. Multi-faceted analysis of discourse combined with learning outcome measurement (domain knowledge gains) aligns with interaction analysis and knowledge building theory. Primary unit is small groups; secondary is the discourse traces themselves.

ijCSCL_7_1_5.title: Collaboration amidst disagreement and moral judgment: The dynamics of Jewish and Arab students’ collaborative inquiry of their joint past
ijCSCL_7_1_5.summary_haiku: Israeli Jewish and Arab students collaboratively investigated a historical event through computer-supported learning, analyzing conflicting narratives via wiki-based discussion. Despite persistent disagreement, students' post-activity individual answers demonstrated enriched historical understanding, incorporating multiple perspectives and reduced one-sidedness. The researchers propose "fission"—moments when opposing voices create cracks in individual perspectives, fostering polyphonic thinking without requiring consensus.
ijCSCL_7_1_5.evidence_span: methods, findings, discussion of fission and polyphonic thinking
ijCSCL_7_1_5.coding_notes: Study centers on micro-analytic examination of collaborative wiki-based discourse between Jewish and Arab students investigating conflicting historical narratives. The concept of 'fission' and polyphonic thinking reflects dialogic theory (Bakhtin). Individual post-activity outcomes analyzed alongside group interaction, justifying secondary unit as individual learner.

ijCSCL_6_3_2.title: Identity presence and knowledge building: Joint emergence in online learning environments?
ijCSCL_6_3_2.authors: Fengfeng Ke & Alicia F. Chavez & Pei-Ni L. Causarano & Antonio Causarano
ijCSCL_6_3_2.summary_haiku: This mixed-method study examined identity presence in seven online courses and its relationship to knowledge building. Using discourse analysis of 1,817 discussion posts, researchers found that posts expressing personal experiences, cultural perspectives, and age-related views elicited significantly more responses and correlated with knowledge-sharing interactions. However, identity presence did not significantly predict higher-level collaborative knowledge construction, suggesting online learners prioritize self-expression over negotiating shared understanding.
ijCSCL_6_3_2.evidence_span: methods (discourse analysis of 1,817 posts across seven courses) + findings (correlation of identity presence with knowledge-sharing; non-significance for collaborative knowledge construction)
ijCSCL_6_3_2.coding_notes: Study explicitly uses discourse analysis of discussion posts as primary method, combined with quantitative correlation analysis, making it mixed-methods. Primary unit is the post/artifact and course cohort. Knowledge building theory frames the inquiry into whether identity presence supports collective knowledge advancement.

ijCSCL_5_2_2.title: Animation and grammar in science education: Learners’ construal of animated educational software
ijCSCL_5_2_2.summary_haiku: This case study examines how two upper-secondary students collaboratively interpret animated biochemical processes through written reports. Using interaction analysis of video-recorded sessions, the research reveals that students' grammatically constructed narratives prioritize perceptually salient animated features as active subjects, deriving noun phrases from animation and educational text while substituting verbs with everyday language. Without sufficient subject-matter knowledge, students cannot evaluate adequacy and rely solely on grammatical correctness, resulting in non-scientific explanations. The findings emphasize that technology-supported science education requires consideration of both cultural and semiotic processes.
ijCSCL_5_2_2.evidence_span: methods (interaction analysis of video-recorded sessions) + findings (grammatical construction patterns, noun/verb substitution)
ijCSCL_5_2_2.coding_notes: The study employs micro-analytic interaction analysis of collaborative interpretation episodes, with secondary content analysis of written reports and grammatical structures. While animation software is present, the focus is on how students interpret it through language rather than on the technology itself; the primary analytical lens is semiotic and linguistic construction of meaning in dialogue.

ijCSCL_6_1_0.title: CSCL in Asia
ijCSCL_6_1_0.summary_haiku: Asian countries are achieving superior educational outcomes through forward-looking policies emphasizing collaborative knowledge building and twenty-first-century skills rather than rote learning. This editorial examines CSCL research and implementation across Asia, highlighting Singapore's multi-level reform approach integrating micro, meso, and macro educational scales, and presenting empirical studies on productive failure, peer review, and inquiry-based learning from Asian contexts.
ijCSCL_6_1_0.coding_notes: This is an editorial overview rather than a primary empirical study. It surveys CSCL research across Asia and emphasizes policy-level reform (micro, meso, macro scales) alongside pedagogical approaches (knowledge building, peer review, inquiry). Methodology is primarily descriptive/synthetic; no specific experimental design is detailed in the excerpt. Confidence is moderate due to the editorial nature and lack of detailed methodological specificity in the summary.

ijCSCL_4_4_1.title: Wikis to support the “collaborative” part of collaborative learning
ijCSCL_4_4_1.summary_haiku: Wikis provide an effective platform for supporting asynchronous, non-collocated collaborative learning when enhanced with awareness, navigation, and communication components. Two case studies demonstrate that prefabricated wiki structures function as coordinating representations, enabling both tightly coupled team design projects and loosely coupled co-blogging activities to maintain adequate intersubjective spaces for productive student collaboration.
ijCSCL_4_4_1.evidence_span: title, abstract, case study design description
ijCSCL_4_4_1.coding_notes: The study uses two bounded case studies of wiki-supported collaborative learning; methodology is qualitative but not explicitly ethnographic. Prefabricated wiki structures function as collaboration scripts; awareness and navigation components support orchestration. No AI/LLM involvement evident.

ijCSCL_5_4_4.title: The collaborative construction of chronotopes during computer-supported collaborative professional tasks
