ijCSCL_2_2_5.evidence_span: methods (multilevel analysis, role assignment design) + findings (knowledge construction, exam performance by role)
ijCSCL_2_2_5.coding_notes: Design-based research comparing two cohorts with role-scripting intervention; multilevel analysis explicitly used to account for nested discussion data within groups and individuals; asynchronous forum is the primary technology; collaboration scripts (role assignment) is the core pedagogical mechanism.

ijCSCL_2_4_3.title: Facilitating argumentative knowledge construction with computer-supported collaboration scripts
ijCSCL_2_4_3.authors: Karsten Stegmann & Armin Weinberger & Frank Fischer
ijCSCL_2_4_3.summary_haiku: Computer-supported collaboration scripts significantly improve argumentative knowledge construction in online discussions. A 2×2 factorial study with 120 educational science students examined scripts supporting single argument construction and argumentation sequences. Results showed scripts substantially enhanced formal argument quality and argumentation sequence quality. Scripts also facilitated knowledge on argumentation but not domain-specific knowledge, suggesting learners focused effort on argumentation skills rather than content mastery.
ijCSCL_2_4_3.evidence_span: methods (2×2 factorial design, 120 students) + findings (argument quality, argumentation sequence quality, knowledge outcomes)
ijCSCL_2_4_3.coding_notes: Classic CSCL experimental study of collaboration scripts in online discussion. Primary focus is controlled comparison of script conditions affecting argumentative discourse quality and learning outcomes. Content analysis of arguments and sequences is secondary to the experimental design.

ijCSCL_9_3_3.title: An examination of CSCL methodological practices and the influence of theoretical frameworks 2005–2009
ijCSCL_9_3_3.authors: Heisawn Jeong & Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver & Yawen Yu
ijCSCL_9_3_3.summary_haiku: This content analysis examined methodological practices in 400 empirical CSCL studies published 2005–2009 across seven leading journals. Researchers coded studies across research designs, settings, data sources, and analysis methods, then examined relationships with theoretical frameworks. Findings revealed descriptive designs dominated (54%), classroom settings predominated (74%), and quantitative analysis was most common (86%), though qualitative and mixed methods were frequent. Cluster analysis identified four distinctive method-theory combinations, demonstrating that theoretical frameworks significantly influenced methodological choices across all dimensions.
ijCSCL_9_3_3.coding_notes: This is a meta-analytic systematic review of 400 CSCL studies using structured content analysis with coding schemes applied to research design, settings, data sources, and analysis methods. The primary unit is the published empirical study (artifact/discourse trace) rather than learner outcomes or pedagogical interventions. Pedagogy and theory are examined as variables across the corpus rather than instantiated in a single intervention.

ijCSCL_8_1_4.title: Recalibrating reference within a dual-space interaction environment
ijCSCL_8_1_4.summary_haiku: # Summary Middle school students collaborating in the Virtual Math Teams system develop shared understanding of mathematical problems through sequential recalibration of referential practices. Using ethnomethodological analysis of chat and whiteboard interactions, the study demonstrates how students progressively specify indexical properties of underspecified problems and solutions. Rather than treating representations as static objects, the research reveals how problem-solving emerges from the situated, interactive work of producing and refining references to mathematical concepts across dual-space modalities.
ijCSCL_8_1_4.evidence_span: methods (ethnomethodological analysis of chat and whiteboard) + findings (sequential recalibration of referential practices)
ijCSCL_8_1_4.coding_notes: The study employs fine-grained, moment-by-moment analysis of collaborative episodes in Virtual Math Teams, characteristic of interaction analysis. Ethnomethodological approach and focus on discourse practices (indexicality, reference) support secondary coding in discourse analysis and ethnographic case study. Dialogic theory is primary because the work emphasizes multi-voiced dialogue and progressive uptake in meaning-making; sociocultural and distributed cognition are secondary because the analysis treats cognition as situated and spread across chat, whiteboard, and participants.

ijCSCL_9_1_1.title: The dialectical potential of Cultural Historical Activity Theory for researching sustainable CSCL practices
ijCSCL_9_1_1.summary_haiku: Cultural Historical Activity Theory (CHAT) offers a relational, dialectical framework for understanding sustainable computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) in authentic educational settings. This study proposes an integrated CHAT methodology that moves beyond descriptive triangle models to analyze contradictions and tensions across multiple activity levels. Through a five-stage analytical process applied to undergraduate online collaboration, the research demonstrates how CHAT's dialectical method reveals complex interrelations between discourse, actions, and community, explaining why collaborative practices succeed or fail to become institutionalized.
ijCSCL_9_1_1.evidence_span: abstract, methodology, findings on undergraduate online collaboration
ijCSCL_9_1_1.coding_notes: The study is framed as a methodological proposal using CHAT as an analytical lens applied to undergraduate online collaboration in an authentic educational setting. The five-stage analytical process and focus on contradictions across activity levels align with activity theory methodology. Secondary methodology reflects the discourse and artifact analysis inherent in CHAT analysis. Technology is inferred as asynchronous given 'online collaboration' context, though not explicitly detailed in the excerpt.

ijCSCL_9_1_3.title: Multi-player epistemic games: Guiding the enactment of classroom knowledge-building communities
ijCSCL_9_1_3.summary_haiku: Researchers extended epistemic games—strategic knowledge-building practices—to "multi-player" versions where students collectively advance ideas through distributed contributions in Knowledge Forum. Using design-based research in Singapore primary science classrooms, they developed scaffolding tools (Think Cards and hypothetical game-configurations) to help students learn the Progressive-Improvement Game. Analyses showed students improved significantly in generating valid knowledge-building moves, supporting classroom enactment of knowledge-building communities.
ijCSCL_9_1_3.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (design-based research in classrooms), findings (scaffolding tools, knowledge-building moves analysis)
ijCSCL_9_1_3.coding_notes: Core study exemplifies design-based research iteratively refining epistemic games and scaffolds in naturalistic classroom settings. Knowledge Forum is the primary collaborative technology; Think Cards and game-configurations are collaboration scripts. Analysis of knowledge-building discourse moves in Knowledge Forum posts supports interaction and content coding.

ijCSCL_8_3_4.title: Inducing socio-cognitive conflict in Finnish and German groups of online learners by CSCL script
ijCSCL_8_3_4.authors: Armin Weinberger & Miika Marttunen & Leena Laurinen
ijCSCL_8_3_4.summary_haiku: This cross-cultural study examined how a peer-critique collaboration script affects socio-cognitive conflict in online learning. Using a 2×2 design with 132 Finnish and German university students, researchers analyzed discussion patterns and knowledge acquisition. Results revealed German groups engaged in more conflict-oriented consensus building than Finnish groups, who preferred integration-oriented approaches. The script strengthened conflict-oriented discourse in German groups but proved incompatible with Finnish collaborative norms, suggesting CSCL environments require culturally sensitive design.
ijCSCL_8_3_4.evidence_span: methods (2×2 design, script manipulation), findings (discourse patterns, cultural differences)
ijCSCL_8_3_4.coding_notes: Study uses a controlled 2×2 factorial design comparing script conditions across cultural groups, with systematic coding of discussion discourse and knowledge outcomes. Primary focus is on how collaboration scripts induce socio-cognitive conflict, analyzed through discourse patterns in online groups.

ijCSCL_3_4_4.title: Alternative goal structures for computer game-based learning
ijCSCL_3_4_4.summary_haiku: This field study examined how cooperative, competitive, and individualistic goal structures in classroom computer math games affect fifth-graders' math performance and attitudes. Using a pretest-posttest design with 160 students across four conditions, results showed all gaming groups outperformed controls on math tests, but cooperative goal structures proved most effective for promoting positive math attitudes. Socioeconomic status significantly moderated outcomes, with disadvantaged students benefiting most from cooperation.
ijCSCL_3_4_4.evidence_span: methods (pretest-posttest design, 160 students, four conditions) + findings (math performance, attitudes, SES moderation)
ijCSCL_3_4_4.coding_notes: Study uses a controlled comparison of goal structures (cooperative, competitive, individualistic) in a classroom setting with random or quasi-random assignment. Primary focus is individual learner outcomes (math performance, attitudes), though goal structures operate at the group/classroom level. Technology (computer math games) is the delivery medium but not the analytical focus; the study examines pedagogical structures (goal structures) rather than technology affordances.

ijCSCL_9_3_1.title: The multi-layered nature of small-group learning: Productive interactions in object-oriented collaboration
ijCSCL_9_3_1.summary_haiku: # Summary This study examines productive interactions in small-group collaborative learning through a 20-week undergraduate research project. Using qualitative analysis and descriptive statistics, the researcher analyzed five student groups' interactions and emerging knowledge objects (research reports). Findings reveal that productive interactions manifest in two primary patterns: discourse-based interactions fostering shared understanding, and object-oriented interactions involving iterative co-construction. Groups demonstrating shared epistemic agency—deliberate, joint engagement with knowledge materialization—produced higher-quality knowledge objects, suggesting that productive collaboration integrates discursive interaction with tangible object development over time.
ijCSCL_9_3_1.evidence_span: methods, findings, discussion of interaction patterns and knowledge objects
ijCSCL_9_3_1.coding_notes: Study employs micro-analytic coding of collaborative episodes (interaction_analysis) combined with descriptive statistics and systematic analysis of research reports as artifacts. Primary focus on small groups' discourse and object co-construction aligns with knowledge-building and sociocultural frameworks; distributed cognition and activity theory are secondary given emphasis on shared epistemic agency and iterative materialization.

ijCSCL_2_4_1.title: Using activity-oriented design methods to study collaborative knowledge-building in e-learning courses within higher education
ijCSCL_2_4_1.summary_haiku: Activity-Oriented Design Methods (AODM) operationalize Activity Theory to analyze collaborative knowledge-building in e-learning courses. Using qualitative case study methodology, researchers applied AODM's six-stage framework to examine course design teams and students in online higher education. Findings revealed that peer collaboration, facilitated through small-group assignments and discussion guidelines, supported students' development of statistical knowledge through exploratory talk and iterative refinement of shared learning objects.
ijCSCL_2_4_1.coding_notes: AODM explicitly operationalizes Activity Theory; qualitative case study with six-stage framework suggests systematic but interpretive analysis. Small-group assignments and discussion guidelines indicate collaboration scripts; asynchronous forum inferred from e-learning context. No AI/LLM involvement evident in 2007 publication.

ijCSCL_2_2_7.title: How do argumentation diagrams compare when student pairs use them as a means for debate or as a tool for representing debate?
ijCSCL_2_2_7.authors: Kristine Lund & Gaelle Molinari & Arnauld Sejourne & Michael Baker
ijCSCL_2_2_7.summary_haiku: This study compared two instructional approaches for using argumentation diagrams during online debates among 36 secondary students. Using the ADAM analysis method, researchers examined individual diagrams created before and after debate, plus collaborative diagrams produced during debate. Results revealed that students instructed to represent their chat debate in diagrams added more non-argumentative relations (examples, causes, consequences), while those using diagrams simultaneously during debate expressed more opinions about arguments. These findings suggest different cognitive mechanisms emerge depending on whether diagrams mediate debate or represent completed debate.
ijCSCL_2_2_7.evidence_span: methods (ADAM analysis, diagram coding) + findings (comparison of diagram types and debate expressions)
ijCSCL_2_2_7.coding_notes: Study uses systematic coding of argumentation diagrams (ADAM method) to analyze collaborative artifacts before/after and during debate, comparing two instructional conditions. Primary methodology is interaction_analysis because the focus is on how students use diagrams to mediate debate; secondary includes content_analysis (diagram coding scheme) and experimental_quasi_experimental (two instructional conditions compared). Unit is dyad because pairs collaborate; artifact_discourse_trace is secondary because diagrams and chat are analyzed objects.

ijCSCL_1_1_5.title: R-U-Typing-2-Me? Evolving a chat tool to increase understanding in learning activities
ijCSCL_1_1_5.summary_ollama: This study investigates the problem of Chat Confusion in educational debates, which occurs when multiple participants converse simultaneously, making it difficult to follow the conversation. The researchers developed successive versions of the Mediated Chat tool to address the identified problems, including Co-text Loss, Dynamics Interruption, Message Overload, and Decontextualization. The study found that improvements to the presentation of messages can effectively reduce Chat Confusion by easing the reading and message-ﬁnding process. The integration of the revised mechanisms in Mediated Chat 6.0 is expected to further alleviate Chat Confusion.
ijCSCL_1_1_5.summary_haiku: This research investigates "Chat Confusion"—difficulties following conversations when multiple participants communicate simultaneously in chat tools used for educational debates. Through iterative design-based development, researchers identified six key problems: co-text loss, dynamics interruption, message overload, lack-of-visibility-of-turn-in-progress, reading difficulties, and decontextualization. Successive Mediated Chat versions implemented targeted solutions including message threading, structured conversation techniques, publication queues, interface improvements, and session history. Case studies demonstrated that combining structured dynamics with interface enhancements effectively reduced confusion and improved understanding in online learning activities.
ijCSCL_1_1_5.evidence_span: methods (iterative design cycles), findings (case studies of Mediated Chat versions)
ijCSCL_1_1_5.coding_notes: Design-based research is primary methodology: iterative design and study of Mediated Chat intervention across successive versions. Interaction analysis and content analysis of chat logs support the identification of confusion patterns. Collaboration scripts (structured dynamics, turn sequences) and synchronous chat technology are central to the intervention addressing 'Chat Confusion.'

ijCSCL_3_2_2.title: Supporting controversial CSCL discussions with augmented group awareness tools
ijCSCL_3_2_2.summary_haiku: Augmented group awareness tools that aggregate and visualize learner ratings of discussion contributions can strengthen minority influence in collaborative learning. An experimental study with groups discussing controversial physics topics found that groups using rating-based awareness tools made significantly better decisions and showed higher individual learning than unsupported groups, particularly by shifting majority members toward scientifically correct minority viewpoints through enhanced informational influence.
ijCSCL_3_2_2.coding_notes: Experimental design comparing groups with and without augmented awareness tools (rating visualizations) during controversial discussions. Primary focus on group decision-making and individual learning outcomes; secondary attention to individual learner gains and discourse analysis of minority influence dynamics.

ijCSCL_3_2_3.title: Annotations and the collaborative digital library: Effects of an aligned annotation interface on student argumentation and reading strategies
ijCSCL_3_2_3.summary_haiku: Aligned annotation interfaces—where reader comments appear in text margins—significantly enhance student critical thinking and argumentation. Two complementary studies found that annotations, particularly pairs presenting conflicting viewpoints, prompted students to move beyond passive comprehension toward active evaluation and perspective-taking. Students receiving annotated materials demonstrated reduced reliance on summary strategies and greater engagement with competing positions, suggesting annotations provide valuable scaffolding for developing critical reading and writing practices.
ijCSCL_3_2_3.coding_notes: Study compares annotated vs. non-annotated conditions (experimental design) and analyzes student reading strategies and argumentation quality through artifact analysis. Aligned annotation interface is a shared workspace tool supporting collaborative meaning-making around texts.

ijCSCL_1_1_4.title: Situating CoWeb: a scholarship of application
ijCSCL_1_1_4.summary_ollama: The study examines the effectiveness of CoWeb, a Wiki-based collaborative learning platform, in various academic settings. The researchers conducted four case studies, situating CoWeb in different socio-cultural contexts, including architecture, English composition, STEM classes, and an introductory computer science course. The results show that CoWeb was successful in architecture and English composition, where the culture of the classroom and the discipline were compatible with the medium. However, in STEM classes, students actively resisted collaboration, and the researchers identified three cultural barriers to collaboration: competition and single-answer assignments, the challenge of seeking help, and faculty attitudes and models of collaboration. The researchers concluded that the culture of the classroom and the discipline must be compatible with the medium for computer-supported collaborative learning to be effective.
ijCSCL_1_1_4.summary_haiku: Researchers developed CoWeb, a wiki-based platform for collaborative learning, and deployed it across diverse academic contexts at Georgia Tech. Through design-based research, they found that collaborative learning success depends critically on cultural compatibility: CoWeb succeeded in architecture and composition where collaboration aligned with disciplinary values, but failed in STEM courses due to competitive cultures. By redesigning an introductory computing course around collaborative principles, they overcame these barriers, demonstrating that culture can be intentionally shaped to support technology adoption.
ijCSCL_1_1_4.evidence_span: methods, findings, discussion of deployment across contexts and cultural factors
ijCSCL_1_1_4.coding_notes: Design-based research is primary methodology: iterative design and study of CoWeb intervention across naturalistic academic settings. Cultural compatibility and disciplinary values are analyzed as socio-cultural factors shaping adoption; wiki platform supports knowledge building and collaborative authoring aligned with disciplinary practices.

ijCSCL_2_2_6.title: Using graphical tools in a phased activity for enhancing dialogical skills: An example with Digalo
ijCSCL_2_2_6.authors: Nathalie Muller Mirza & Valerie Tartas & Anne-Nelly Perret-Clermont & Jean-Francois de Pietro
ijCSCL_2_2_6.summary_haiku: This study examined how university students developed argumentative and historical knowledge through a phased learning activity using Digalo, graphical argument-mapping software. Using descriptive analysis of two collective debates about the Valladolid Controversy, researchers found that students constructed complex understanding of the historical topic while developing sophisticated argument-counterargument-reply sequences. The software's visual representations and structured functionalities supported both topic meaning-making and argumentative processes, enabling students to elaborate justifications and integrate opposing perspectives into their reasoning.
ijCSCL_2_2_6.evidence_span: methods, findings, discussion of phased activity and argument-mapping analysis
ijCSCL_2_2_6.coding_notes: Study uses micro-analytic coding of collaborative debate episodes (interaction_analysis) combined with systematic examination of argument structures in Digalo traces (content_analysis). Primary unit is small-group collective debates; secondary is the graphical artifacts themselves. Dialogic theory is central to the focus on argument-counterargument-reply sequences and multi-voiced meaning-making.

ijCSCL_2_4_0.title: CSCL and its flash themes
ijCSCL_2_4_0.summary_haiku: Stahl examines how "flash themes"—coordinated collections of papers on emerging research topics—develop within the CSCL community through collaborative, iterative processes involving workshops, peer review, and journal publication. Using a dialectical metaphor of logs and fire, he argues that scientific ideas emerge not from individual minds but through situated, institutionally-mediated interactions among researchers, editors, and the broader academic community.
ijCSCL_2_4_0.coding_notes: Stahl's meta-analysis of CSCL community knowledge production itself exemplifies sociocultural and dialogic theory; the study examines how scientific ideas emerge through situated institutional interactions rather than individual cognition. Confidence is moderate because the article is primarily a conceptual/theoretical reflection on CSCL research practices rather than an empirical study with explicit methods section.

ijCSCL_9_3_0.title: CSCL artifacts
ijCSCL_9_3_0.authors: G. Stahl & S. Ludvigsen & N. Law & U. Cress
ijCSCL_9_3_0.summary_haiku: Artifacts are central to computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL), serving multiple roles including communication media, knowledge representation structures, and collaborative products. This editorial examines how artifacts mediate group meaning-making processes and presents four papers analyzing artifact roles in CSCL settings and trends in CSCL research publications, advancing understanding of the post-cognitive CSCL paradigm emphasizing group-level processes over individual learning outcomes.
ijCSCL_9_3_0.coding_notes: This is an editorial/review article examining artifact roles in CSCL rather than a primary empirical study. Coded as content_analysis because the editorial systematically examines how artifacts function across CSCL research. Primary unit is artifact_discourse_trace since artifacts and their mediating role in meaning-making are the focal analytical objects. Theory emphasizes sociocultural mediation and distributed cognition aligned with post-cognitive CSCL paradigm.

ijCSCL_3_4_5.title: Automatic coding of dialogue acts in collaboration protocols
ijCSCL_3_4_5.summary_haiku: Researchers developed an automatic coding system to identify dialogue acts (communicative functions) in online collaboration protocols using discourse markers. Testing on 1,000 messages showed 79% agreement with manual coding (Cohen's kappa=0.75). Validity analyses confirmed the system reliably distinguished gender differences in communication patterns and detected experimental intervention effects, supporting its utility for analyzing collaborative learning processes.
ijCSCL_3_4_5.evidence_span: methods + findings (automatic coding system, validation against manual coding, kappa=0.75)
ijCSCL_3_4_5.coding_notes: Study develops an automated NLP-based system to code dialogue acts in online collaboration messages using discourse markers. Primary focus is computational linguistics applied to discourse analysis; secondary methods include systematic content coding and learning analytics validation. Theory grounded in dialogic interaction and sociocultural collaboration.

ijCSCL_8_3_5.title: Dialogical positions as a method of understanding identity trajectories in a collaborative blended university course
ijCSCL_8_3_5.authors: M. Beatrice Ligorio & Fedela Feldia Loperfido & Nadia Sansone
ijCSCL_8_3_5.summary_haiku: # Summary This study proposes a three-step qualitative-quantitative method for tracking identity trajectories in collaborative learning using Bakhtinian concepts of polyphony and chronotopes as dialogical indicators. Applied to online notes from two university students in a blended course, the method reveals unique, context-sensitive identity development patterns, demonstrating how students' positioning shifts across course modules in response to activities and personal circumstances.
ijCSCL_8_3_5.evidence_span: title, summary, methods (Bakhtinian discourse analysis of online notes)
ijCSCL_8_3_5.coding_notes: Study explicitly uses Bakhtinian dialogical concepts (polyphony, chronotopes) to analyze identity trajectories through discourse in online course notes. Combines qualitative-quantitative tracking of positioning shifts, grounded in dialogic theory and discourse-analytic method applied to asynchronous written artifacts from individual learners in a blended collaborative course.

ijCSCL_8_3_1.title: Vocational education approach: New TEL settings—new prospects for teachers’ instructional activities?
ijCSCL_8_3_1.summary_haiku: This design-based research study examined vocational teachers' instructional activities in a 3D game environment using content analysis of 8,188 utterances from four teacher-student groups. Findings revealed teachers employed two distinct approaches: "knowledge-providing" and "joint problem-solving," with different student responses. Teachers asked more contextual questions and engaged in shared problem-solving than students, while students provided more knowledge. The study demonstrates teachers spontaneously develop innovative instructional strategies in technology-enhanced vocational learning settings, shifting from classroom management toward empowering collaborative knowledge construction.
ijCSCL_8_3_1.evidence_span: methods (design-based research, content analysis of 8,188 utterances, four teacher-student groups) + findings (two instructional approaches, teacher vs. student discourse patterns, collaborative knowledge construction)
ijCSCL_8_3_1.coding_notes: Study is explicitly design-based research iteratively examining teacher instructional moves in a 3D game environment. Primary unit is teacher facilitation within small groups; secondary is the dyad/small-group context. Pedagogy centers on teacher-orchestrated dialogue and joint problem-solving. Technology is the 3D game environment (tabletop/immersive interface). Sociocultural and dialogic theories underpin the focus on mediated, multi-voiced collaborative learning.

ijCSCL_3_4_1.title: Leveraging online communities in fostering adaptive schools
ijCSCL_3_4_1.authors: David Hung & Kenneth Y. T. Lim & Der-Thanq Victor Chen & Thiam Seng Koh
ijCSCL_3_4_1.summary_haiku: Online communities function as "para-communities" that should remain distinct from formal schools rather than being integrated into them. Through conceptual analysis, the authors argue that schools and online communities serve fundamentally different goals: schools emphasize intentional learning and efficiency, while online communities prioritize intrinsic motivation and innovation. They propose that adaptive schools leverage external para-communities through internal Communities of Interest, enabling complementary relationships that cultivate social capital and innovation without compromising organizational efficiency.
ijCSCL_3_4_1.evidence_span: abstract, conceptual analysis, discussion of para-communities and adaptive schools
ijCSCL_3_4_1.coding_notes: This is primarily a conceptual/theoretical paper analyzing the relationship between online communities and formal schools rather than an empirical study. Coded as ethnographic_case_study as a proxy for qualitative conceptual analysis; however, the work is better characterized as theoretical argumentation. Community_network reflects the focus on online communities as units; communities_of_practice and distributed_cognition capture the theoretical framing of learning through participation and socially distributed activity.

ijCSCL_9_3_4.title: Contemporary intellectual structure of CSCL research (2006–2013): a co-citation network analysis with an education focus
ijCSCL_9_3_4.authors: Kai-Yu Tang & Chin-Chung Tsai & Tzu-Chiang Lin
ijCSCL_9_3_4.summary_haiku: This study employed document co-citation analysis, exploratory factor analysis, and social network analysis to map the intellectual structure of CSCL research (2006–2013). Analyzing 403 source papers and 5,351 citing articles, researchers identified six research subfields: representation and discourse patterns, factors influencing CSCL, intervention and comparison, critical reasoning, social construction processes, and design and modeling. Results revealed seminal works and core publications, with representation and discourse emerging as the dominant research stream, demonstrating the field's maturity and interconnectedness.
ijCSCL_9_3_4.coding_notes: This is a meta-analytic bibliometric study mapping the intellectual structure of CSCL research itself, not an empirical CSCL intervention study. Co-citation network analysis and exploratory factor analysis are the core methodologies; pedagogy and theory are not applicable as this analyzes the field rather than studying learning. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

ijCSCL_8_1_3.title: Student sensemaking with science diagrams in a computer-based setting
ijCSCL_8_1_3.authors: Anniken Furberg & Anders Kluge & Sten Ludvigsen
ijCSCL_8_1_3.summary_haiku: This study examined how upper secondary students collaboratively made sense of solar panel diagrams in a computer-based learning environment. Using interaction analysis of one student group's expert-group session, researchers found that science diagrams functioned as productive social and cognitive resources, enabling students to slow conceptual reasoning and negotiate scientific meanings. However, students faced significant challenges translating oral accounts into written explanations and coordinating multiple diagram representations. The analysis reveals that students' sensemaking involved not only conceptual understanding but also navigating institutional norms and practices embedded within schooling contexts.
ijCSCL_8_1_3.evidence_span: methods (interaction analysis of one student group) + findings (sensemaking with diagrams, negotiation of meanings)
ijCSCL_8_1_3.coding_notes: The study employs micro-analytic interaction analysis of moment-by-moment collaborative episodes around science diagrams in a computer-based environment. Diagrams and written explanations are treated as artifacts mediating sensemaking, grounded in sociocultural theory emphasizing social and cognitive resources.

ijCSCL_2_4_4.title: The role of floor control and of ontology in argumentative activities with discussion-based tools
ijCSCL_2_4_4.summary_haiku: This study examined how informal argumentative ontologies and floor control in synchronous e-discussions affect knowledge co-elaboration among 54 seventh-grade students using the Digalo tool. Using a 2×2 factorial design, researchers compared conditions with/without ontology and with/without floor control. Results showed that combining informal ontology with floor control produced significantly more relevant claims and arguments while reducing chat-style expressions and non-productive peer references, suggesting these design features facilitate collaborative knowledge construction.
ijCSCL_2_4_4.evidence_span: methods (2×2 factorial design, Digalo tool, floor control, ontology conditions) + findings (claims, arguments, chat-style expressions coded and compared)
ijCSCL_2_4_4.coding_notes: Clear experimental design with two independent variables (ontology and floor control) manipulated across conditions. Content analysis of argumentative moves (claims, arguments, non-productive references) serves as primary outcome measure. Digalo is a synchronous discussion tool; floor control and ontology are collaboration-scripting features that structure the interaction space.

ijCSCL_1_3_2.title: The affordance of anchored discussion for the collaborative processing of academic texts
ijCSCL_1_3_2.authors: J. van der Pol & W. Admiraal & P.R.J. Simons
ijCSCL_1_3_2.summary_haiku: Anchored discussion systems, which integrate texts directly into online forums with message anchoring capabilities, promote more text-focused and constructive collaboration than traditional forum discussion. Comparing these systems with standard discussion boards in a pedagogy course, the study found anchored discussion produced more meaning-oriented discourse, more efficient communication, and fewer social digressions, making it more suitable for collaborative academic text comprehension among undergraduate students.
ijCSCL_1_3_2.evidence_span: title, abstract, summary describing comparison of anchored discussion vs. standard forums
ijCSCL_1_3_2.coding_notes: Study compares two conditions (anchored vs. standard forums) in a pedagogy course, analyzing discourse quality and collaboration patterns. Primary methodology is quasi-experimental comparison; secondary methods include discourse and content analysis of forum messages. Technology focus is asynchronous forum with anchoring as a design affordance.

ijCSCL_2_2_2.title: Supporting collaborative learning and problem-solving in a constraint-based CSCL environment for UML class diagrams
ijCSCL_2_2_2.authors: Nilufar Baghaei & Antonija Mitrovic & Warwick Irwin
ijCSCL_2_2_2.summary_haiku: COLLECT-UML is a constraint-based intelligent tutoring system that teaches UML class diagram design while supporting collaborative learning. Using meta-constraints to model collaboration alongside domain constraints, the system provides feedback on both problem-solving and teamwork. Evaluation studies with 48 students showed significant improvements in UML knowledge and collaboration skills, with experimental group participants acquiring greater declarative knowledge about effective collaboration and demonstrating more balanced, active participation.
ijCSCL_2_2_2.evidence_span: methods (48 students, experimental design) + findings (significant improvements in UML knowledge and collaboration skills, balanced participation)
ijCSCL_2_2_2.coding_notes: COLLECT-UML is a constraint-based ITS using meta-constraints to scaffold both domain problem-solving and collaborative teamwork; the study compares experimental and control groups on learning outcomes and collaboration quality, making it a controlled comparison design. AI involvement is rule-based constraint modeling rather than LLM-based.

ijCSCL_1_1_0.title: ijCSCL—a journal for research in CSCL
ijCSCL_1_1_0.summary_ollama: This article presents the inaugural issue of the International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (ijCSCL), a peer-reviewed journal that aims to serve as a communication vehicle for the CSCL community. The journal's mission is to share seminal innovations and proposals from around the world, contributing to the development of the CSCL field. The first issue features articles that propose new directions for CSCL, including research on the CSCL community, a relational approach to CSCL technologies, student assessment of collaborative inquiry, and the application of wiki technology.
ijCSCL_1_1_0.summary_haiku: The International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (ijCSCL) was established to advance the maturing CSCL field by providing a peer-reviewed publication venue for an increasingly global research community. The journal aims to foster interdisciplinary collaboration, develop CSCL-specific theories and methodologies, and disseminate high-quality research through open-access online platforms alongside traditional publication formats.
ijCSCL_1_1_0.coding_notes: This is an editorial/journal-establishment article, not an empirical research study. It describes the journal's mission and scope rather than reporting methodology, units of analysis, pedagogy, technology, or theory applied to a specific research question or intervention.

ijCSCL_1_1_1.title: The CSCL community in its ﬁrst decade: development, continuity, connectivity
ijCSCL_1_1_1.summary_ollama: This study examines the development, continuity, and connectivity of the Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) community over its first decade (1995-2005). Using a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative analysis of conference proceedings and qualitative study of policies and motives, the researchers investigate the growth of the CSCL community, its international connectivity, and the factors influencing its development. The findings suggest that the community is increasingly international, with a growing number of international co-authorships and citations across different countries. However, the study also reveals a relatively low continuity of participation, with only a small number of people participating continuously in the community. The researchers conclude that the CSCL community is a lively and mature community with a stable ratio of new and recurring members, and recommend maintaining internationality in the program committee and rotating meeting locations to support its further development.
ijCSCL_1_1_1.summary_haiku: The CSCL community's first decade (1995–2005) demonstrates growth and increasing internationalization despite low individual continuity. Using quantitative analysis of conference proceedings, participant lists, and program committees combined with qualitative surveys, researchers found that while 79% of authors contributed to only one conference, international connectivity grew substantially through citations and co-authorships across countries, with conference location rotation and diverse program committee composition supporting this development.
ijCSCL_1_1_1.evidence_span: methods + findings (conference proceedings analysis, participant lists, program committees, surveys)
ijCSCL_1_1_1.coding_notes: This is a meta-analysis of the CSCL research community itself rather than a study of collaborative learning. Methodology relies on quantitative frequencies (79% single-conference authors) and qualitative survey data. Primary focus is community structure, connectivity, and continuity—not pedagogical intervention or learning outcomes.

ijCSCL_2_2_3.title: Dealing with multiple documents on the WWW: The role of metacognition in the formation of documents models
ijCSCL_2_2_3.summary_haiku: This study examined whether metacognitive prompting helps laypersons form documents models—integrated representations of content and sources—when researching medical information online. Using an experimental design with 79 participants assigned to groups receiving evaluation prompts, monitoring prompts, both, or neither, researchers found that monitoring prompts enhanced factual knowledge acquisition, while evaluation prompts improved source knowledge and source attribution in essays, supporting metacognition's importance in multiple-document comprehension.
ijCSCL_2_2_3.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (experimental design with 4 conditions), findings (knowledge and attribution outcomes)
ijCSCL_2_2_3.coding_notes: Experimental design with random assignment to four conditions (evaluation prompts, monitoring prompts, both, neither) examining metacognitive support for document comprehension. Primary focus is individual learner outcomes (factual knowledge, source knowledge, attribution) measured via post-task assessments. Information processing theory dominates (metacognitive monitoring and evaluation as regulatory mechanisms), though sociocultural elements present in collaborative online research context.

ijCSCL_1_3_3.title: Code talk: Student discourse and participation with networked handhelds
ijCSCL_1_3_3.summary_haiku: Networked handheld computers in a middle school mathematics classroom expanded collaborative problem-solving participation beyond traditional discourse. Through interactional analysis of two student groups using the Code Breaker cryptography software, the study found that students demonstrating largest achievement gains gave more instructions and responded less frequently. Importantly, shared mathematical objects across devices enabled non-discursive participation forms, allowing lower-status students to contribute meaningfully despite limited verbal participation.
ijCSCL_1_3_3.evidence_span: methods (interactional analysis of two student groups) + findings (discourse patterns, achievement gains, participation forms)
ijCSCL_1_3_3.coding_notes: Study employs fine-grained interactional analysis of moment-by-moment collaborative episodes with networked handhelds. The focus on how shared mathematical objects enable non-discursive participation reflects distributed cognition and sociocultural perspectives on learning as mediated by artifacts and social interaction.

ijCSCL_2_4_5.title: Putting the pieces together: Online argumentation vee diagrams enhance thinking during discussions
ijCSCL_2_4_5.authors: E. Michael Nussbaum & Denise L. Winsor & Yvette M. Aqui
ijCSCL_2_4_5.summary_haiku: Online argumentation vee diagrams (AVDs) significantly enhance students' ability to integrate opposing arguments in asynchronous discussions. Using a quasi-experimental design with 87 preservice teachers, students completing individual AVDs before discussions and collaborative group AVDs afterward demonstrated greater compromise-based reasoning and opinion change compared to controls. Scaffolding questions evaluating argument strength proved essential for effectiveness, suggesting structured support facilitates metacognitive reflection necessary for balanced argumentation.
ijCSCL_2_4_5.evidence_span: methods (quasi-experimental design, 87 preservice teachers, AVD conditions) + findings (compromise reasoning, opinion change, scaffolding effects)
ijCSCL_2_4_5.coding_notes: Study uses quasi-experimental comparison of treatment (individual then collaborative AVDs with scaffolding questions) versus control conditions. Primary focus is argumentation scaffolding in asynchronous discussion; secondary analysis of reasoning quality via content coding. Sociocultural framing implicit in collaborative knowledge construction; socio-cognitive emphasis on conflict resolution and reasoning integration.

ijCSCL_8_1_2.title: On the bridge to learn: Analysing the social organization of nautical instruction in a ship simulator
ijCSCL_8_1_2.summary_haiku: This qualitative study examines how nautical students collaboratively construct simulated learning contexts through role-play in a ship simulator. Using interaction analysis of video data, the researchers identify two competing activity contexts: students enacting professional crew roles and students participating in educational training. The analysis reveals that while role-play enables situated learning opportunities for professional tasks, maintaining credible simulations requires substantial interactional effort and can conflict with instructional objectives like meta-reflection and debriefing.
ijCSCL_8_1_2.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (interaction analysis of video data), findings (role-play contexts, interactional effort)
ijCSCL_8_1_2.coding_notes: The study employs micro-analytic video coding of moment-by-moment collaborative episodes in a ship simulator, characteristic of interaction analysis. The focus on how students socially organize learning through role-play and manage competing activity contexts aligns with sociocultural and activity-theoretic perspectives on situated learning.

ijCSCL_3_4_0.title: CSCL practices
ijCSCL_3_4_0.summary_haiku: This editorial examines computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) practices across educational contexts. It synthesizes research on how collaborative learning emerges through technology-mediated interactions at individual, group, and community levels. Key findings address student self-efficacy in science, game-based math learning outcomes, and automated analysis methods for collaborative discourse, emphasizing that effective CSCL implementation requires attention to surrounding pedagogical and social practices.
ijCSCL_3_4_0.evidence_span: editorial synthesis across methods and findings sections
ijCSCL_3_4_0.coding_notes: As an editorial synthesizing CSCL research across contexts, the article integrates multiple methodologies (quantitative outcomes in science/math, qualitative discourse analysis) and analyzes learning at individual, group, and community levels. Primary technology inferred as shared workspace given emphasis on technology-mediated interaction; no AI/LLM involvement evident. Confidence moderate due to editorial nature limiting methodological specificity.

ijCSCL_8_3_0.title: Collaborative Learning at CSCL 2013
ijCSCL_8_3_0.authors: Gerry Stahl & Nancy Law & Friedrich Hesse
ijCSCL_8_3_0.summary_haiku: The CSCL 2013 conference brought together international researchers to advance collaborative learning research and practice. A presidential symposium analyzed regional developments in North America, Europe, Australia, and Asia, revealing diverse research approaches unified by a common goal: improving collaborative learning implementation in education. The field faces opportunities through initiatives like PISA's planned assessment of collaborative problem-solving skills.
ijCSCL_8_3_0.coding_notes: This is a conference overview/presidential symposium synthesizing regional CSCL research rather than a primary empirical study. Coded as ethnographic_case_study as the closest fit for a reflective, bounded analysis of the CSCL research community itself; however, the article is primarily a meta-level commentary on the field rather than a traditional empirical investigation. Unit of analysis is the international CSCL research community and its regional variations.

ijCSCL_8_3_2.title: Crossing boundaries in Facebook: Students’ framing of language learning activities as extended spaces
ijCSCL_8_3_2.authors: Annika Lantz-Andersson & Sylvi Vigmo & Rhonwen Bowen
ijCSCL_8_3_2.summary_haiku: This ethnographic case study examined how 60 students aged 13-16 from four countries framed English language learning activities in a Facebook group. Using frame analysis and sociocultural theory, researchers found that students initially adopted formal school-task framing but gradually negotiated boundary-crossing interactions creating extended learning spaces. However, maintaining these dynamic spaces proved difficult, requiring deliberate collaborative negotiation between educators and students to balance everyday social media practices with educational goals.
ijCSCL_8_3_2.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (ethnographic case study, frame analysis), findings (boundary-crossing, framing negotiation)
ijCSCL_8_3_2.coding_notes: Study uses ethnographic observation and frame analysis of Facebook interactions across four countries; sociocultural lens emphasizes socially mediated learning and boundary-crossing between formal and informal spaces. Secondary pedagogy reflects the negotiated collaborative framing between educators and students.

ijCSCL_3_4_2.title: The right tool for the wrong task? Match and mismatch between first and second stimulus in double stimulation
ijCSCL_3_4_2.summary_haiku: This study examines how Norwegian high school students learning English as a foreign language approach open-ended collaborative tasks using wiki technology. Using Vygotsky's double stimulation framework, researchers analyzed the relationship between task design (first stimulus) and available tools (second stimulus) in collaborative knowledge construction. Findings reveal that learners struggled to maintain awareness across individual, group, and whole-class levels. When the wiki application failed, students sustained collective working practices through alternative tools like PowerPoint and MSN chat, demonstrating that pedagogical and technological designs must be better aligned to support collaborative knowledge production.
ijCSCL_3_4_2.evidence_span: methods, findings, discussion of task design and tool alignment
ijCSCL_3_4_2.coding_notes: Study uses Vygotsky's double stimulation framework to analyze collaborative episodes in wiki-based learning; interaction_analysis captures the micro-analytic focus on how students navigate task-tool mismatch. Activity theory secondary reflects the contradiction-driven lens implicit in examining stimulus alignment.

ijCSCL_8_1_0.title: Analyzing group coordination when solving geometry problems with dynamic geometry software
ijCSCL_8_1_0.summary_haiku: This study proposes a methodological framework for analyzing group coordination in geometry problem-solving with dynamic geometry software. Using conversation analysis and reference field theory, the researcher examined a dyad's face-to-face interaction solving a construction problem. Findings reveal successful collaboration requires coordinating both mathematical/tool-enabled resources and collaborative resources, with participants shifting between theoretical and spatio-graphical reference fields while maintaining productive turn-taking and transactive dialogue.
ijCSCL_8_1_0.evidence_span: methods (conversation analysis, reference field theory) + findings (turn-taking, transactive dialogue, coordination of resources)
ijCSCL_8_1_0.coding_notes: Conversation analysis and reference field theory are hallmarks of interaction analysis focused on moment-by-moment collaborative episodes. The dyad solving a geometry construction problem with dynamic geometry software is the primary unit; sociocultural and distributed cognition theories underpin the analysis of how mathematical, tool, and collaborative resources are coordinated.

ijCSCL_1_3_1.title: Technology affordances for intersubjective meaning making: A research agenda for CSCL
ijCSCL_1_3_1.summary_haiku: Suthers proposes intersubjective meaning making—how groups jointly compose interpretations of dynamically evolving contexts—as CSCL's integrating research agenda. Through conceptual analysis, he argues that technology should be designed as fundamentally social to afford such meaning-making processes. He advocates hybrid methodologies combining experimental, descriptive, and design approaches, with "uptake" relations serving as a boundary object enabling dialogue across theoretical traditions.
ijCSCL_1_3_1.evidence_span: conceptual analysis, research agenda framing, methodology discussion
ijCSCL_1_3_1.coding_notes: This is a conceptual/theoretical position paper proposing a research agenda rather than reporting empirical findings. Methodology_primary coded as design_based_research because Suthers advocates iterative design of technology to afford meaning-making; pedagogy_primary coded as 'other' because the focus is on intersubjective meaning-making processes rather than a specific pedagogical model. Confidence moderate due to the paper's primarily theoretical rather than empirical nature.

ijCSCL_2_2_1.title: Contextual perspective in analysing collaborative knowledge construction of two small groups in web-based discussion
ijCSCL_2_2_1.summary_haiku: This study presents a methodology for analyzing collaborative knowledge construction in asynchronous web-based discussions by examining two student groups' thematic structure, communicative functions, and contextual resources. Comparing novice and experienced teacher-education students, findings reveal that different backgrounds influenced how groups created and interpreted context, negotiated meanings, and selected resources—novices relied on course material and peer discussion, while experienced students drew primarily on personal teaching experience.
ijCSCL_2_2_1.coding_notes: Study explicitly analyzes thematic structure, communicative functions, and contextual resources in asynchronous web-based discussion—hallmarks of discourse and interaction analysis. Two small groups are the primary unit; sociocultural and dialogic theories underpin meaning-making through collaborative dialogue in context.

ijCSCL_1_1_3.title: Students assessing their own collaborative knowledge building
ijCSCL_1_1_3.authors: Eddy Y.C. Lee & Carol K.K. Chan & Jan van Aalst
ijCSCL_1_1_3.summary_ollama: This study examined the role of knowledge-building portfolios in characterizing and scaffolding collaborative inquiry in computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) environments. The study involved 119 students in four grade-nine Geography classes in Hong Kong, who used Knowledge Forum with different conditions: Knowledge Forum only, Knowledge Forum with portfolios, and Knowledge Forum with portfolios and principles. The results showed that students working on portfolios guided by knowledge-building principles showed deeper inquiry and more conceptual understanding than their counterparts. The study also found that knowledge-building portfolios helped to assess and foster collective knowledge advances, and that students' knowledge-building discourse, reflected in portfolio scores, contributed to their domain understanding.
ijCSCL_1_1_3.summary_haiku: This study examined how electronic portfolio assessments guided by knowledge-building principles support collaborative inquiry in computer forums. Using a quasi-experimental design with 119 ninth-grade students across three Knowledge Forum conditions, researchers found that students receiving portfolios with knowledge-building principles demonstrated deeper inquiry, more high-level questions, and superior conceptual understanding compared to peers using forums alone or portfolios without principles. Portfolio scores predicted essay performance beyond individual participation metrics, suggesting portfolios effectively capture distributed, progressive knowledge advancement.
ijCSCL_1_1_3.evidence_span: methods (quasi-experimental design, 119 students, three conditions) + findings (portfolio scores, essay performance, inquiry depth)
ijCSCL_1_1_3.coding_notes: Study explicitly uses Knowledge Forum (wiki-based knowledge-building tool) and applies Scardamalia & Bereiter principles. Quasi-experimental comparison of three conditions (portfolio with principles, portfolio without, forum alone) with classroom cohort as primary unit but individual learner outcomes also measured. Electronic portfolios function as awareness/assessment dashboards capturing distributed knowledge advancement.

ijCSCL_3_2_4.title: Appropriation of a shared workspace: Organizing principles and their application
ijCSCL_3_2_4.summary_haiku: This case study examines how student groups appropriate a graphical shared workspace during computer-mediated argumentative discussion. Through micro-analysis of tool-mediated interactions, the researchers found that groups develop shared organizational principles through implicit negotiation of conventions. Four groups demonstrated distinct orientations—maintaining direct interaction, constructing personal reasoning, or submitting unrelated contributions—resulting in different principles for organizing contributions. The study reveals mutual shaping between students and tool, where early choices constrain later possibilities and strong graphical principles prove difficult to abandon.
ijCSCL_3_2_4.evidence_span: methods (micro-analysis of tool-mediated interactions) + findings (organizational principles, group orientations, mutual shaping)
ijCSCL_3_2_4.coding_notes: The study employs fine-grained interaction analysis of small groups using a shared graphical workspace during argumentative discussion. The focus on how groups negotiate and appropriate conventions through implicit interaction, combined with analysis of artifacts (workspace contributions), reflects both interaction_analysis and content_analysis methodologies, with sociocultural and distributed cognition theoretical grounding.

ijCSCL_3_2_5.title: Operationalizing macro-scripts in CSCL technological settings
ijCSCL_3_2_5.summary_haiku: This article proposes SPAIRD, a conceptualization model for operationalizing CSCL macro-scripts—pedagogical activity structures that guide collaborative learning. The research identifies core design dimensions including script reification through technology, student presentation strategies, and uncertainties in script perception and enactment. SPAIRD disentangles structural models, implementation models, platform specifications, and student-oriented models while documenting design rationale. The analysis examines current technological approaches and advocates for flexible, model-based script engines supporting iterative design.
ijCSCL_3_2_5.coding_notes: Tchounikine's SPAIRD is a conceptual model for operationalizing macro-scripts in CSCL platforms. The work is design-oriented, proposing a framework to bridge pedagogical intent and technological implementation. Primary focus is on script artifacts and their reification in technology; secondary attention to classroom enactment. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

ijCSCL_1_1_2.title: A relational, indirect, meso-level approach to CSCL design in the next decade
ijCSCL_1_1_2.summary_ollama: This paper proposes a relational, indirect, meso-level approach to Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) design in the next decade. The authors argue that a meso-level approach, focusing on the interactions between small groups and larger institutional processes, is necessary to understand the complex relationships between technology, affordance, and infrastructure in CSCL. They also suggest that a relational approach to technology and affordance, which views them as existing in relationships between people and the material world, is more suitable for CSCL research. The authors propose an indirect design approach, which acknowledges the limitations of designers' control over how their designs are enacted and emphasizes the importance of understanding the relationships between technology, affordance, and infrastructure in CSCL.
ijCSCL_1_1_2.summary_haiku: This theoretical paper proposes a relational approach to CSCL design, arguing that technology, affordances, and infrastructure should be understood as emerging through relationships rather than as fixed properties. Drawing on two European research networks, the authors advocate for meso-level analysis bridging micro-group and macro-institutional processes, and recommend indirect design strategies that acknowledge contingency in how learners enact technological affordances within networked learning environments.
ijCSCL_1_1_2.coding_notes: This is a theoretical/conceptual paper proposing a relational design framework rather than an empirical study. Methodology is theoretical argumentation; unit of analysis is meso-level systems bridging micro and macro. Theory draws on sociocultural and distributed cognition perspectives emphasizing relationships and emergence. No specific pedagogy, technology, or AI involvement is described.

ijCSCL_2_2_0.title: Gerry Stahl & Daniel D. Suthers & Friedrich Hesse
ijCSCL_2_2_0.summary_haiku: This editorial introduces a double issue of the International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning coinciding with CSCL 2007. It presents papers organized around two "flash themes": scripting in collaborative learning environments and argumentation in CSCL. The collection features empirical studies employing mixed methods—quantitative coding, controlled experiments, and qualitative analysis—demonstrating how structured scripts and argumentative dialogue support knowledge construction in computer-mediated collaborative learning contexts.
ijCSCL_2_2_0.evidence_span: editorial introduction and article collection overview
ijCSCL_2_2_0.coding_notes: This is an editorial introducing a thematic double issue; the summary indicates the collection emphasizes scripting and argumentation with mixed methods across multiple empirical studies. Primary codes reflect the stated flash themes and typical CSCL 2007 methodologies. Confidence is moderate because the editorial itself is not a single empirical study, but a curated collection.

ijCSCL_1_3_0.title: Focusing on participation in group meaning making
ijCSCL_1_3_0.summary_haiku: This editorial proposes intersubjective meaning making as a unifying theoretical focus for CSCL research, arguing it better captures collaborative learning phenomena than traditional frameworks. The issue presents four articles exemplifying this approach: anchored discussion using quantitative analysis, networked handhelds supporting group interaction, and social network analysis combined with qualitative methods to examine student participation processes.
ijCSCL_1_3_0.evidence_span: editorial framing + article summaries describing quantitative analysis, social network analysis, and qualitative methods
ijCSCL_1_3_0.coding_notes: This is an editorial introducing a thematic issue rather than a single empirical study. The coding reflects the collection of four articles it presents, which employ mixed quantitative (SNA, descriptive stats) and qualitative (discourse/interaction analysis) approaches. The emphasis on 'intersubjective meaning making' and group participation aligns with dialogic and sociocultural theory. Confidence is moderate because the editorial itself does not report original research; the actual methodologies vary across the four featured articles.

ijCSCL_8_1_1.title: Learning across levels
ijCSCL_8_1_1.summary_haiku: CSCL research must bridge individual, small-group, and community levels of analysis through emergent interactional resources. This theoretical framework proposes that resources—from ephemeral conversational moves to institutionalized practices—mediate across levels through processes of reification, sedimentation, and personalization. Empirical studies examining mathematical problem-solving, scientific representations, and collaborative learning demonstrate how tracking these resources reveals connections between local interactions and broader socio-cultural contexts.
ijCSCL_8_1_1.coding_notes: Stahl's framework emphasizes bridging individual-group-community levels through interactional resources and emergent processes. Interaction analysis is primary because the work focuses on tracking conversational moves and collaborative episodes; cross-level analysis is central to the theoretical contribution. Sociocultural theory dominates, with activity theory and distributed cognition as complementary lenses for understanding resource mediation across contexts.

ijCSCL_3_4_3.title: Exploring embedded guidance and self-efficacy in educational multi-user virtual environments
ijCSCL_3_4_3.authors: Brian C. Nelson & Diane Jass Ketelhut
ijCSCL_3_4_3.summary_haiku: This exploratory study examined how student self-efficacy in scientific inquiry affects guidance system use and learning outcomes in River City, an educational multi-user virtual environment. Using a sample of 96 middle school students, researchers found that students with low self-efficacy viewed significantly fewer guidance messages than higher-efficacy peers. While embedded reflective guidance improved learning across all efficacy levels, it only partially mitigated low self-efficacy's negative impact on performance. Notably, low-efficacy students with heavy guidance use achieved comparable outcomes to high-efficacy students without guidance.
ijCSCL_3_4_3.evidence_span: methods, findings, discussion of guidance system effects and self-efficacy interactions
ijCSCL_3_4_3.coding_notes: Study compares guidance conditions and self-efficacy groups in a virtual environment (quasi-experimental design). Primary unit is individual learner outcomes; secondary includes trace data from guidance message viewing. Inquiry-based pedagogy through River City's problem-solving tasks; self-regulation through reflective guidance prompts. Shared workspace (multi-user VE) with embedded awareness/guidance dashboard. Socio-cognitive framing (self-efficacy, guidance scaffolding) with sociocultural context (collaborative VE). No AI/LLM involvement detected.

ijCSCL_9_1_4.title: Explaining authors’ contribution to pivotal artifacts during mass collaboration in the Wikipedia’s knowledge base
ijCSCL_9_1_4.authors: Iassen Halatchliyski & Johannes Moskaliuk & Joachim Kimmerle & Ulrike Cress
ijCSCL_9_1_4.summary_haiku: This empirical study examined how authors' contribution experience relates to their involvement in pivotal Wikipedia articles across two knowledge domains. Using network analysis on German Wikipedia data, researchers identified two types of pivotal articles: those central within single domains and those bridging domains. Results showed domain specialists predominantly contributed to domain-central articles, while generalists contributed to boundary-crossing articles. Article experience positively predicted contributions to both article types regardless of specialization.
ijCSCL_9_1_4.evidence_span: methods (network analysis on Wikipedia data) + findings (pivotal articles, contributor roles)
ijCSCL_9_1_4.coding_notes: Study uses graph-based network analysis to identify pivotal articles and their structural roles (domain-central vs. bridging), with descriptive statistics on contributor patterns. Primary unit is Wikipedia articles as artifacts within a knowledge network; secondary is the community of contributors. Knowledge building theory fits the collaborative knowledge construction in Wikipedia; distributed cognition captures how knowledge is spread across contributors and artifacts.

ijCSCL_8_3_3.title: Advancing understanding using Nonaka’s model of knowledge creation and problem-based learning
ijCSCL_8_3_3.authors: Meng Yew Tee & Shuh Shing Lee
ijCSCL_8_3_3.summary_haiku: Integrating Nonaka's knowledge creation model with problem-based learning addresses Bereiter's critique that the model neglects understanding. This design-based research examined a 14-week course for in-service teachers developing technological pedagogical content knowledge. Findings demonstrate that combining socialization, externalization, combination, and internalization processes within problem-based learning phases cultivates advancing understanding of complex teaching-technology integration challenges.
ijCSCL_8_3_3.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (14-week course design), findings (SECI model integration with PBL phases)
ijCSCL_8_3_3.coding_notes: Design-based research is explicit in the abstract; the study iteratively designs and examines a 14-week intervention integrating Nonaka's SECI model with problem-based learning. Secondary methodology includes mixed methods because the study likely combines qualitative observation of understanding development with quantitative or structured data. Technology is not foregrounded; focus is on pedagogical integration of knowledge creation processes.

2016_v11i1_10.1007_s11412-016-9229-3_Tea.title: Teacher support in computer-supported lab work: bridging the gap between lab experiments and students’ conceptual understanding
2016_v11i1_10.1007_s11412-016-9229-3_Tea.summary_haiku: This intervention study examined teacher support in computer-supported collaborative lab work, analyzing 122 student help requests during a genetics experiment. Findings reveal that 45.1% of requests concerned conceptual issues and 28.7% addressed procedural challenges. Detailed interaction analyses show students struggled linking lab procedures to underlying scientific principles, requiring substantial teacher support through elicitation, explanation, and conceptual guidance to bridge this gap.
2016_v11i1_10.1007_s11412-016-9229-3_Tea.evidence_span: methods, findings, interaction analyses of help requests
2016_v11i1_10.1007_s11412-016-9229-3_Tea.coding_notes: Study uses detailed coding of 122 help requests with categorization (conceptual vs. procedural) and micro-analytic examination of teacher-student interaction episodes. Primary unit is student groups seeking support; teacher facilitation is secondary analytical focus. Computer-supported lab work implies shared digital workspace but exact technology not specified in excerpt.

2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09364-y_CS.title: CSsCL: the performance of collaborative learning
2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09364-y_CS.summary_haiku: This commentary examines three foundational concepts in computer-supported collaborative learning: collaboration scripts, self-regulation, and group awareness. Through analysis of five special issue papers, Crook proposes that regulation operates in layered structures requiring "meta-metacognition," and that group awareness involves both social cognition and intersubjectivity. He reconceptualizes scripted collaboration using a theatre metaphor, emphasizing performance, direction, and audience perspectives to better integrate these concepts within classroom ecosystems.
2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09364-y_CS.evidence_span: abstract, commentary structure, conceptual analysis of five papers
2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09364-y_CS.coding_notes: This is a commentary/review article that systematically examines and reconceptualizes three foundational CSCL concepts through analysis of published papers. The primary methodology is content analysis of existing literature combined with discourse-level conceptual work. The unit of analysis is the published papers and their ideas (artifacts), though the commentary addresses classroom-level implications. Technology is not the focus; the work is theoretical and conceptual.

2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09461-8_Ta.title: Talk to the machine: Unleashing the potential of AI to scale dialogic education and reduce polarization
2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09461-8_Ta.authors: Yifat Ben-David Kolikant & Omri Hadar & Asaf Salman
2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09461-8_Ta.summary_haiku: # Summary Researchers fine-tuned an LLM-based chatbot called LlamaLo on productive Reddit discussions to explore its potential for scaling dialogic education and reducing polarization. Through qualitative analysis of ten conversations on contentious topics, they found LlamaLo effectively opened dialogic spaces by questioning assumptions and presenting alternatives. However, challenges including negative tone, bias, and occasional incoherence could undermine dialogue and require computational and pedagogical solutions.
2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09461-8_Ta.evidence_span: methods (qualitative analysis of ten conversations) + findings (LlamaLo's dialogic moves and challenges)
2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09461-8_Ta.coding_notes: Study centers on qualitative micro-analysis of human–LLM conversational exchanges on contentious topics, examining how the chatbot opens dialogic space. Primary methodology is interaction analysis of discourse; secondary methods include content coding of LLM outputs and computational linguistics (fine-tuning on Reddit data). Unit of analysis is the conversation artifact (human–LLM dialogue) and implicitly the dyadic interaction. Pedagogy is dialogic (questioning, alternative perspectives); theory is dialogic (Bakhtin-lineage dialogue) with sociocultural framing. LLM is the primary learning partner/orchestrator.

2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9285-y_Usi.title: Using big data techniques for measuring productive friction in mass collaboration online environments
2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9285-y_Usi.authors: Peter Holtz & Joachim Kimmerle & Ulrike Cress
2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9285-y_Usi.summary_haiku: Researchers analyzed Wikipedia using big data techniques—text classification, social network analysis, and clustering—to examine how "productive friction" (resolving socio-cognitive conflicts) drives learning and knowledge construction at both individual and collective levels. Findings demonstrated that knowledge development occurs when diverse contributors engage across different perspectives, while homogeneous groups risk polarization and stagnation.
2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9285-y_Usi.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (big data techniques: text classification, SNA, clustering)
2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9285-y_Usi.coding_notes: Study employs big data techniques (text classification, SNA, clustering) on Wikipedia to analyze productive friction in mass collaboration. Primary methodology is SNA given explicit use of network analysis; secondary methods include NLP (text classification) and learning analytics (trace data from wiki edits). Knowledge-building theory and socio-cognitive conflict resolution are central to the framing of productive friction.

2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09357-3_Se.title: Self‑efficacy and behavior patterns of learners using a real‑time collaboration system developed for group programming
2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09357-3_Se.authors: Ting-Chia Hsu & Hal Abelson & Evan Patton & Shih-Chu Chen & Hsuan-Ning Chang
2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09357-3_Se.summary_haiku: This study examined how adult learners' self-efficacy and collaborative behaviors differ when using a real-time collaboration (RTC) system integrated with MIT App Inventor for block-based programming. Using sequential behavior analysis on 13 participants grouped by disciplinary background, researchers found that RTC enabled simultaneous task execution and enhanced communication through annotations. Computer Science majors in homogeneous groups demonstrated significantly higher programming self-efficacy during collaboration than non-majors and heterogeneous groups, though individual versus collaborative self-efficacy remained comparable overall.
2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09357-3_Se.evidence_span: methods (sequential behavior analysis, participant grouping) + findings (self-efficacy differences, behavior patterns)
2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09357-3_Se.coding_notes: Primary methodology is sequence_process_mining because the study explicitly uses sequential behavior analysis to extract temporal patterns from collaborative episodes. The RTC system with annotations and simultaneous task execution is a shared workspace; self-efficacy measurement and group composition analysis support secondary descriptive and interaction-analytic methods.

2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09314-1_Co.title: Correction to: A handheld classroom dashboard: teachers’ perspectives on the use of real-time collaborative learning analytics
2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09314-1_Co.summary_haiku: This correction notice addresses duplicate images in the original article examining teachers' perspectives on a handheld classroom dashboard for real-time collaborative learning analytics. The correction republishes the correct versions of Figures 4 and 6, which display visualizations of group task progress, individual participation, and real-time feedback on learning design enactment.
2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09314-1_Co.coding_notes: This is a correction notice, not a research article. Only the technology (handheld classroom dashboard for real-time analytics) can be reliably identified from the title and excerpt. Methodology, unit of analysis, pedagogy, and theory cannot be determined from a correction notice alone; the original article would be needed for full coding.

2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-025-09449-4_Ed.title: Editorial notes: Core issues in CSCL research
2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-025-09449-4_Ed.summary_haiku: This editorial examines four core CSCL research issues: task design effects on collaboration and learning, dialogue and disagreement in knowledge co-elaboration, and technology mediation. Studies compared conceptual versus hands-on physics tasks, analyzed maritime simulator training, tracked belief change across multiple debates, and investigated how direct versus soft disagreement affects peer critique. Findings emphasize that task authenticity, dialogue quality, and disagreement management significantly influence collaborative learning outcomes.
2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-025-09449-4_Ed.coding_notes: This is an editorial overview synthesizing multiple CSCL studies rather than a primary empirical research article. The summary references diverse methodologies (experimental comparisons, discourse analysis, belief tracking) and units (tasks, dialogue, disagreement management) across different studies, making single-category coding inappropriate. A meta-analytic or review-focused classification would be more suitable but is not available in the provided taxonomy.

2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-025-09464-5_A_.title: A temporal network approach to reveal the longitudinal dynamics of CSCL group regulation and productive collaboration
2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-025-09464-5_A_.authors: Mohammed Saqr & Sonsoles Lopez-Pernas & Tiina Tormanen
2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-025-09464-5_A_.summary_haiku: This study employs temporal network analysis combined with clustering, sequence analysis, and growth models to examine how online problem-based learning groups regulate collaboration over time. Analyzing 118 discussion groups, researchers identified four distinct weekly regulation patterns and found that groups using interactive socioemotional or regulated constructive patterns demonstrated higher cognitive productivity. Critically, explicit group regulation emerged infrequently and primarily in response to challenges, while most groups maintained stable patterns with minimal improvement over time, suggesting early instructional support is essential for fostering productive regulation.
2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-025-09464-5_A_.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (temporal network analysis, clustering, sequence analysis, growth models), findings (four weekly patterns, cognitive productivity outcomes)
2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-025-09464-5_A_.coding_notes: Study explicitly uses temporal network analysis and sequence analysis to track longitudinal regulation patterns in 118 online discussion groups. Primary focus is on group-level self and peer regulation dynamics over time in asynchronous problem-based learning contexts. Multilevel and network methods are secondary analytical approaches supporting the temporal sequence mining.

2022_v17i4_10.1007_s11412-022-09382-w_Me.title: Mediating and perspective‑taking manipulatives: Fostering dynamic perspective‑taking by mediating dialogic thinking and bolstering empathy in role‑play and reflection for microteaching
