2022_v17i4_10.1007_s11412-022-09382-w_Me.authors: Toshio Mochizuki & Hiroshi Sasaki & Takehiro Wakimoto & Yoshihiko Kubota & Brendan Eagan & Ryoya Hirayama & Yuta Yamaguchi & Natsumi Yuki & Hideo Funaoi & Hideyuki Suzuki & Hiroshi Kato
2022_v17i4_10.1007_s11412-022-09382-w_Me.summary_haiku: This study examined how tangible puppets and 3D manipulable animations support student teachers' perspective-taking in microteaching. Using epistemic network analysis on discourse from 72 preservice teachers across three sessions, results showed that combining mediating manipulatives (puppets) with perspective-taking manipulatives (3D viewpoint switching) significantly enhanced student-centered reflection compared to video-only conditions. The intervention fostered authentic imaginary student voices and sustained dialogic teaching perspectives in subsequent role-plays.
2022_v17i4_10.1007_s11412-022-09382-w_Me.evidence_span: methods (epistemic network analysis, discourse coding), findings (perspective-taking outcomes, role-play reflection)
2022_v17i4_10.1007_s11412-022-09382-w_Me.coding_notes: Study uses epistemic network analysis on discourse to examine how tangible manipulatives (puppets and 3D animations) mediate perspective-taking in microteaching. Primary focus is interaction analysis of dialogic discourse; secondary methods include discourse analysis and learning analytics via trace data from role-play sessions. Dialogic theory is central to the intervention design and analysis framework.

2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09391-3_Co.title: Correction: An artificial intelligence‑driven learning analytics method to examine the collaborative problem‑solving process from the complex adaptive systems perspective
2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09391-3_Co.authors: Fan Ouyang & Weiqi Xu & Mutlu Cukurova
2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09391-3_Co.summary_haiku: This is a correction notice for an article on artificial intelligence-driven learning analytics examining collaborative problem-solving through complex adaptive systems theory. The correction addresses an erroneous figure that appeared in the original publication, replacing it with the correct framework diagram of complex adaptive systems theory adapted from Holland's work.
2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09391-3_Co.coding_notes: This is a correction notice rather than a full empirical study, limiting detail available for precise coding. The original article examines collaborative problem-solving using AI-driven learning analytics and complex adaptive systems theory; the correction only addresses a figure replacement. Coding reflects the inferred methodology and theory from the title and context, but confidence is moderate due to lack of methods/findings sections in the correction document itself.

2020_v15i1_10.1007_s11412-020-09316-4_Go.title: Good for learning, bad for motivation? A meta-analysis on the effects of computer-supported collaboration scripts
2020_v15i1_10.1007_s11412-020-09316-4_Go.authors: Anika Radkowitsch & Freydis Vogel & Frank Fischer
2020_v15i1_10.1007_s11412-020-09316-4_Go.summary_haiku: This meta-analysis of 53 studies examined computer-supported collaboration scripts' effects on learner outcomes. Results showed scripts produced non-significant positive effects on motivation, small positive effects on domain learning, and medium positive effects on collaboration skills. Contrary to widespread criticism, scripts did not undermine motivation. However, combining multiple collaborative activity prompts generally reduced effectiveness compared to single-activity scripts, suggesting simpler designs may be more beneficial for learning.
2020_v15i1_10.1007_s11412-020-09316-4_Go.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (meta-analysis of 53 studies), findings (effect sizes on motivation, learning, collaboration skills)
2020_v15i1_10.1007_s11412-020-09316-4_Go.coding_notes: Meta-analysis synthesizes quantitative effect sizes across multiple studies using inferential statistics (meta-regression, heterogeneity testing). Primary unit is the study/intervention artifact (collaboration scripts); secondary is cross-level because meta-analyses aggregate individual and group outcomes. Pedagogy centers on collaboration scripts; theory draws on socio-cognitive (explanation, conflict) and sociocultural (mediated activity) frameworks implicit in script design.

2022_v17i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09372-y_Co.title: Collaborative analytics-supported reflective Assessment for Scaffolding Pre-service Teachers’ collaborative Inquiry and Knowledge Building
2022_v17i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09372-y_Co.authors: Yuqin Yang & Gaoxia Zhu & Daner Sun & Carol K. K. Chan
2022_v17i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09372-y_Co.summary_haiku: This study examined how collaborative analytics-supported reflective assessment enhances pre-service teachers' competencies in collaborative inquiry and knowledge building. Using a quasi-experimental design with 40 experimental and 28 comparison pre-service teachers over 18 weeks, the experimental group engaged in knowledge building enriched by KBDeX visualizations and rubrics, while the comparison group used portfolio assessment. Analysis of Knowledge Forum discourse revealed that the experimental group demonstrated significantly higher-level epistemic engagement, collaborative interactions, and metacognitive reflection. Epistemic network analysis showed stronger connections between higher-level actions in the experimental group, and cumulative degree centrality indicated greater community knowledge advancement. Results suggest collaborative analytics-supported reflective assessment effectively scaffolds pre-service teachers' development of collaborative inquiry competencies.
2022_v17i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09372-y_Co.evidence_span: methods (quasi-experimental design, 18-week intervention, Knowledge Forum discourse analysis, epistemic network analysis) + findings (higher epistemic engagement, stronger network connections, centrality measures)
2022_v17i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09372-y_Co.coding_notes: Study combines quantitative comparison (quasi-experimental with control group) and qualitative discourse/network analysis of Knowledge Forum interactions. Primary focus is knowledge building pedagogy scaffolded by collaborative analytics (KBDeX visualizations and rubrics). Epistemic network analysis and cumulative degree centrality are secondary quantitative methods applied to discourse data.

2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09368-8_Co.title: Correction to: Many are the ways to learn: Identifying multi‑modal behavioral profiles of collaborative learning in constructivist activities
2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09368-8_Co.authors: Jauwairia Nasir & Aditi Kothiyal & Barbara Bruno & Pierre Dillenbourg
2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09368-8_Co.summary_haiku: This correction document addresses formatting and citation errors in the original 2021 article examining multi-modal behavioral profiles in collaborative constructivist learning. The researchers identified and corrected a missing colon in the title and multiple misattributed or incorrectly formatted citations throughout the paper, ensuring accurate reference to their prior work on collaborative learning analytics.
2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09368-8_Co.coding_notes: This is a correction/erratum notice, not a research article. It addresses formatting and citation errors in a 2021 original study but provides no substantive methodological, pedagogical, or technological content to code. The original 2021 article would be the appropriate source for detailed coding.

2024_v19i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09413-0_Ex.title: Exploring students’ immersive VR experiences as resources for collaborative meaning making and learning
2024_v19i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09413-0_Ex.authors: Kenneth Silseth & Rolf Steier & Hans Christian Arnseth
2024_v19i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09413-0_Ex.summary_haiku: Students viewing a cinematic VR film about exclusion and discrimination, followed by teacher-facilitated group dialogues, experienced the VR as highly social. Through interaction analysis of reflective dialogues, researchers identified four dimensions characterizing meaning-making: feeling part of conversations, attending to others' bodily expressions, students' own bodily responses, and teacher guidance. The study demonstrates how immersive VR experiences become collaborative learning resources when integrated into structured activity sequences emphasizing dialogue.
2024_v19i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09413-0_Ex.evidence_span: methods (interaction analysis of dialogues) + findings (four dimensions of meaning-making)
2024_v19i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09413-0_Ex.coding_notes: VR film is the artifact/stimulus, but the primary analytical focus is micro-analytic coding of moment-by-moment collaborative dialogue and bodily interaction during teacher-facilitated group discussions. Technology is peripheral to the core CSCL analysis of collaborative meaning-making.

2024_v19i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09412-1_Le.title: Learning within fiber‑crafted algorithms: Posthumanist perspectives for capturing human‑material collaboration
2024_v19i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09412-1_Le.summary_haiku: This study employs posthumanist analysis to examine how middle school students and fiber craft materials collaboratively produce algorithms during weaving and fabric manipulation activities. Using video data, the researcher identifies how youth-material intra-actions create computational performances through repeated, patterned movements. Findings reveal that both humans and materials actively contribute to algorithmic production, with variations in these patterns enabling algorithmic expansion over time. The study proposes human-material collaboration as a productive analytical unit for understanding computational learning in CSCL contexts.
2024_v19i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09412-1_Le.evidence_span: methods (video analysis, posthumanist framework) + findings (human-material intra-actions, algorithmic patterns)
2024_v19i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09412-1_Le.coding_notes: The study's core methodology is micro-analytic video coding of moment-by-moment human-material interactions during weaving, making interaction_analysis primary. The artifact (woven patterns/algorithms) and material traces are central analytical objects. Distributed cognition and activity theory best capture the posthumanist framing of cognition as spread across humans and materials; sociocultural theory also relevant given the collaborative learning context.

2025_v20i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09443-2_En.title: Enhancing students’ dialogic reflection through classroom discourse visualisation
2025_v20i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09443-2_En.authors: Pengjin Wang & Fan Chen & Deliang Wang & Gaowei Chen
2025_v20i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09443-2_En.summary_haiku: Visualisation-supported dialogic reflection (VSDR) using classroom discourse analysis enhanced primary students' collaborative learning. A 3-month intervention with 53 students showed significant knowledge gains in the high-dose group and increased student participation across both groups. Qualitative analysis revealed students engaged in deeper reflection on problem-solving strategies, group collaboration, and whole-class participation when reviewing visualised classroom discourse through discussion forums.
2025_v20i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09443-2_En.coding_notes: Study combines quantitative outcome measures (knowledge gains, participation frequency) with qualitative discourse analysis of reflection episodes. Classroom discourse visualisation functions as an awareness dashboard enabling reflective dialogue; asynchronous forums support the reflection process. Dialogic theory is primary because the intervention explicitly targets dialogic reflection through multi-voiced classroom discourse review.

2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-026-09471-0_Ed.title: Editorial notes: Collaboration, feedback and dynamics
2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-026-09471-0_Ed.summary_haiku: This editorial examines foundational CSCL concepts through five empirical papers. It explores whether collaboration extends to human-AI interactions and large-group collective intelligence, reconceptualizes feedback as multimodal and embodied rather than unidirectional, and argues that describing collaborative dynamics requires deeper ontological models beyond flat variable relationships—integrating layered processes, functional analysis, and mechanist explanations to understand how learning actually emerges.
2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-026-09471-0_Ed.coding_notes: This is an editorial/commentary piece that synthesizes and reflects on five empirical papers rather than reporting original empirical research. It does not employ a single methodology but instead critiques and reconceptualizes foundational CSCL concepts (collaboration, feedback, dynamics). The primary contribution is theoretical and meta-analytical, examining ontological models for understanding collaborative learning emergence. Confidence is low because the piece's nature as a framing editorial makes standard CSCL methodology and unit-of-analysis categories poorly applicable.

2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09451-w_Ac.title: Accomplishing collaboration at scale: How professionals jointly frame problems on Stack Overflow
2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09451-w_Ac.summary_haiku: # Summary This study investigates how software developers collaboratively frame programming problems on Stack Overflow through asynchronous, fluid participation. Using trace ethnography and sequential analysis of selected threads, the research reveals that minimal reproducible examples (MREs) structured within the platform's dual-space design enable collaboration at scale. Standardized norm-enforcing requests and explicit referencing practices ensure mutual intelligibility among unknown contributors, facilitating effective problem-solving in large-scale online environments.
2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09451-w_Ac.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (trace ethnography, sequential analysis)
2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09451-w_Ac.coding_notes: Study uses trace ethnography and sequential analysis of Stack Overflow threads to examine how developers collaboratively frame problems through asynchronous interaction. Primary focus is on discourse artifacts (MREs, posts, referencing practices) and their role in enabling large-scale collaboration; secondary attention to community-level participation patterns. Standardized norms and explicit referencing practices function as collaboration scripts.

2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09414-z_St.title: Studying teacher withitness in the wild: comparing a mirroring and an alerting & guiding dashboard for collaborative learning
2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09414-z_St.authors: Reet Kasepalu & Pankaj Chejara & Luis P. Prieto & Tobias Ley
2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09414-z_St.summary_haiku: This quasi-experiment examined how dashboards affect teacher withitness—situational awareness and interventions—during collaborative learning. Twenty-four teachers used three conditions: no dashboard, mirroring-only dashboard, and AI-assisted alerting & guiding dashboard. Results show mirroring dashboards increased situational awareness, while alerting & guiding dashboards significantly reduced teacher workload, particularly frustration and perceived failure. However, intervention rates didn't increase as hypothesized, suggesting teachers need extended training to effectively implement AI-suggested coregulation strategies in authentic classroom settings.
2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09414-z_St.coding_notes: Study compares three dashboard conditions (none, mirroring, AI-assisted alerting) in authentic classrooms with 24 teachers; primary focus is teacher withitness and workload rather than student learning outcomes. AI involvement is rule-based alerting and guidance rather than LLM-based, though the 'alerting & guiding' system may incorporate some predictive/ML components for coregulation suggestions.

2021_v16i3_10.1007_s11412-021-09351-9_De.title: Deconstructing orchestration load: comparing teacher support through mirroring and guiding
2021_v16i3_10.1007_s11412-021-09351-9_De.authors: Ishari Amarasinghe & Davinia Hernandez-Leo & H. Ulrich Hoppe
2021_v16i3_10.1007_s11412-021-09351-9_De.summary_haiku: This study compared how mirroring and guiding support in teacher dashboards influence orchestration load during scripted collaborative learning. Six teachers conducted Pyramid-pattern activities under three conditions: no dashboard, mirroring support, and guiding support with alerts. Using epistemic network analysis, researchers found that guiding support enabled more targeted interactions and announcements compared to mirroring support. The findings deconstruct orchestration load into situation evaluation, goal formation, and action-taking facets.
2021_v16i3_10.1007_s11412-021-09351-9_De.evidence_span: methods (epistemic network analysis, dashboard conditions) + findings (orchestration load facets, interaction patterns)
2021_v16i3_10.1007_s11412-021-09351-9_De.coding_notes: The study uses epistemic network analysis to examine teacher orchestration moves across dashboard conditions, focusing on how awareness tools mediate teacher decision-making during scripted collaborative activities. Primary focus is teacher facilitation and orchestration load rather than learner outcomes.

2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09389-x_Ed.title: Editorial: Nine elements for robust collaborative learning analytics: A constructive collaborative critique
2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09389-x_Ed.authors: Alyssa Friend Wise & Carolyn Rose & Sanna Jarvela
2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09389-x_Ed.summary_haiku: This editorial proposes nine essential elements for robust collaborative learning analytics, bridging computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) and learning analytics (LA) communities. The framework emphasizes data-driven improvement, careful construct mapping, temporal and multi-level theorization, multi-channel data integration, user-centered design, human-centered approaches, real-world implementation examination, and ethical considerations. The authors evaluate four journal articles against these elements, identifying strengths in theory development and intervention design while highlighting gaps in closing the loop between analysis and actionable support.
2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09389-x_Ed.evidence_span: title, abstract, editorial framing of nine elements and evaluation of four articles
2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09389-x_Ed.coding_notes: This is a meta-analytical editorial proposing a framework for evaluating CSCL/LA research rather than reporting original empirical findings. Primary methodology coded as learning_analytics because the editorial's core contribution is a framework for LA practice and evaluation. Unit of analysis is artifact_discourse_trace because the editorial evaluates how four studies analyze collaborative traces and discourse. No AI/LLM involvement detected in the editorial's own methodology or the framework proposed.

2024_v19i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09425-4_Co.title: Collaborative Problem‑Solving in Knowledge‑Rich Domains: A Multi‑Study Structural Equation Model
2024_v19i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09425-4_Co.authors: Laura Brandl & Matthias Stadler & Constanze Richters & Anika Radkowitsch & Martin R. Fischer & Ralf Schmidmaier & Frank Fischer
2024_v19i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09425-4_Co.summary_haiku: This study tested the Collaborative Diagnostic Reasoning (CDR) model using structural equation modeling across three medical education studies (N=504). Analyzing simulation-based diagnostic tasks, researchers found that content and collaboration knowledge influenced collaborative diagnostic activities (evidence elicitation and sharing), which subsequently affected diagnostic accuracy, justification, and efficiency. Notably, collaboration knowledge emerged as more critical than social skills, and diagnostic activities independently predicted outcomes beyond individual characteristics, highlighting the multidimensional nature of collaborative problem-solving in knowledge-rich domains.
2024_v19i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09425-4_Co.evidence_span: methods (SEM across three studies, N=504), findings (model fit, path coefficients, mediation effects)
2024_v19i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09425-4_Co.coding_notes: SEM is the primary inferential method testing a theoretical model; multilevel structure implied by nested data across three studies. Dyads engage in collaborative diagnostic reasoning tasks; cross-level analysis examines individual knowledge and group activities predicting outcomes. Pedagogy centers on structured diagnostic problem-solving with emphasis on collaboration knowledge. No AI/LLM or specialized CSCL technology mentioned; focus is on face-to-face simulation-based collaboration.

2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09388-y_Fo.title: Fostering regulation of learning processes among programming students using computational scaffolding
2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09388-y_Fo.authors: Leonardo Silva & Antonio Mendes & Anabela Gomes & Gabriel Fortes
2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09388-y_Fo.summary_haiku: # Summary This randomized controlled trial evaluated RESPE, a computer-supported collaborative learning platform embedding computational scaffolding for self-regulation and socially shared regulation of learning in introductory programming. With 71 students across three conditions (self-regulation support only, combined self and social regulation support, and control), results showed regulatory support significantly improved course grades. Notably, only students receiving social regulation support achieved superior collaborative activity performance, confirming the importance of social-cognitive perspectives in learning regulation.
2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09388-y_Fo.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (RCT design with three conditions), findings (regulatory support effects on grades and collaborative performance)
2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09388-y_Fo.coding_notes: RCT with three experimental conditions (self-regulation, combined self+social regulation, control) is clearly experimental. RESPE platform embeds computational scaffolding for regulation, classified as collaboration_scripting_tools. Primary unit is individual learner outcomes (grades), but social regulation condition involves dyadic/group collaboration. Socio-cognitive theory emphasized in abstract ('social-cognitive perspectives'); sociocultural framing implicit in socially shared regulation concept.

2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09367-9_In.title: Integrating collaboration scripts, group awareness, and self‑regulation in computer‑supported collaborative learning
2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09367-9_In.summary_haiku: This special issue examines three interconnected concepts in computer-supported collaborative learning: group awareness, collaboration scripts, and self-regulation. Through conceptual and empirical papers, the collection explores how these mechanisms—which support learners' social interactions, cognitive processes, and metacognitive monitoring—can be combined to enhance collaborative learning design. The papers demonstrate that integrating these approaches yields more effective CSCL environments than addressing them separately.
2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09367-9_In.coding_notes: This is a special issue editorial/overview synthesizing multiple empirical and conceptual papers on collaboration scripts, group awareness, and self-regulation in CSCL. Primary methodology coded as mixed_methods because the collection integrates both conceptual and empirical work; confidence is moderate because the summary does not detail specific methodologies of individual papers. Pedagogy and technology reflect the three core mechanisms highlighted (scripts, awareness, self-regulation).

2022_v17i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09373-x_Re.title: Relations Matter – CSCL Research Informing and Developing CL Competencies
2022_v17i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09373-x_Re.summary_haiku: This editorial examines how interpersonal relations and interactions in computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) influence learning outcomes. Through empirical studies employing social network analysis, epistemic network analysis, and collaborative analytics, the four featured papers demonstrate that strategic relations matter in two ways: interventions designed from empirical findings support successful collaborative interactions, and CSCL environments foster key learner competencies in problem-solving, teamwork, and knowledge-building communities.
2022_v17i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09373-x_Re.evidence_span: title, abstract, editorial framing of featured papers
2022_v17i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09373-x_Re.coding_notes: Editorial synthesizing four empirical CSCL studies emphasizing social network analysis and epistemic network analysis of collaborative interactions. Primary methodology coded as social_network_analysis based on explicit mention; secondary methods reflect learning_analytics and interaction_analysis as supporting approaches. Pedagogy emphasizes structured collaboration and knowledge-building communities. No AI/LLM involvement evident in this editorial overview.

2020_v15i1_10.1007_s11412-020-09319-1_Ex.title: Experiencing CSCL: from motivation to the embodied experience and beyond
2020_v15i1_10.1007_s11412-020-09319-1_Ex.authors: Carolyn Rose & Sanna Jarvela & Sten Ludvigsen
2020_v15i1_10.1007_s11412-020-09319-1_Ex.summary_haiku: This editorial introduces a journal transition emphasizing empirical CSCL research grounded in deep theory. Featured articles include a meta-analysis of collaboration scripts showing non-significant positive motivational effects, and three papers advancing embodied CSCL through Activity Theory frameworks, physiological synchrony measurement instruments, and augmented reality sandbox environments for authentic collaborative learning experiences.
2020_v15i1_10.1007_s11412-020-09319-1_Ex.evidence_span: abstract and summary; editorial framing of featured articles
2020_v15i1_10.1007_s11412-020-09319-1_Ex.coding_notes: This is an editorial introducing a journal issue rather than a single empirical study. The coding reflects the collection of featured articles described: meta-analysis of collaboration scripts, embodied CSCL work using Activity Theory, physiological synchrony measurement, and augmented reality environments. Mixed methods and multilevel modeling inferred from meta-analysis and multi-paper scope; multimodal sensors from physiological synchrony focus. Confidence is moderate because the editorial does not detail full methodological or theoretical commitments of each paper.

2019_v14i1_10.1007_s11412-019-09296-0_Im.title: Improving the quality of vocational students’ collaboration and knowledge acquisition through instruction and joint reflection
2019_v14i1_10.1007_s11412-019-09296-0_Im.authors: Judith ter Vrugte & Anjo Anjewierden & Lars Bollen & Elise H. Eshuis & Jakob Sikken & Ton de Jong
2019_v14i1_10.1007_s11412-019-09296-0_Im.summary_haiku: Combining conventional instruction with an online reflection tool incorporating self-assessment, peer feedback, and goal-setting significantly improved vocational students' collaborative behavior and knowledge acquisition in computer-supported learning environments. Analysis of chat logs and knowledge tests from 198 first-year technical students revealed that instruction alone proved ineffective, but instruction paired with the reflection tool fostered higher-quality collaboration and superior learning outcomes compared to control conditions.
2019_v14i1_10.1007_s11412-019-09296-0_Im.evidence_span: methods, findings, and results sections describing experimental design, chat log analysis, and knowledge test outcomes
2019_v14i1_10.1007_s11412-019-09296-0_Im.coding_notes: Study employs a controlled comparison of instruction + reflection tool versus instruction alone and control, with analysis of chat logs (learning analytics) and knowledge tests. Primary focus is on individual learner outcomes and collaborative behavior in dyads/small groups. The reflection tool (self-assessment, peer feedback, goal-setting) is the core pedagogical intervention supporting self and peer regulation.

2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09450-x_Th.title: The CoMPAS Framework for Modeling Individual Participation in Collaborative Learning Processes: a Systematic Review
2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09450-x_Th.summary_haiku: This systematic review of 66 studies (2005-2024) proposes the CoMPAS framework for modeling individual participation in collaborative learning using process data. The framework identifies six forms of participation—cognitive interactions, coordinative interactions, metacognitive interactions, passive participation, solo active participation, and socio-emotional interactions—analyzed through oral conversational, textual, log, and nonverbal physical data using descriptive, content, network, and clustering methods. Findings reveal bidirectional relationships between individual participation and group performance.
2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09450-x_Th.evidence_span: title, abstract, framework description, methodology overview
2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09450-x_Th.coding_notes: This is a systematic review proposing the CoMPAS framework for analyzing participation forms in collaborative learning. Primary methodology is content analysis (systematic coding of participation types across multiple data modalities). Secondary methods include descriptive statistics (frequencies of participation forms) and social network analysis (interaction patterns). The review examines individual learners and small groups through discourse and log traces, grounded in sociocultural and distributed cognition perspectives on collaborative learning.

2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09399-9_Mo.title: Mobile augmented reality supporting families’ immersive collaborative learning: Learning‑on‑the‑move for place‑based geoscience sense‑making
2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09399-9_Mo.authors: Heather Toomey Zimmerman & Susan M. Land & Lillyanna Faimon & Yu-Chen Chiu
2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09399-9_Mo.summary_haiku: This study investigated how families experienced immersion while using a mobile augmented reality app called Time Explorers to collaboratively learn about geologic time and geoscience processes during outdoor learning-on-the-move. Using interaction analysis of video recordings and interviews from 17 families (51 participants), researchers found that sensory and social immersion supported sense-making conversations and observational inquiry, while narrative and actional immersion enabled deep engagement with geoscience content about rock-water interactions shaping Appalachia.
2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09399-9_Mo.evidence_span: methods (interaction analysis of video + interviews) + findings (immersion types supporting sense-making)
2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09399-9_Mo.coding_notes: Study uses micro-analytic coding of collaborative episodes (interaction analysis) with 17 families in outdoor, place-based geoscience learning. Mobile AR app (Time Explorers) is the primary technology enabling shared workspace and immersive exploration. Sociocultural framing emphasizes socially mediated sense-making through immersion; distributed cognition fits the embodied, environment-embedded nature of learning-on-the-move.

2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09360-8_A_.title: A theory‑driven reflection on context‑aware support for collaborative discussions in light of analytics, affordances, and platforms
2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09360-8_A_.summary_haiku: This editorial reflection examines context-aware support for collaborative discussions through three lenses: learning analytics, platform affordances, and technological platforms. The authors synthesize four empirical studies employing network analysis, multimodal data integration, experimental manipulation, and platform evaluation to understand collaborative learning processes. They argue that bridging small-scale classroom research with large-scale societal dialogue requires integrating diverse datasets across multiple timescales using combined automatic and human analyses guided by coherent theoretical frameworks.
2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09360-8_A_.evidence_span: abstract, editorial framing, synthesis of four empirical studies
2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09360-8_A_.coding_notes: This is a theory-driven editorial reflection synthesizing multiple empirical studies rather than reporting a single primary study. The primary methodology is mixed_methods because it integrates network analysis, multimodal data, experimental manipulation, and platform evaluation. Unit of analysis is artifact_discourse_trace (collaborative discussions) with secondary cross-level analysis. No AI/LLM involvement is evident in the reflection itself, though individual synthesized studies may employ analytics tools.

2024_v19i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09423-6_Le.title: Learning to notice collaboration: examining the impact of professional development on mathematics teachers’ enhanced awareness in CSCL settings
2024_v19i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09423-6_Le.summary_haiku: # Summary This study examined how professional development affects mathematics teachers' ability to notice dialogue in computer-supported collaborative learning. Fourteen teachers analyzed video excerpts of student pairs solving parabola tasks before and after an 80-minute intervention focused on Bakhtinian dialogic concepts. Using think-aloud interviews and dialogic framework analysis, results showed significant improvements in teachers' attending to and responding to dialogic attributes, particularly regarding student relationships, inter-animation, and multivoicedness, though challenges remain in balancing mathematical correctness with dialogue support.
2024_v19i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09423-6_Le.evidence_span: methods (think-aloud interviews, video analysis, intervention design) + findings (pre/post improvements in dialogic noticing)
2024_v19i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09423-6_Le.coding_notes: Study uses a quasi-experimental pre–post design with 14 teachers as the primary unit, examining how an 80-minute PD intervention changes their ability to notice dialogic features in student video. Bakhtinian dialogic theory and discourse analysis of think-aloud protocols are central. No AI/LLM or advanced CSCL technology is involved; focus is on teacher awareness and professional development.

2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09460-9_Le.title: Learning to deal with hate speech: An online collective intelligence experiment on the Collective Learning platform
2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09460-9_Le.authors: Tatiana Iniguez-Berrozpe & Carmen Elboj-Saso & Francesco Marcaletti
2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09460-9_Le.summary_haiku: This study examined whether collective intelligence can help adolescents manage online hate speech using the Collective Learning platform. Spanish teenagers (ages 15–16) were divided into one large group (n=123) and two smaller groups (n=18, n=23). Results showed that collective intelligence conditions emerged only in the large group, which demonstrated significant improvements in responses across four questions assessing moral reasoning and prosocial action regarding hate speech. Small groups showed minimal improvement, suggesting group size and heterogeneity are critical for collective intelligence to facilitate learning about hate speech prevention.
2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09460-9_Le.coding_notes: Study compares three group-size conditions (large n=123 vs. small n=18, n=23) on a collaborative platform, measuring moral reasoning and prosocial action via pre–post assessment. Collective intelligence and knowledge-building theory are central; the Collective Learning platform likely supports asynchronous discussion. No AI/LLM involvement detected. Confidence reduced slightly due to limited detail on exact platform affordances and whether discourse analysis was performed beyond quantitative outcome measures.

2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09329-z_Bu.title: Building community together: towards equitable CSCL practices and processes
2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09329-z_Bu.summary_haiku: This editorial examines five qualitative studies investigating collaborative learning processes across diverse contexts—data visualization, problem-based learning, maker spaces, online professional development, and equity in automated systems. The collection emphasizes the critical role of human facilitation in scaffolding collaboration, while addressing contemporary concerns about equity, diversity, and fairness in computer-supported collaborative learning technologies.
2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09329-z_Bu.evidence_span: title, abstract, editorial framing of five qualitative studies
2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09329-z_Bu.coding_notes: This is an editorial synthesizing five qualitative studies rather than a single empirical study. Primary coding reflects the dominant themes (ethnographic/case-study orientation, teacher facilitation, sociocultural theory, equity focus). Secondary choices capture the multi-context nature and emphasis on scaffolding and collaborative processes. No AI/LLM involvement evident in the editorial's scope.

2022_v17i4_10.1007_s11412-022-09380-y_Ev.title: Evolution of the academic emotions of academically low‑achieving students in knowledge building
2022_v17i4_10.1007_s11412-022-09380-y_Ev.authors: Yuqin Yang & Gaoxia Zhu & Carol K. K. Chan
2022_v17i4_10.1007_s11412-022-09380-y_Ev.summary_haiku: Low-achieving secondary students engaged in Knowledge Building through Knowledge Forum exhibited predominantly positive emotions, with joy comprising 53% of expressed emotions. Sequential pattern analysis revealed emotions tend to transition to similar emotions, and five primary emotional evolution paths emerged, with confusion serving as a critical juncture determining whether students progress toward joy or negative emotions like boredom and frustration.
2022_v17i4_10.1007_s11412-022-09380-y_Ev.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (sequential pattern analysis), findings (emotional evolution paths)
2022_v17i4_10.1007_s11412-022-09380-y_Ev.coding_notes: The study explicitly uses sequential pattern analysis to extract temporal emotional transitions and identifies five primary emotional evolution paths, making sequence/process mining the primary methodology. Knowledge Building via Knowledge Forum is the core pedagogical and technological context. Low-achieving students' individual emotional trajectories are the primary unit of analysis.

2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09431-6_Ca.title: Capturing temporal pathways of collaborative roles: A multilayered analytical approach using community of inquiry
2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09431-6_Ca.authors: Ramy Elmoazen & Mohammed Saqr & Laura Hirsto & Matti Tedre
2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09431-6_Ca.summary_haiku: This longitudinal study analyzed 135 dental students' online problem-based learning discussions across four courses using Community of Inquiry framework coding combined with latent class analysis, epistemic network analysis, and process mining. Three distinct roles emerged: leaders, social mediators, and peripheral explorers. Students exhibited stable role trajectories across time, with active trajectories achieving higher grades than free riders, suggesting roles function as stable dispositions requiring intentional teacher intervention for change.
2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09431-6_Ca.evidence_span: methods (latent class analysis, epistemic network analysis, process mining) + findings (role trajectories, grade outcomes)
2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09431-6_Ca.coding_notes: Primary methodology is sequence/process mining given explicit temporal pathway and trajectory analysis. Community of Inquiry framework and epistemic network analysis support secondary social network coding. Longitudinal design with role stability across time and multilevel structure (individuals within courses within cohort) justifies cross-level secondary unit.

2017_v12i4_10.1007_s11412-017-9268-4_Fut.title: Future direction for the CSCL field: Methodologies and eight controversies
2017_v12i4_10.1007_s11412-017-9268-4_Fut.authors: Sten Ludvigsen & Ulrike Cress & Nancy Law & Gerry Stahl & Carolyn P. Rose
2017_v12i4_10.1007_s11412-017-9268-4_Fut.summary_haiku: This editorial introduces four papers addressing methodological advances and foundational questions in computer-supported collaborative learning. Three award-winning conference papers present novel analytical approaches: interaction geography for analyzing museum visitors' movements and talk, the SQuILD method for quantifying informal dialogue in interactive exhibits, and research on self-efficacy in peer tutoring. A fourth paper presents eight controversies debated among CSCL experts regarding theoretical frameworks, learner agency, computational approaches, and the field's future direction.
2017_v12i4_10.1007_s11412-017-9268-4_Fut.coding_notes: This is a meta-level editorial/position paper surveying methodologies and controversies in CSCL rather than reporting a single empirical study. It reviews multiple analytical approaches (interaction geography, SQuILD, self-efficacy analysis) and theoretical debates, making it difficult to assign a single primary methodology or pedagogy. Coded as content_analysis (systematic review of methods and frameworks) with secondary discourse and interaction analysis. Primary unit is artifact/discourse because the paper analyzes and discusses research approaches and scholarly debate rather than direct learner outcomes.

2019_v14i1_10.1007_s11412-019-09297-z_Hi.title: Highlighting tools and technologies for collaborative learning
2019_v14i1_10.1007_s11412-019-09297-z_Hi.authors: Carolyn P. Rose & Nancy Law & Ulrike Cress & Sten Ludvigsen
2019_v14i1_10.1007_s11412-019-09297-z_Hi.summary_haiku: This editorial examines four research articles investigating technology's role in collaborative learning, distinguishing between tools that scaffold group reflection and awareness versus those enabling student creativity and expression. The collection demonstrates that technologies—whether supporting metacognitive processes, joint reflection, design practices, or multimodal representation creation—constitute first-class scientific contributions to computer-supported collaborative learning research.
2019_v14i1_10.1007_s11412-019-09297-z_Hi.evidence_span: editorial framing and article collection overview
2019_v14i1_10.1007_s11412-019-09297-z_Hi.coding_notes: This is an editorial synthesizing four research articles rather than a primary empirical study. Coding reflects the dominant themes across the collection: tools supporting group reflection/awareness and metacognitive processes (self-regulation), multimodal representation (shared workspace), and sociocultural framing of collaborative learning. Confidence is moderate due to the meta-level nature of the editorial and lack of detailed methodology description.

2020_v15i4_10.1007_s11412-020-09337-z_St.title: Students’ multimodal knowledge practices in a makerspace learning environment
2020_v15i4_10.1007_s11412-020-09337-z_St.summary_haiku: This sociocultural study examined how students' collaborative knowledge practices are mediated multimodally in a school makerspace during STEAM challenges. Through discourse and multimodal interaction analysis of 350 minutes of video data from two student groups, researchers identified four intertwined knowledge practices: orienting to, interpreting, concretizing, and expanding knowledge. Findings reveal that discourse, materials, embodied actions, and spatial arrangements jointly mediated students' joint attention and knowledge creation, with peer guidance proving more influential than teacher support or pre-given instructions.
2020_v15i4_10.1007_s11412-020-09337-z_St.evidence_span: methods (video analysis, discourse and multimodal interaction coding) + findings (four knowledge practices, role of materials and embodied actions)
2020_v15i4_10.1007_s11412-020-09337-z_St.coding_notes: Study employs fine-grained video analysis of moment-by-moment collaborative episodes in a makerspace, coding discourse and multimodal interaction (gestures, materials, spatial positioning). Sociocultural framing emphasizes mediation through multiple semiotic resources; distributed cognition captures how knowledge emerges across people, artifacts, and environment.

2016_v11i1_10.1007_s11412-016-9230-x_CSC.title: CSCL towards the future: The second decade of ijCSCL
2016_v11i1_10.1007_s11412-016-9230-x_CSC.summary_haiku: The editorial outlines emerging challenges for CSCL research as the field enters its second decade. It emphasizes the need for interdisciplinary expertise, particularly in computer science and statistics, and identifies key research gaps: integrating individual and group-level analysis, designing computational support for emerging collaboration forms, and developing methodologies addressing mass collaboration and learning analytics. The journal maintains its commitment to rigorous, diverse methodological approaches across cognitive, socio-cognitive, and socio-cultural perspectives.
2016_v11i1_10.1007_s11412-016-9230-x_CSC.coding_notes: This is an editorial/position paper surveying the CSCL field rather than reporting an empirical study. It discusses methodological and theoretical directions (sociocultural, socio-cognitive perspectives) and identifies research gaps (individual/group analysis, computational support, learning analytics) but does not itself conduct research with a specific methodology, unit of analysis, pedagogy, or technology focus. Coded as 'other' across primary fields to reflect its meta-analytical, agenda-setting nature.

2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09361-1_Gr.title: Group awareness and regulation in
2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09361-1_Gr.summary_haiku: This article conceptualizes group awareness (GA) in computer-supported collaborative learning as a conscious, current, individual cognitive construct about social entities that learners perceive as valid. The authors identify six defining aspects of GA and propose it operates within three regulatory cycles: regulating GA itself through metacognitive monitoring, regulating social interaction based on GA, and regulating partner schema building. The framework connects GA to working memory processes and suggests implications for designing support tools and conducting empirical research on collaborative learning mechanisms.
2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09361-1_Gr.evidence_span: abstract and conceptual framework; no empirical data reported
2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09361-1_Gr.coding_notes: This is a conceptual/theoretical paper proposing a framework for group awareness and regulatory cycles in CSCL. It does not report empirical data collection or analysis; instead, it synthesizes existing literature and proposes a model. Coded as content_analysis (systematic conceptual decomposition) with discourse_analysis as secondary because the framework addresses how awareness and regulation operate through interaction. Technology is coded as awareness_dashboard because the paper discusses implications for designing support tools that make group activity visible.

2024_v19i4_10.1007_s11412-024-09432-5_Em.title: Emergent group understanding: Investigating intersubjectivity in sociotechnical interdependencies
2024_v19i4_10.1007_s11412-024-09432-5_Em.authors: Anders I. Mørch & Renate Andersen & Siv Eie & Louise Mifsud
2024_v19i4_10.1007_s11412-024-09432-5_Em.summary_haiku: This study investigates how shared understanding emerges in computer-mediated learning using Minecraft for social studies. Through design-based research with student teachers reconstructing historical industrial sites, researchers identified "emergent group understanding"—a phenomenon where spontaneous individual knowledge contributions trigger focused group action toward shared learning goals. The framework integrates sociotechnical congruence, intersubjectivity, and emergence theories, revealing how social and technological objects co-evolve through six states of intersubjectivity toward knowledge objects.
2024_v19i4_10.1007_s11412-024-09432-5_Em.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods, findings on emergent group understanding and intersubjectivity states
2024_v19i4_10.1007_s11412-024-09432-5_Em.coding_notes: Design-based research iteratively studying how shared understanding emerges in Minecraft-mediated collaborative learning. Sociotechnical congruence and intersubjectivity frameworks align with sociocultural and distributed cognition theories. Minecraft functions as a shared workspace enabling co-evolution of social and technological objects.

2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09410-3_Co.title: Correction: Contesting sociocomputational norms: computer programming instructors and students’ stancetaking around refactoring
2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09410-3_Co.authors: Morgan M. Fong & David DeLiema & Virginia J. Flood & Oia Walker-van Aalst
2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09410-3_Co.summary_haiku: This correction clarifies a discrepancy in the theoretical framework section of an interaction analysis study examining how computer programming instructors and students contest sociocomputational norms through classroom discourse. The researchers use stancetaking analysis to investigate participatory and relational inequities without assuming participants' inner experiences, focusing on how meanings are publicly negotiated.
2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09410-3_Co.coding_notes: Study employs micro-analytic stancetaking analysis of classroom discourse between instructors and students around programming norms. Dialogic theory is primary (multi-voiced negotiation of meaning); sociocultural secondary (sociocomputational norms as culturally mediated). Unit of analysis spans dyadic/small-group interactions within classroom context. No AI/LLM involvement evident in this correction notice.

2024_v19i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09422-7_Zo.title: Zooming in: The role of nonverbal behavior in sensing the quality of collaborative group engagement
2024_v19i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09422-7_Zo.authors: Lisa Paneth & Loris T. Jeitziner & Oliver Rack & Klaus Opwis & Carmen Zahn
2024_v19i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09422-7_Zo.summary_haiku: This study examined how nonverbal behaviors relate to collaborative group engagement quality in computer-supported learning. Using video analysis of 38 university groups completing a design task, researchers applied quantitative mixed-effects models to 2,617 one-minute sequences and qualitative case analysis. Findings revealed that nodding, eye contact, and gesturing positively correlate with social, cognitive, and conceptual engagement, while laughing shows complex relationships across dimensions. The research demonstrates nonverbal behaviors serve as meaningful indicators of multifaceted, dynamic group engagement in collaborative learning contexts.
2024_v19i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09422-7_Zo.evidence_span: methods (video analysis, mixed-effects models on 2,617 sequences) + findings (nonverbal behavior correlations with engagement dimensions)
2024_v19i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09422-7_Zo.coding_notes: Mixed-effects models applied to nested temporal sequences (one-minute units within groups) is the primary quantitative approach; video-based interaction analysis of nonverbal behaviors (nodding, eye contact, gestures) and qualitative case analysis provide secondary depth. Study focuses on embodied, multimodal indicators of group engagement without AI/LLM involvement.

2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09404-1_Fo.title: Fostering collaborative and embodied learning
2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09404-1_Fo.summary_haiku: Extended reality (XR) environments—including augmented, virtual, and mixed reality—offer significant potential for collaborative and embodied learning by enabling learners to use body-based resources for meaning-making. This special issue examines empirical research demonstrating how XR technologies support collaborative embodied learning across diverse contexts, from family geoscience exploration to teacher mathematics reasoning, addressing the gap between XR adoption in education and research grounded in collaborative learning theory.
2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09404-1_Fo.coding_notes: This is a special issue introduction/editorial, not an empirical study. It frames XR for collaborative embodied learning theoretically but does not report a specific methodology, unit of analysis, or pedagogy. The primary contribution is conceptual positioning rather than research design or findings.

2025_v20i3_10.1007_s11412-025-09455-6_Ed.title: Editorial notes: Extending perennial topics in CSCL
2025_v20i3_10.1007_s11412-025-09455-6_Ed.summary_haiku: This editorial examines how CSCL research extends perennial topics through technological innovation and theoretical advancement. Papers address reflective dialogue using visualization and immersive virtual reality, collaboration quality assessment via self-evaluation scales, and dialogue analysis through positioning theory. The editors argue that balancing theoretical expansion with knowledge accumulation across established themes strengthens the field's scientific foundations.
2025_v20i3_10.1007_s11412-025-09455-6_Ed.coding_notes: This is an editorial note surveying perennial CSCL topics rather than a primary empirical study. It does not employ a single methodology, unit of analysis, pedagogy, or technology; instead, it synthesizes and reflects on multiple papers addressing reflective dialogue, collaboration assessment, and dialogue analysis. No specific empirical methods, pedagogical approach, or technology platform is the focus of the editorial itself.

2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09347-5_Gu.title: Guidance in computer‑supported collaborative inquiry learning: Capturing aspects of affect and teacher support in science classrooms
2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09347-5_Gu.authors: Tarja Pietarinen & Tuire Palonen & Marja Vauras
2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09347-5_Gu.summary_haiku: Teachers in computer-supported collaborative science inquiry learning primarily focused on task management and content knowledge while extensively observing groups. Mixed-methods analysis of four classrooms revealed teachers preferentially guided groups perceived as motivated and collaborative, regardless of prior competence. Notably, socio-emotional support was minimal. Teachers' positive affect correlated with student affect, suggesting reciprocal emotional influences on learning outcomes.
2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09347-5_Gu.evidence_span: methods + findings; teacher guidance patterns, affect analysis, group observation
2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09347-5_Gu.coding_notes: Study combines quantitative observation frequencies and qualitative interaction coding across four classrooms. Primary focus on teacher facilitation decisions and affect dynamics during computer-supported inquiry; secondary units include small-group collaboration and cross-level analysis of teacher–student emotional reciprocity.

2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9252-z_Exp.title: Experiences, appearances, and interprofessional training: The instructional use of video in post-simulation debriefings
2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9252-z_Exp.authors: Oskar Lindwall & Hans Rystedt & Elin Johansson
2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9252-z_Exp.summary_haiku: This study uses conversation analysis to examine 40 video-supported debriefings following simulation-based healthcare training. The research reveals that video enables students to discuss their interprofessional teamwork from a third-person perspective, while facilitators' instructional questions guide students to reconceptualize their performance by contrasting audiovisual appearances with their subjective experiences, facilitating collaborative sense-making about professional conduct.
2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9252-z_Exp.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (conversation analysis of 40 video-supported debriefings)
2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9252-z_Exp.coding_notes: Conversation analysis is the explicit methodology; video-supported debriefing is the artifact and shared workspace. Facilitators' questions and student dialogue are the primary analytical focus, supporting interaction_analysis as primary and discourse_analysis as secondary. Dialogic theory (multi-voiced meaning-making through video-mediated reflection) and sociocultural framing (collaborative sense-making in professional context) are evident.

2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-026-09485-8_Ed.title: Editorial Notes: the CSCL universe is still expanding
2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-026-09485-8_Ed.summary_haiku: This editorial examines four CSCL research papers addressing technology-mediated collaborative learning. Studies investigate anger's productive role in educational games, knowledge synthesis through technological artifacts, temporal network analysis revealing group regulatory patterns, and intergenerational learning in smart home environments. Findings demonstrate that emotional dynamics, meaning reification, temporal group dynamics, and expanded social contexts significantly influence collaborative learning outcomes, while the field continues expanding its analytical scope.
2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-026-09485-8_Ed.evidence_span: editorial summary only; no primary research methods or data presented
2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-026-09485-8_Ed.coding_notes: This is an editorial overview synthesizing four separate CSCL studies rather than a primary research article. The summary mentions diverse methodologies (emotional dynamics, artifact analysis, temporal network analysis, intergenerational contexts) and technologies without sufficient detail to code any single study's approach. Coding reflects the meta-analytical nature of the editorial rather than a specific empirical investigation.

2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09462-7_Ed.title: Editorial notes: Mechanisms as a unifying construct for CSCL research
2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09462-7_Ed.summary_haiku: This editorial proposes mechanistic explanation as a unifying framework for CSCL research. Drawing on realist philosophy of science, the authors argue that identifying generative mechanisms—organized configurations producing outcomes through spatiotemporal continuity—provides deeper explanations than variable-based approaches. They illustrate this through stratification in collaborative learning, demonstrating how Directed Acyclic Graphs and Bayesian Networks model causal relationships, while agent-based modeling captures micro-to-macro mechanisms linking individual actions to group outcomes.
2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09462-7_Ed.evidence_span: entire editorial; conceptual framework and illustrative examples
2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09462-7_Ed.coding_notes: This is a theoretical/philosophical editorial proposing mechanistic explanation as a unifying framework for CSCL, not a primary empirical study. It discusses methodological approaches (DAGs, Bayesian Networks, agent-based modeling) as illustrative examples rather than conducting original research. Coded as 'other' for methodology (meta-theoretical commentary), unit_of_analysis (framework-level analysis), and pedagogy (no specific pedagogical intervention studied).

2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9253-y_Fos.title: Fostering targeted group practices as a Core focus for CSCL task and technology design
2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9253-y_Fos.authors: Nancy Law & Sten Ludvigsen & Ulrike Cress & Carolyn P. Rose
2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9253-y_Fos.summary_haiku: # Summary This editorial examines how computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) can be designed to foster specific group practices essential for productive collaboration. Through analysis of five empirical studies across diverse contexts—from mathematics to medical education—the authors identify common collaborative mechanisms (pointing, turn-taking, boundary spanning, perspective-taking) necessary for effective learning. The research demonstrates that targeted group practices emerge through intentional task design, technology selection, and instructor facilitation rather than automatically, providing systematic guidance for advancing CSCL environments.
2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9253-y_Fos.evidence_span: abstract, summary, editorial framing of five empirical studies
2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9253-y_Fos.coding_notes: This is an editorial synthesizing five empirical studies rather than a single primary research report. The primary methodology is systematic content analysis of collaborative mechanisms across diverse contexts. Secondary methods reflect the underlying studies' use of interaction analysis and ethnographic observation. No AI/LLM involvement evident in the editorial or referenced studies.

2019_v14i2_10.1007_s11412-019-09305-2_In.title: Investigating the complexity of
2019_v14i2_10.1007_s11412-019-09305-2_In.authors: U. Cress & C. P. Rose & N. Law & S. Ludvigsen
2019_v14i2_10.1007_s11412-019-09305-2_In.summary_haiku: Contemporary CSCL research increasingly examines real-world complexity beyond controlled laboratory settings, investigating how core peer-learning processes interact with broader social systems and contextual factors. This editorial synthesizes five journal articles demonstrating that authentic learning contexts, socio-cognitive openness, emotional engagement, learner agency, and multi-level analysis are essential for understanding collaborative learning dynamics in practice.
2019_v14i2_10.1007_s11412-019-09305-2_In.evidence_span: editorial abstract and summary; synthesis of five articles examining real-world CSCL complexity
2019_v14i2_10.1007_s11412-019-09305-2_In.coding_notes: This is an editorial synthesizing multiple studies rather than a single empirical study. The emphasis on multi-level analysis, authentic contexts, and interaction of peer-learning with broader systems suggests cross-level multilevel analysis as primary unit. Methodology coded as mixed_methods because the editorial integrates quantitative and qualitative findings across diverse studies; confidence is moderate due to the meta-level nature of the piece and limited methodological detail in the excerpt.

2024_v19i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09420-9_Di.title: Dialogues across time and space in a video‑based collaborative learning environment
2024_v19i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09420-9_Di.summary_haiku: # Summary This design-based research study examines how pre-service teachers' dialogues emerged across time and space as they collaboratively constructed video-based mind maps using a Padlet platform. Through interaction analysis of 28 hours of video recordings, the researchers found that video-based mind maps supported multiple space-time constellations—synchronous small-group conversations, asynchronous group-to-group exchanges, and whole-class dialogues—enabling meaning-making across learning levels. The study demonstrates how shared video dialogues functioned as mediational artifacts connecting individual contributions into networked conversations that supported collaborative learning and exam preparation.
2024_v19i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09420-9_Di.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (28 hours video recordings, interaction analysis), findings (space-time constellations, mediational artifacts)
2024_v19i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09420-9_Di.coding_notes: Study explicitly uses interaction analysis of video recordings to examine dialogues across multiple temporal and spatial scales. Design-based research framing evident in iterative study of Padlet intervention. Dialogic theory central to analysis of meaning-making through multi-voiced exchanges; distributed cognition relevant to networked conversations across levels.

2016_v11i4_10.1007_s11412-016-9245-3_Tow.title: Toward a classification of discourse patterns in asynchronous online discussions
2016_v11i4_10.1007_s11412-016-9245-3_Tow.authors: Jan van Aalst & Carol K. K. Chan & Ella L. F. Fu
2016_v11i4_10.1007_s11412-016-9245-3_Tow.summary_haiku: This study developed a classification of nine discourse patterns in asynchronous online discussions using qualitative coding and narrative analysis of Knowledge Forum databases across three classes. The patterns distinguished three modes of discourse—knowledge sharing, knowledge construction, and knowledge building—revealing how students engage in collaborative interactions. Knowledge-sharing discourse predominated, while knowledge-building discourse was rare, suggesting that supporting productive discourse requires explicit pedagogical guidance aligned with learning principles.
2016_v11i4_10.1007_s11412-016-9245-3_Tow.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (qualitative coding and narrative analysis of Knowledge Forum databases)
2016_v11i4_10.1007_s11412-016-9245-3_Tow.coding_notes: Study uses systematic qualitative coding of discourse patterns in Knowledge Forum (a wiki-based knowledge repository) across three classes. Primary unit is the discourse trace/post artifact analyzed for knowledge-sharing, construction, and building modes. Knowledge-building theory and sociocultural framing are explicit in the conceptual framework.

2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09365-x_Su.title: ‘Supporting socially shared regulation during collaborative task‑oriented reading’
2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09365-x_Su.authors: Jolique Kielstra & Inge Molenaar & Roel van Steensel & Ludo Verhoeven
2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09365-x_Su.summary_haiku: A collaboration script designed to support socially shared regulation during task-oriented reading facilitated mainly low-level metacognitive discussions among 44 prevocational students working in groups. While the script elicited metacognitive regulation through role-based information distribution, deep-level co-construction remained rare. However, students individually improved their ability to recognize high-level task characteristics and reflect on appropriate reading strategies post-intervention.
2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09365-x_Su.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (44 students, groups, script intervention), findings (metacognitive discussions, individual post-intervention gains)
2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09365-x_Su.coding_notes: Study employs a collaboration script intervention with 44 prevocational students in small groups, examining socially shared regulation during reading. Interaction analysis of metacognitive discussions and content analysis of task-oriented talk are evident. Primary focus is on group-level regulation processes, with secondary attention to individual learning outcomes post-intervention.

2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09435-2_To.title: Toward multimodal learning analytics in simulation‑based collaborative learning: A design ethnography of maritime training
2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09435-2_To.summary_haiku: # Summary This design ethnography examines maritime simulator-based training to inform multimodal learning analytics (MMLA) development. Through detailed video analysis of master mariner students' collaborative bridge activities, the researchers identified how instructors deliver embedded assessments and feedback using multiple social and material resources. The study proposes specific technologies—system logs, eye-tracking, and speech recognition—necessary for capturing professional performance, communication, and collaboration in simulation-based learning environments.
2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09435-2_To.evidence_span: methods (design ethnography, video analysis), findings (instructor feedback, multimodal resource use)
2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09435-2_To.coding_notes: Design ethnography with detailed video analysis of collaborative maritime simulator training is the core methodology. Multimodal sensors (eye-tracking, speech recognition, system logs) are proposed technologies for future MMLA development rather than deployed in this study, hence primary technology is multimodal_sensors. Instructor orchestration of embedded assessment and feedback is central to findings.

2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09456-5_Ag.title: Age‑related differences in explanatory activities during collaborative learning with concept maps: experimental investigation using epistemic network analysis
2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09456-5_Ag.summary_haiku: Younger adults demonstrated significantly higher learning performance and concept map quality than older adults during collaborative learning with concept maps using attribution theory. While younger adults engaged more frequently in active utterances and showed stronger connections between constructive and interactive behaviors, older adults exhibited higher constructive and interactive utterance frequencies but stronger active-interactive connections. Epistemic network analysis revealed that older adults required knowledge reactivation during elaboration, suggesting age-related cognitive decline hinders knowledge integration in computer-supported collaborative learning environments.
2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09456-5_Ag.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (epistemic network analysis), findings (age-related differences in utterance patterns and network connections)
2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09456-5_Ag.coding_notes: Study uses epistemic network analysis (ENA) to examine moment-by-moment collaborative utterances and their connections during concept-map-based learning, making interaction_analysis primary. Social network analysis is secondary because ENA explicitly models network ties between epistemic actions. Attribution theory and age-related cognitive decline suggest sociocultural framing of collaborative learning with individual differences.

2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9274-1_Mul.title: Multiple forms of regulation and coordination across levels in educational settings
2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9274-1_Mul.authors: Sten Ludvigsen & Ulrike Cress & Nancy Law & Gerry Stahl & Carolyn P. Rose
2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9274-1_Mul.summary_haiku: This editorial examines how collaborative learning processes vary based on contextual factors including participant differences, small-group regulation forms, and cross-activity coordination. Four empirical studies investigate computer-supported collaboration using multi-touch tables, wiki environments, and classroom technology. Findings demonstrate that shared understanding, appropriate regulation strategies, and integration across individual, group, and institutional levels are essential for productive collaborative learning in educational settings.
2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9274-1_Mul.evidence_span: title, abstract, summary of four empirical studies examining regulation and coordination
2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9274-1_Mul.coding_notes: Editorial synthesizing multiple studies on regulation and coordination across individual, group, and institutional levels. Primary methodology coded as mixed_methods because the editorial integrates findings from four empirical studies using varied approaches (multi-touch tables, wikis, classroom technology). Cross-level multilevel analysis is central to the editorial's framing. Activity theory and sociocultural perspectives align with the focus on contextual factors and coordination across levels.

2023_v18i3_10.1007_s11412-023-09394-0_Ex.title: Exploring the impact of chat‑based collaborative activities and SRL‑focused interventions on students’ self‑regulation profiles, participation in collaborative activities, retention, and learning in MOOCs
2023_v18i3_10.1007_s11412-023-09394-0_Ex.authors: Georgios Psathas & Stergios Tegos & Stavros N. Demetriadis & Thrasyvoulos Tsiatsos
2023_v18i3_10.1007_s11412-023-09394-0_Ex.summary_haiku: This study examined how self-regulated learning (SRL) interventions combined with chat-based collaborative activities affect MOOC students' outcomes. Using a programming MOOC with 1,807 participants, researchers compared control, general intervention, and personalized intervention groups. Results showed personalized interventions significantly improved SRL profiles and course retention (87.5% vs. 62.5%), while both intervention types increased collaborative participation and learning outcomes compared to controls, demonstrating that targeted SRL support enhances engagement and completion in MOOCs.
2023_v18i3_10.1007_s11412-023-09394-0_Ex.evidence_span: methods (three-group comparison design, MOOC platform, chat-based activities, SRL interventions) + findings (retention rates, SRL profiles, participation metrics, learning outcomes)
2023_v18i3_10.1007_s11412-023-09394-0_Ex.coding_notes: Study uses a controlled comparison of three conditions (control, general intervention, personalized intervention) with large-scale MOOC data (n=1,807), making it quasi-experimental. Primary focus is individual learner outcomes (retention, SRL profiles, learning) measured via learning analytics traces from chat and platform logs. SRL interventions and chat-based collaboration are the core pedagogical mechanisms; no AI/LLM involvement detected.

2019_v14i2_10.1007_s11412-019-09303-4_So.title: Socio-cognitive openness in online knowledge building discourse: does openness keep conversations going?
2019_v14i2_10.1007_s11412-019-09303-4_So.authors: Frank P. C. M. de Jong & Jan van Aalst & Natascha de Hoog & Hennie van Heijst & Paul A. Kirschner
2019_v14i2_10.1007_s11412-019-09303-4_So.summary_haiku: This study analyzes socio-cognitive openness in online knowledge-building discourse among Master's students using a framework with four social and four cognitive components. Analyzing 638 Knowledge Forum contributions, researchers found moderate openness levels with higher social than cognitive openness. Cognitive openness indicators—particularly elaboration, justification, and inviting response—positively predicted follow-up contributions, while social openness showed no significant relationship. Expressing uncertainty emerged as key to sustaining knowledge-building conversations.
2019_v14i2_10.1007_s11412-019-09303-4_So.evidence_span: methods (framework, 638 contributions coded), findings (openness levels, predictive relationships)
2019_v14i2_10.1007_s11412-019-09303-4_So.coding_notes: Study systematically codes Knowledge Forum posts using a socio-cognitive openness framework, then uses inferential statistics (regression) to predict follow-up contributions. Primary focus is content analysis of discourse artifacts; secondary methods include statistical inference and discourse-level interpretation aligned with knowledge-building theory.

2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09442-3_Ho.title: How does collaborative task design shape collaborative knowledge construction and group‑level regulation of learning? A study of secondary school students’ interactions in two varied tasks
2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09442-3_Ho.authors: Kateryna Zabolotna & Liv Nøhr & Megumi Iwata & Daniel Spikol & Jonna Malmberg & Hanna Jarvenoja
2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09442-3_Ho.summary_haiku: Task design significantly shapes collaborative learning processes. This study compared a conceptual physics drawing task and a hands-on robotics task involving secondary students, analyzing collaborative knowledge construction and group-level regulation using video coding and network analysis. Conceptually oriented tasks promoted prolonged cognitive engagement and stronger connections between cognitive regulation and negotiation, while hands-on tasks featured frequent but brief knowledge construction episodes emphasizing socioemotional interactions for maintaining collaboration.
2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09442-3_Ho.evidence_span: methods (video coding, network analysis) + findings (task design effects on knowledge construction and regulation)
2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09442-3_Ho.coding_notes: Study uses video-based micro-analytic coding of collaborative episodes and network analysis to examine how task design (conceptual vs. hands-on) shapes group-level knowledge construction and regulation. Primary methodology is interaction analysis; secondary methods include social network analysis of connections and content analysis of coded episodes. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

2022_v17i3_10.1007_s11412-022-09378-6_Su.title: Supporting perspective taking across chasms of thinking: Do real‑time analytics hold the key?
2022_v17i3_10.1007_s11412-022-09378-6_Su.summary_haiku: This editorial examines how real-time learning analytics can support perspective-taking and growth in collaborative learning across diverse contexts. Four featured articles integrate collaborative learning theory with novel analytical methods and digital trace data to design technologies that prompt learner growth, particularly when addressing challenging topics requiring cross-cultural understanding and meaningful dialogue.
2022_v17i3_10.1007_s11412-022-09378-6_Su.coding_notes: This is an editorial synthesizing four featured articles on real-time analytics for collaborative learning. Primary coding reflects the overarching focus on learning analytics and real-time dashboards supporting perspective-taking in dialogue; secondary methods and units reflect the diversity of approaches across the featured studies. No explicit mention of AI/LLM involvement in the editorial itself.

2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09363-z_Ad.title: Adaptable scaffolding of mathematical argumentation skills: The role of self‑regulation when scaffolded with CSCL scripts and heuristic worked examples
2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09363-z_Ad.authors: Freydis Vogel & Ingo Kollar & Frank Fischer & Kristina Reiss & Stefan Ufer
2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09363-z_Ad.summary_haiku: Two experiments examined adaptable versus non-adaptable scaffolding for mathematical argumentation skills in collaborative learning. University students (N=167) learned with either adaptable or fixed CSCL scripts and heuristic worked examples. Results showed maximal scaffolding supported domain-specific skills, while adaptable scaffolds benefited students with higher self-regulation abilities. Self-regulation skills proved crucial for effectively utilizing adaptable scaffolding, particularly for socio-discursive argumentation development.
2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09363-z_Ad.coding_notes: Two-condition experimental design comparing adaptable vs. fixed CSCL scripts with worked examples. Primary focus on collaboration scripts and self-regulation as moderator of scaffolding effectiveness. Sociocultural framing evident in emphasis on socio-discursive argumentation development within collaborative dyads.

2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09346-6_Im.title: Improving learning and writing outcomes: Influence of cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools in wikis
2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09346-6_Im.authors: Lisa Ollesch & Sven Heimbuch & Daniel Bodemer
2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09346-6_Im.summary_haiku: This study examined how cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools affect wiki-based collaborative learning through a 2×2 factorial experiment with 158 participants. Results show both tool types influence thread selection and discussion engagement, with behavioral awareness particularly motivating contributions. Critically, only the combination of cognitive and behavioral awareness improved article quality, suggesting complementary effects outweigh individual benefits in supporting wiki-based learning outcomes.
2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09346-6_Im.evidence_span: methods (2×2 factorial design, 158 participants) + findings (tool effects on thread selection, engagement, article quality)
