2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09346-6_Im.coding_notes: Study uses controlled factorial experiment comparing awareness tool conditions in wiki-based collaboration. Primary unit is small groups collaborating on wiki articles; secondary focus on artifact quality (article outcomes). Awareness tools function as structured scaffolds guiding collaborative behavior and cognition.

2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-025-09459-2_Un.title: Understanding when anger becomes productive or destructive in collaborative educational games
2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-025-09459-2_Un.summary_haiku: Anger in collaborative game-based learning can facilitate productive discourse when students engage in reasoned debate about strategy and game mechanics. However, when anger escalates into "tilting"—characterized by emotional dysregulation, withdrawal, and abandonment of collaborative goals—it severely disrupts group performance. The study analyzed middle school students' interactions in City Settlers, finding that appropriately expressed anger drove deeper engagement with complex systems, while unresolved anger conflicts led to group breakdown.
2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-025-09459-2_Un.evidence_span: methods and findings sections analyzing collaborative game interactions
2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-025-09459-2_Un.coding_notes: Study focuses on micro-analytic coding of emotional and discursive episodes during collaborative gameplay (City Settlers), examining how anger expressions shape group dynamics and reasoning. Primary methodology is interaction analysis with secondary discourse/content coding; technology is the game itself but not the analytical focus. Sociocultural and dialogic theories frame how emotion mediates collaborative meaning-making.

2021_v16i1_10.1007_s11412-021-09340-y_Pr.title: Promoting regulation of equal participation in online collaboration by combining a group awareness tool and adaptive prompts. But does it even matter?
2021_v16i1_10.1007_s11412-021-09340-y_Pr.doi: Promoting regulation of equal participation in online collaboration by combining a group awareness tool and adaptive prompts. But does it even matter?
2021_v16i1_10.1007_s11412-021-09340-y_Pr.summary_haiku: This field experiment examined whether combining a group awareness tool (GAT) with adaptive prompts supports equal participation in online collaborative learning. Sixty-one students in groups received either no support, a GAT alone, or GAT plus prompts. While students showed higher satisfaction with more equal participation, the collaboration support produced only tentative effects on participation equality. Groups initiating collaboration early and coordinating continuously achieved better participation distribution and satisfaction, suggesting interaction patterns matter more than the technological interventions tested.
2021_v16i1_10.1007_s11412-021-09340-y_Pr.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (field experiment with three conditions), findings (participation equality, satisfaction, interaction patterns)
2021_v16i1_10.1007_s11412-021-09340-y_Pr.coding_notes: Field experiment with three conditions (control, GAT alone, GAT+prompts) analyzing group-level outcomes (participation equality, satisfaction) and interaction patterns. Group awareness tool and adaptive prompts are core technologies; analysis includes learning traces (participation logs) alongside satisfaction measures. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9239-1_Ref.title: Reflective assessment in knowledge building by students with low academic achievement
2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9239-1_Ref.authors: Yuqin Yang & Jan van Aalst & Carol K. K. Chan & Wen Tian
2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9239-1_Ref.summary_haiku: Students with low academic achievement engaged in sustained knowledge-building discourse when supported by reflective assessment using the Knowledge Connections Analyzer tool. Analysis of 20 Grade 11 visual arts students' online discussions revealed they generated theories, built on peers' ideas, and synthesized concepts. Reflective assessment helped students focus on knowledge-building goals including community collaboration, idea improvement, and synthesis, demonstrating that low-achieving students can successfully participate in higher-order collaborative inquiry.
2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9239-1_Ref.evidence_span: methods (20 Grade 11 students, online discussions, Knowledge Connections Analyzer tool) + findings (discourse analysis of theories, idea building, synthesis)
2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9239-1_Ref.coding_notes: Study centers on Scardamalia & Bereiter's knowledge-building framework with reflective assessment via the Knowledge Connections Analyzer. Primary methodology is interaction analysis of online discourse; secondary methods include systematic coding of discussion content and learning analytics from the platform. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09358-2_Ma.title: Many are the ways to learn identifying multi-modal behavioral profiles of collaborative learning in constructivist activities
2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09358-2_Ma.authors: Jauwairia Nasir & Aditi Kothiyal & Barbara Bruno
2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09358-2_Ma.summary_haiku: This study identifies three distinct multi-modal behavioral profiles of dyads engaged in collaborative open-ended learning with interactive tabletops and a robot mediator. Using combined learning analytics and interaction analysis on video, audio, and log data from 32 teams, researchers discovered two learning profiles—Expressive Explorers and Calm Tinkerers—and one non-learning profile, Silent Wanderers. Key findings reveal that speech overlap and reflection behaviors strongly distinguish learners from non-learners, while problem-solving strategy interacts with emotional expressivity to characterize different pathways to learning.
2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09358-2_Ma.evidence_span: methods (video, audio, log data; interaction analysis; learning analytics) + findings (behavioral profiles; speech overlap; reflection behaviors)
2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09358-2_Ma.coding_notes: Study combines micro-analytic coding of collaborative episodes (interaction_analysis) with trace data from tabletop and robot (learning_analytics, multimodal sensors). Primary unit is dyads; open-ended constructivist activity aligns with inquiry-based pedagogy. Sociocultural framing evident in focus on collaborative meaning-making and distributed cognition across human-robot-artifact system.

2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09454-7_Co.title: Collaboration in virtual and remote laboratories for education: A systematic literature review
2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09454-7_Co.summary_haiku: This systematic literature review examined 62 educational virtual and remote laboratories published 2011-2025 to assess collaboration support. While communication and group awareness tools are well-integrated, guidance and regulation tools remain underrepresented. Most laboratories support synchronous, non-co-located collaboration in STEM disciplines. Evaluation studies show predominantly positive learning outcomes, yet only one-third assess collaboration quality, indicating a significant research gap requiring future investigation.
2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09454-7_Co.evidence_span: abstract, methods (systematic review protocol), findings (tool categorization and outcome synthesis)
2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09454-7_Co.coding_notes: This is a systematic literature review that codes and synthesizes 62 primary studies on virtual/remote labs. The primary methodology is content analysis of published lab designs and evaluation reports. Secondary descriptive statistics summarize tool prevalence and learning outcomes. Unit of analysis is the lab artifact/platform itself and the cohorts studied within those labs. Pedagogy emphasizes structured collaboration (scripts) and inquiry-based STEM tasks. Technology spans shared workspaces (lab simulations), synchronous tools, and awareness features. No AI/LLM involvement in the review or technologies reviewed.

2022_v17i4_10.1007_s11412-022-09383-9_No.title: Novel CSCL design processes prompted by exploration of role‑playing and emotions
2022_v17i4_10.1007_s11412-022-09383-9_No.summary_haiku: This editorial synthesizes four empirical studies examining role-playing and emotions in computer-supported collaborative learning. Research employs behavioral trace analysis, epistemic network analysis, and content analysis to investigate how role-play scripts scaffold group regulation and how emotions function in digital discussions and knowledge-building. Findings demonstrate that targeted scripts promote learning behaviors, manipulatives foster perspective-taking, and emotions serve as dialogic instruments facilitating collaborative interactions.
2022_v17i4_10.1007_s11412-022-09383-9_No.coding_notes: Editorial synthesizing four empirical studies on role-play scripts and emotions in CSCL. Primary methodology coded as content_analysis because the editorial emphasizes systematic coding of discourse and behavioral traces; secondary methods include interaction_analysis (role-play episodes) and learning_analytics (trace data from digital platforms). Collaboration_scripts is the dominant pedagogy given explicit focus on role-play scaffolding; sociocultural theory underpins the work given emphasis on socially mediated learning and dialogic functions of emotion.

2022_v17i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09369-7_Pa.title: Patterns of action transitions in online collaborative problem solving: A network analysis approach
2022_v17i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09369-7_Pa.authors: Shupin Li & Johanna Poysa-Tarhonen & Paivi Hakkinen
2022_v17i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09369-7_Pa.summary_haiku: This study examined 166 Finnish sixth graders' action transition patterns during computer-based collaborative problem-solving using social network analysis. Researchers created transition networks from log file data and calculated network measures including density, centralization, and reciprocity. Results showed pairs with at least one member possessing high social and cognitive skills conducted significantly more actions with higher transition frequencies, suggesting more productive collaborative problem-solving than other pair compositions.
2022_v17i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09369-7_Pa.coding_notes: Study uses graph-based network analysis (density, centralization, reciprocity) on action transition patterns from log data, with learning analytics as secondary method. Primary unit is dyad pairs, though individual skill composition is also analyzed. Computer-based problem-solving environment suggests shared workspace technology.

2020_v15i4_10.1007_s11412-020-09333-3_Ga.title: Gaze awareness and metacognitive suggestions by a pedagogical conversational agent: an experimental investigation on interventions to support collaborative learning process and performance
2020_v15i4_10.1007_s11412-020-09333-3_Ga.summary_haiku: A 2×2 experimental study examined how real-time gaze feedback and pedagogical conversational agent suggestions independently and jointly affect collaborative learning. Eighty dyads completed a knowledge integration task while receiving various combinations of these interventions. Results showed gaze feedback more effectively facilitated coordination processes, while agent suggestions better improved learning gains. Combined interventions produced synergistic effects on performance, with successful coordination strongly predicting learning outcomes only when both supports were present.
2020_v15i4_10.1007_s11412-020-09333-3_Ga.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (2×2 experimental design), findings (gaze feedback, agent suggestions, synergistic effects)
2020_v15i4_10.1007_s11412-020-09333-3_Ga.coding_notes: Study is a controlled 2×2 factorial experiment with dyads as primary unit. Gaze tracking (eye-tracking sensor) and pedagogical conversational agent (LLM-like orchestration providing metacognitive suggestions) are core technologies. Collaboration scripts implicit in structured task and agent prompts. Sociocultural framing evident in focus on coordination and joint learning processes.

2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09452-9_Op.title: Optimizing group formation with a mixed genetic algorithm: an empirical study in active reading using marker data
2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09452-9_Op.authors: Changhao Liang & Yuko Toyokawa & Hiroaki Ogata
2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09452-9_Op.summary_haiku: A mixed genetic algorithm embedded in a learning platform optimizes group formation for EFL active reading by balancing homogeneous and heterogeneous student characteristics using marker data. Implemented in a Japanese high school classroom with 39 students, the system significantly improved vocabulary learning gains and demonstrated positive group dynamics through Wordcloud visualization, with 85% of students reporting the tool's helpfulness for collaborative tasks.
2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09452-9_Op.evidence_span: methods (genetic algorithm implementation, classroom design) + findings (vocabulary gains, group dynamics, student perception)
2025_v20i4_10.1007_s11412-025-09452-9_Op.coding_notes: The study uses a genetic algorithm (non-LLM AI) to optimize group formation and measures learning outcomes (vocabulary gains) and collaboration quality in a quasi-experimental classroom setting. The Wordcloud visualization and marker data suggest learning analytics and awareness features. Confidence is moderate because the paper emphasizes algorithmic optimization and empirical outcomes rather than deep discourse or interaction analysis.

2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09411-2_Th.title: The role of first‑language heterogeneity in the acquisition of online interaction self‑efficacy in CSCL
2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09411-2_Th.authors: Natalia Reich-Stiebert & Jennifer Raimann & Stefan Sturmer
2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09411-2_Th.summary_haiku: Students in linguistically heterogeneous CSCL groups exhibited lower gains in online interaction self-efficacy than those in homogeneous groups, regardless of their own language status. This nine-week pretest-posttest study of 1,525 distance education students found that task-related communication during initial collaboration moderated this negative effect, while social bonding activities paradoxically amplified perceived heterogeneity and impaired self-efficacy development.
2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09411-2_Th.evidence_span: methods (pretest-posttest design, 1,525 students, nine weeks) + findings (self-efficacy gains, moderation by task-related communication)
2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09411-2_Th.coding_notes: Study employs a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest design comparing linguistically homogeneous vs. heterogeneous groups, with inferential statistics testing moderation effects. Primary unit is individual learner self-efficacy outcomes, nested within groups. Pedagogy involves structured task-related communication and social bonding activities. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09444-9_Ed.title: Editorial notes: Unity in diversity at the CSCL crossroads
2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09444-9_Ed.summary_haiku: # Summary This editorial examines whether CSCL constitutes a unified scientific field or an interdisciplinary crossroads. Rather than seeking a single unifying framework, the authors argue CSCL exhibits "family resemblances"—partial commonalities across diverse theoretical and methodological approaches. Four featured articles demonstrate this diversity through temporal analysis of collaborative problem-solving, role dynamics, stance-taking in programming, and scripting/reflection scaffolding, collectively illustrating how CSCL research maintains creative vitality through methodological pluralism.
2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09444-9_Ed.coding_notes: This is an editorial/position paper reflecting on the CSCL field itself rather than reporting empirical research. It does not employ a primary research methodology, analyze a specific unit of learning, instantiate a particular pedagogy, or deploy technology. The article discusses methodological pluralism and theoretical diversity across four featured studies but does not itself conduct primary research. Coded as 'other' across dimensions because the article's primary function is meta-analytical commentary on the field rather than empirical investigation.

2016_v11i4_10.1007_s11412-016-9247-1_Col.title: Collaboration scripts and scaffolding
2016_v11i4_10.1007_s11412-016-9247-1_Col.authors: Sten Ludvigsen & Ulrike Cress & Nancy Law & Carolyn P. Rose & Gerry Stahl
2016_v11i4_10.1007_s11412-016-9247-1_Col.summary_haiku: This editorial examines four CSCL studies investigating computational support for collaborative learning. Research employs experimental designs, discourse analysis, and ethnographic methods to analyze group formation, automatic feedback, conversational agents, and interaction patterns. Findings demonstrate that computational tools effectively scaffold student learning when combined with teacher support, though students perceive automated interventions differently. Results highlight how design features leveraging text-mining, agent technology, and detailed interaction analysis enhance productive academic collaboration.
2016_v11i4_10.1007_s11412-016-9247-1_Col.evidence_span: title, abstract, summary of four constituent studies
2016_v11i4_10.1007_s11412-016-9247-1_Col.coding_notes: Editorial synthesizing four CSCL studies using computational scaffolding (text-mining, agents, interaction analysis). Mixed methods inferred from mention of experimental designs, discourse analysis, and ethnographic methods. AI involvement coded as non-LLM (conversational agents, text-mining) with potential LLM feedback component, though specific LLM use not explicitly confirmed in excerpt.

2023_v18i3_10.1007_s11412-023-09408-x_En.title: Enhancing student learning and achievement through orchestration of group processes and group composition
2023_v18i3_10.1007_s11412-023-09408-x_En.summary_haiku: This editorial examines how explicit and implicit scaffolding enhance collaborative learning. Four empirical studies demonstrate that supportive interventions promoting productive group processes—including self-regulated learning support in MOOCs, meta-discourse enrichment in knowledge building, and strategically designed peer feedback—significantly improve student learning and retention. Fine-grained peer matching by skill level proves particularly effective for optimizing collaborative outcomes.
2023_v18i3_10.1007_s11412-023-09408-x_En.evidence_span: title, abstract, editorial framing of four empirical studies
2023_v18i3_10.1007_s11412-023-09408-x_En.coding_notes: Editorial synthesizing multiple studies on scaffolding and group composition; mixed methods inferred from mention of multiple empirical studies with different designs. Peer matching and meta-discourse suggest structured collaboration and self-regulation. No explicit AI/LLM involvement mentioned in summary.

2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09299-x_Wh.title: What information should CSCL teacher dashboards provide to help teachers interpret CSCL situations?
2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09299-x_Wh.authors: Anouschka van Leeuwen & Nikol Rummel & Tamara van Gog
2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09299-x_Wh.summary_haiku: Teachers struggle to interpret collaborative learning situations from dashboards. This experimental study (n=53) compared three dashboard types—mirroring, alerting, and advising—examining how different support levels affect teachers' detection and interpretation of student collaboration problems in fraction tasks. Results showed dashboard type did not influence detection speed or accuracy, but advising dashboards significantly improved interpretation depth, with teachers adopting more analytical stances toward situations.
2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09299-x_Wh.evidence_span: methods (experimental design, n=53, three dashboard conditions) + findings (detection speed/accuracy, interpretation depth)
2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09299-x_Wh.coding_notes: Study is a controlled experiment manipulating dashboard design (mirroring, alerting, advising) to examine teacher interpretation of CSCL situations. Primary focus is teacher awareness and decision-making supported by visualization tools; secondary analysis likely involved coding teacher responses or interpretations (content analysis). No AI/LLM involvement detected.

2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9291-0_Dev.title: Developing understanding beyond the given knowledge and new methodologies for analyses in CSCL
2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9291-0_Dev.authors: Sten Ludvigsen & Ulrike Cress & Carolyn P. Rose & Nancy Law & Gerry Stahl
2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9291-0_Dev.summary_haiku: This editorial examines four papers addressing how students develop understanding beyond curriculum-provided knowledge using digital resources, and introduces new analytical methodologies for CSCL research. Key findings include: teacher scaffolding proves essential for student comprehension of computational artifacts; epistemic network analysis better captures temporal learning patterns than traditional coding-and-counting approaches; and theoretically-grounded big data methods reveal knowledge development mechanisms in collaborative online environments.
2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9291-0_Dev.coding_notes: This is an editorial/review article synthesizing four papers rather than reporting a single empirical study. It discusses methodological innovation (epistemic network analysis, big data methods) and theoretical frameworks without a bounded primary methodology, unit, pedagogy, or technology focus. The sociocultural and activity-theory framing reflects the CSCL field's dominant theoretical orientation.

2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09415-y_Re.title: Reflecting on what counts as collaboration: Reaching forward without losing what is behind
2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09415-y_Re.summary_haiku: This editorial reflection examines the core question "What counts as collaboration?" within computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL). Through qualitative analysis of journal submissions over four years, the authors identify four emerging themes: new technologies enabling collaboration, multimodal data collection methods, societal responsiveness including equity concerns, and generative artificial intelligence integration. The work argues CSCL must balance theoretical grounding with openness to innovation while maintaining disciplinary identity.
2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09415-y_Re.evidence_span: abstract, methods (qualitative analysis of journal submissions), findings (four emerging themes)
2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09415-y_Re.coding_notes: This is a meta-analytical editorial reflection on CSCL research trends rather than an empirical study of learner collaboration. Primary methodology is systematic coding of journal submissions (content_analysis); unit is the corpus of published articles/discourse traces. Technology_primary coded as 'other' because the editorial discusses technology broadly as a theme rather than studying a specific technology. AI involvement is secondary (mentioned as an emerging theme) but coded as llm_supported_analytics since the editorial itself may use AI for analysis of submissions.

2021_v16i3_10.1007_s11412-021-09354-6_So.title: Socio‑technical configurations for productive talk
2021_v16i3_10.1007_s11412-021-09354-6_So.summary_haiku: CSCL research employs collaboration scripts, prompting, and awareness technologies to foster productive talk in group learning. This editorial reviews four studies demonstrating methodological maturity through synergistic integration of quantitative and qualitative approaches, particularly Epistemic Network Analysis and Social Network Analysis. Research ranges from small-scale classroom interventions to large-scale museum studies and year-long knowledge-building projects, establishing that structural-configurational methods enable theory testing beyond data description.
2021_v16i3_10.1007_s11412-021-09354-6_So.evidence_span: title, abstract, editorial framing of four reviewed studies
2021_v16i3_10.1007_s11412-021-09354-6_So.coding_notes: This is an editorial reviewing multiple CSCL studies on productive talk. Primary methodology is mixed_methods because the editorial explicitly highlights synergistic integration of quantitative and qualitative approaches (Epistemic Network Analysis + Social Network Analysis). Primary pedagogy is collaboration_scripts as the editorial identifies scripts, prompting, and awareness as core interventions. Primary technology is awareness_dashboard given emphasis on awareness technologies. No AI/LLM involvement evident in the editorial's scope.

2020_v15i4_10.1007_s11412-020-09331-5_So.title: Social practices in teacher knowledge creation and innovation adoption: a large-scale study in an online instructional design community for inquiry learning
2020_v15i4_10.1007_s11412-020-09331-5_So.authors: Luis P. Prieto & Tobias Ley & Ton de Jong & Maria Jesus Rodriguez-Triana & Denis Gillet
2020_v15i4_10.1007_s11412-020-09331-5_So.summary_haiku: This large-scale study analyzed 40,235 inquiry learning designs created in Graasp, an online platform used by 35,000+ teachers, to examine how social practices relate to classroom implementation of pedagogical innovations. Using the Knowledge Appropriation Model framework, researchers found that knowledge maturation, expert scaffolding, and knowledge appropriation practices were significantly associated with increased adoption rates of learning designs in classrooms, with maturation showing the strongest effect.
2020_v15i4_10.1007_s11412-020-09331-5_So.coding_notes: Study uses trace data from 40,235 learning designs on Graasp platform to model adoption patterns; Knowledge Appropriation Model and focus on social practices in a large online teacher community align with knowledge-building and distributed cognition frameworks. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

2025_v20i3_10.1007_s11412-025-09445-8_Me.title: Measuring the quality of collaborative group engagement: Development and validation of the QCGE self‑assessment scale (QCGE‑SAS)
2025_v20i3_10.1007_s11412-025-09445-8_Me.authors: Loris T. Jeitziner & Lisa Paneth & Oliver Rack & Susanne Bleisch & Carmen Zahn
2025_v20i3_10.1007_s11412-025-09445-8_Me.summary_haiku: This study developed and validated the QCGE-SAS, a 13-item self-assessment scale measuring quality of collaborative group engagement across four dimensions: behavioral, social, cognitive, and conceptual-to-consequential engagement. Using confirmatory factor analysis with 246 higher education students, the scale demonstrated good model fit and construct validity through correlations with related measures. Three subscales showed acceptable reliability; however, the social engagement subscale exhibited suboptimal internal consistency, warranting future refinement.
2025_v20i3_10.1007_s11412-025-09445-8_Me.evidence_span: methods (CFA, scale development) + findings (model fit, reliability, validity)
2025_v20i3_10.1007_s11412-025-09445-8_Me.coding_notes: Study is primarily a psychometric validation using confirmatory factor analysis and correlation analysis with 246 students. The scale measures self-reported collaborative engagement dimensions; unit of analysis is individual learners reporting on their group experience. Sociocultural framing implicit in engagement construct; no explicit technology platform or AI involvement reported.

2016_v11i2_10.1007_s11412-016-9236-4_CSC.title: CSCL: connecting the social, emotional and cognitive dimensions
2016_v11i2_10.1007_s11412-016-9236-4_CSC.summary_haiku: This editorial examines how computer-supported collaborative learning integrates social, emotional, and cognitive dimensions. It identifies four core themes: how collaboration emerges and builds common ground, the interplay of emotions and identities in learning, group formation and performance prediction, and shared understanding through mutual modeling. The analysis emphasizes that emotions function within cognitive work, identities shape knowledge construction, machine learning can predict group performance, and mutual modeling requires bidirectional awareness.
2016_v11i2_10.1007_s11412-016-9236-4_CSC.coding_notes: This is an editorial/position paper synthesizing CSCL research themes rather than reporting original empirical work. No specific methodology, unit of analysis, or pedagogy is instantiated; the piece is conceptual and integrative. Sociocultural and socio-cognitive theories are invoked to frame the social-emotional-cognitive nexus.

2024_v19i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09433-4_CS.title: CSCL: a learning and collaboration science?
2024_v19i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09433-4_CS.summary_haiku: # Summary Computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) has evolved significantly over thirty years. Collaboration now operates at larger scales with asynchronous, technology-mediated interactions across epistemic communities, rather than small synchronous groups. To address theoretical fragmentation across interdisciplinary frameworks, the authors propose adopting formalized languages—particularly Bayesian Networks—as a unifying approach. This formalization enables explicit theorizing, generative modeling, and counterfactual reasoning, exemplified through shared meaning-making analysis, strengthening CSCL's scientific foundation.
2024_v19i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09433-4_CS.coding_notes: This is a theoretical/position paper proposing formalized languages (Bayesian Networks) as a unifying framework for CSCL rather than reporting empirical research. Methodology is conceptual analysis and theory synthesis; unit of analysis is the CSCL field itself. Coded pedagogy and technology as representative of CSCL's scope, but the paper's primary contribution is metatheoretical rather than empirical.

2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09310-5_Re.title: Real-time orchestrational technologies in
2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09310-5_Re.summary_haiku: Real-time dashboards in computer-supported collaborative learning environments enable teachers to monitor student progress and provide timely, targeted guidance during complex collaborative activities. This special issue examines five empirical studies investigating how real-time data visualization supports classroom orchestration, finding that effective designs partner with teachers rather than replace their functions, balance automated support with teacher autonomy, and require participatory design involving educators throughout development.
2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09310-5_Re.evidence_span: title, abstract, and summary describing real-time dashboards, teacher monitoring, classroom orchestration, and participatory design
2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09310-5_Re.coding_notes: This is a special issue editorial/overview examining five empirical studies on real-time orchestrational dashboards. The primary focus is on teacher awareness and decision-making during collaborative learning, supported by data visualization tools. Design-based research is inferred from the emphasis on iterative, participatory design involving educators; learning analytics is secondary because trace data visualization is central to the intervention.

2021_v16i1_10.1007_s11412-021-09342-w_Ex.title: Exploring multilayered collaboration designs
2021_v16i1_10.1007_s11412-021-09342-w_Ex.authors: Nancy Law & Sanna Jarvela & Carolyn Rose
2021_v16i1_10.1007_s11412-021-09342-w_Ex.summary_haiku: This editorial examines how multilayered collaboration designs scaffold productive learning through socio-organizational and technological supports. Analyzing four empirical studies, the authors demonstrate that layering different social units (individual, intra-group, inter-group, whole-class) and technological tools (awareness tools, adaptive prompts, multitouch interfaces) effectively regulates collaborative processes. Findings reveal that pedagogical scripting and interface design significantly influence collaboration quality and regulatory behaviors, though spontaneous regulatory action requires explicit support.
2021_v16i1_10.1007_s11412-021-09342-w_Ex.evidence_span: abstract, editorial framing, and empirical study descriptions
2021_v16i1_10.1007_s11412-021-09342-w_Ex.coding_notes: This is an editorial synthesizing four empirical studies rather than a single primary study. The primary methodology is coded as content_analysis because the editorial systematically examines and compares findings across studies. The multilayered design focus and explicit attention to socio-organizational scaffolding across individual, group, and class levels justify cross_level_multilevel as the primary unit of analysis. Collaboration scripts and awareness tools are central to the designs reviewed.

2025_v20i3_10.1007_s11412-025-09447-6_Un.title: Understanding the role of I‑positions facilitating knowledge construction in a computer‑supported collaborative learning environment
2025_v20i3_10.1007_s11412-025-09447-6_Un.authors: Aaron J. Peltoniemi & Joni Lamsa & Sami Lehesvuori
2025_v20i3_10.1007_s11412-025-09447-6_Un.summary_haiku: This qualitative study applies discourse analysis and dialogical self theory to investigate how interpersonal and intrapersonal voices facilitate knowledge construction in computer-supported collaborative learning. Analyzing ten physics students in two groups, researchers identified discourse functions and I-positions (I–it, I–me, I–you, I–we) within dialogues. The successful group employed both interpersonal and intrapersonal voices, with intrapersonal voices peaking during empirical evaluation, while the unsuccessful group relied predominantly on interpersonal voices focused on individual-level concerns rather than collective elaboration.
2025_v20i3_10.1007_s11412-025-09447-6_Un.coding_notes: Study explicitly applies discourse analysis and dialogical self theory to examine I-positions and voices in collaborative dialogue. Primary unit is two small groups of physics students; analysis focuses on discourse functions and interpersonal/intrapersonal voices as artifacts. Knowledge building and argumentation are implicit in the focus on collective elaboration and empirical evaluation.

2020_v15i2_10.1007_s11412-020-09322-6_Ca.title: Capturing the participation and social dimensions of
2020_v15i2_10.1007_s11412-020-09322-6_Ca.authors: Mohammed Saqr & Olga Viberg & Henriikka Vartiainen
2020_v15i2_10.1007_s11412-020-09322-6_Ca.summary_haiku: This study validates social network analysis centrality measures for analyzing computer-supported collaborative learning. Using data from 12 university courses with 598 students, researchers examined how different network configurations (multigraph, simplified, weighted) affect the reproducibility of centrality measures as indicators of student performance. Results show multigraph configuration produces the most consistent and robust measures, with degree centralities reliably indicating participation and eigenvector centrality consistently reflecting social dimensions across configurations.
2020_v15i2_10.1007_s11412-020-09322-6_Ca.coding_notes: Study is methodological validation of SNA centrality measures applied to CSCL data across 12 courses (n=598). Primary focus is on network configuration effects on reproducibility of centrality indices as proxies for participation and social position; no specific pedagogical intervention or technology platform is the focus. Distributed cognition and sociocultural framing implicit in treating collaboration as network-embedded social activity.

2017_v12i2_10.1007_s11412-017-9257-7_Fra.title: Frameworks for mass collaboration, adaptable scripts, complex systems theory, and collaborative writing
2017_v12i2_10.1007_s11412-017-9257-7_Fra.authors: Sten Ludvigsen & Nancy Law & Carolyn P. Rose & Gerry Stahl
2017_v12i2_10.1007_s11412-017-9257-7_Fra.summary_haiku: This editorial examines four emerging themes in computer-supported collaborative learning: mass collaboration frameworks, complex adaptive systems theory, adaptable scripting for self-regulation, and collaborative writing processes. The authors synthesize research using diverse methodologies—including experimental designs and multi-method analyses—to demonstrate how different interaction types, self-organization principles, adaptive scripts, and non-linear writing phases contribute to understanding collaborative learning phenomena.
2017_v12i2_10.1007_s11412-017-9257-7_Fra.evidence_span: title, abstract, editorial framing of four themes
2017_v12i2_10.1007_s11412-017-9257-7_Fra.coding_notes: This is a synthetic editorial synthesizing multiple research streams rather than a single empirical study. The primary methodology is coded as mixed_methods because the editorial explicitly references diverse methodologies (experimental designs, multi-method analyses). Unit of analysis is cross_level because the themes span individual self-regulation, small-group interaction, and mass/community-scale collaboration. Pedagogy emphasizes adaptable scripts and self-regulation; theory draws on activity theory (complex systems, self-organization) and sociocultural perspectives. No AI/LLM involvement evident in the 2017 timeframe and editorial scope.

2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09348-4_Fo.title: Forms of collaboration matters: CSCL across the contexts
2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09348-4_Fo.summary_haiku: This editorial examines how different forms of collaboration function across diverse contexts in computer-supported collaborative learning. Through four empirical studies and a position paper, the authors analyze collaboration using network analysis, instructional representations, and awareness tools. Key findings reveal that transitivity and contact duration influence partner selection, network visualizations scaffold historical reasoning, combined awareness information enhances learning outcomes, and teacher guidance significantly impacts collaborative processes. The authors advocate for integrating cognitive and social perspectives while prioritizing social sensitivity in CSCL research.
2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09348-4_Fo.evidence_span: abstract, editorial framing, empirical studies overview
2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09348-4_Fo.coding_notes: This is an editorial synthesizing four empirical studies on collaboration forms across contexts. Network analysis is prominent (partner selection, transitivity, contact duration); awareness tools and instructional representations are analyzed. Teacher guidance and social sensitivity are emphasized, suggesting sociocultural framing. Confidence is moderate because the editorial summarizes diverse methodologies; primary coding reflects the dominant analytical approach (network analysis) and the cross-level focus (individual choices within group/classroom structures).

2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09387-z_An.title: An artificial intelligence-driven learning analytics method to examine the collaborative problem-solving process from the complex adaptive systems perspective
2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09387-z_An.authors: Fan Ouyang & Weiqi Xu & Mutlu Cukurova
2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09387-z_An.summary_haiku: This study proposes a three-layered AI-driven analytical framework integrating learning analytics to examine collaborative problem-solving from a complex adaptive systems perspective. Analyzing multimodal data from 24 online group sessions using optimal matching, clustering, and hidden Markov modeling, researchers identified three distinct collaborative patterns: behavior-oriented (medium performance), communication-behavior-synergistic (high performance), and communication-oriented (low performance), revealing the multimodal, dynamic, and synergistic nature of group collaboration.
2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09387-z_An.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (multimodal data, optimal matching, clustering, hidden Markov modeling), findings (three collaborative patterns)
2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09387-z_An.coding_notes: The study is fundamentally a learning analytics investigation using AI-driven methods (optimal matching, clustering, HMM) to analyze multimodal trace data from online collaborative problem-solving sessions. The complex adaptive systems framing and dynamic pattern identification align with sequence/process mining and distributed cognition theory. AI involvement is primarily in analytics/pattern detection rather than LLM-based feedback or orchestration.

2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09439-y_Co.title: Correction: Collaborative Problem‑Solving in Knowledge‑Rich Domains: A Multi‑Study Structural Equation Model
2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09439-y_Co.authors: Laura Brandl & Matthias Stadler & Constanze Richters & Anika Radkowitsch & Martin R. Fischer & Ralf Schmidmaier & Frank Fischer
2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09439-y_Co.summary_haiku: This is a correction notice for a structural equation modeling study examining collaborative problem-solving in knowledge-rich domains. The original article contained a sign error in Table 5, where most coefficients were incorrectly prefixed with negative signs. The corrected version has been published online.
2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09439-y_Co.coding_notes: This is a correction notice rather than a full research article; the original study used structural equation modeling (SEM) to examine collaborative problem-solving in dyads or small groups within knowledge-rich domains. Pedagogy inferred from 'collaborative problem-solving' framing; technology assumed minimal given no mention of digital tools in the excerpt. Confidence is moderate due to limited detail available in the correction notice alone.

2019_v14i4_10.1007_s11412-019-09313-2_Ca.title: Capturing the dynamic and cyclical nature of regulation: Methodological Progress in understanding socially shared regulation in learning
2019_v14i4_10.1007_s11412-019-09313-2_Ca.summary_haiku: This review examines methodological progress in researching socially shared regulation (SSRL) of learning in collaborative and computer-supported collaborative learning contexts. The authors identify three key challenges: capturing regulation's cyclical, temporal nature; understanding how self-regulation, co-regulation, and SSRL jointly contribute to learning; and studying SSRL in authentic contexts. They advocate for multimodal data collection methods, technological tools for prompting regulation, and analyzing learning challenges as triggers for regulatory processes.
2019_v14i4_10.1007_s11412-019-09313-2_Ca.evidence_span: abstract, introduction, and methodological discussion sections
2019_v14i4_10.1007_s11412-019-09313-2_Ca.coding_notes: This is a methodological review article examining SSRL research rather than an empirical study. The primary methodology reflects the mixed-methods nature of studies reviewed and the emphasis on capturing temporal, cyclical regulation through multimodal data. Secondary units reflect the nested individual-group-class dynamics central to SSRL theory.

2025_v20i3_10.1007_s11412-025-09446-7_Ac.title: Activity‑based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning
2025_v20i3_10.1007_s11412-025-09446-7_Ac.summary_haiku: Paulsen and Davidsen propose Activity-Based Collaborative Virtual Reality (ABC-VR), a conceptual framework grounded in activity theory for designing and researching collaborative learning in immersive 360-degree video environments. Unlike existing individual-focused concepts, ABC-VR emphasizes social knowledge construction through analyzing recorded real-world activities at multiple levels—examining what actions occur, how they're performed, and why. The framework positions learners collaboratively engaging with situated practices from educational, social, and work contexts.
2025_v20i3_10.1007_s11412-025-09446-7_Ac.coding_notes: This is a conceptual/theoretical paper proposing ABC-VR framework grounded in activity theory for immersive VR collaborative learning. Coded as design-based research because it presents a framework for designing and researching interventions; however, the excerpt does not clearly indicate empirical implementation or iteration. Technology coded as tabletop_tangible_interface as a proxy for immersive 360-degree video environments (closest fit for embodied, situated collaborative spaces), though 'other' might be more precise. Confidence moderate due to reliance on summary rather than full paper methods section.

2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-025-09463-6_Ad.title: Advancing collaborative discourse through knowledge synthesis
2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-025-09463-6_Ad.authors: Xinran Zhu & Bodong Chen & David DeLiema
2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-025-09463-6_Ad.summary_haiku: # Summary This study investigates a knowledge synthesis intervention designed to support collaborative discourse in a graduate course. Using qualitative methods including content and interaction analysis, researchers examined how students' individual synthesis artifacts—created from social annotations—facilitated group collaboration. Findings reveal that synthesis artifacts guided discourse progression, enabled key knowledge practices, and supported group artifact development, though effectiveness depended on both artifact quality and collaborative engagement patterns.
2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-025-09463-6_Ad.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (qualitative, content and interaction analysis), findings (discourse progression, knowledge practices, group artifacts)
2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-025-09463-6_Ad.coding_notes: Study uses qualitative interaction and content analysis of collaborative discourse around synthesis artifacts from social annotations. Primary focus is on how artifacts mediate group collaboration and knowledge practices, aligning with knowledge-building theory and distributed cognition. Secondary methods include discourse analysis. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9286-x_Ren.title: Rendering controversial socioscientific issues legible through digital mapping tools
2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9286-x_Ren.authors: Asa Makitalo & Thomas Hillman & Anne Solli
2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9286-x_Ren.summary_haiku: Digital mapping tools developed for Science and Technology Studies enable upper secondary students to collaboratively explore controversial socioscientific issues online. Through video analysis of students using network visualization software (Gephi), researchers found that tool-mediated activity slowed categorization processes, prompting productive negotiation of how to interpret controversies. Misalignments between algorithmic tool logic and students' content-focused reasoning generated valuable collaborative discussion about distinguishing controversies from their visualizations.
2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9286-x_Ren.evidence_span: methods (video analysis, Gephi tool use) + findings (negotiation, misalignments, collaborative discussion)
2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9286-x_Ren.coding_notes: Study uses video analysis of moment-by-moment collaborative episodes with digital mapping tools (Gephi network visualization). Primary focus is on how tool-mediated activity shapes student reasoning about controversial issues through interaction. Sociocultural framing emphasizes mediation by cultural tools; distributed cognition captures how cognition is distributed across students, the tool, and the controversy representation.

2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09397-x_Co.title: Coordinating modalities of mathematical collaboration in shared VR environments
2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09397-x_Co.authors: Wen Huang & Candace Walkington & Mitchell J. Nathan
2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09397-x_Co.summary_haiku: This study examines how in-service teachers collaboratively construct geometric knowledge in shared VR environments using a novel multimodal analysis method. Analyzing 108 episodes across three groups, researchers identified strong simultaneous relationships between actions on virtual objects and collaborative speech, plus five emergent interaction themes. Results demonstrate that virtual objects effectively mediate collaborative knowledge-building, with structured activity design and moderate avatar realism supporting equitable, adaptable learning.
2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09397-x_Co.evidence_span: methods (multimodal analysis of 108 episodes), findings (interaction themes, object-mediated collaboration)
2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09397-x_Co.coding_notes: Study employs fine-grained interaction analysis of moment-by-moment collaborative episodes in VR, examining how virtual objects mediate knowledge construction. Multimodal analysis integrates speech, gesture, and object manipulation; distributed cognition and knowledge-building theory align with emphasis on object-mediated collaborative knowledge construction.

2024_v19i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09427-2_Kn.title: Knowledge creation through maker practices and the role of teacher and peer support in collaborative invention projects
2024_v19i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09427-2_Kn.authors: Sini Davies & Pirita Seitamaa-Hakkarainen & Kai Hakkarainen
2024_v19i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09427-2_Kn.summary_haiku: Student teams engaged in open-ended collaborative invention projects applied maker practices—design, computer engineering, product design, and science—in iterative, nonlinear processes. Video analysis of three seventh-grade teams revealed that embodied practices like sketching and material experimentation were essential for advancing shared epistemic objects. Teacher scaffolding and peer tutoring effectively supported knowledge creation, though excessive direction could oversimplify designs and reduce engagement.
2024_v19i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09427-2_Kn.evidence_span: methods (video analysis of three teams) + findings (embodied practices, scaffolding effects)
2024_v19i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09427-2_Kn.coding_notes: Video analysis of moment-by-moment collaborative episodes in maker projects is core interaction_analysis. Open-ended invention projects with iterative design processes align with inquiry-based learning. Embodied sketching and material experimentation reflect distributed cognition across people and artifacts; teacher scaffolding and peer tutoring are key sociocultural supports.

2018_v13i3_10.1007_s11412-018-9284-z_For.title: Forming social systems by coupling minds at different levels of cognition: Design, tools, and research methods
2018_v13i3_10.1007_s11412-018-9284-z_For.authors: U. Cress & G. Stahl & C. Rose & N. Law & S. Ludvigsen
2018_v13i3_10.1007_s11412-018-9284-z_For.summary_haiku: This article examines how digital tools and collaborative learning environments couple individual minds at different cognitive levels—visual attention, core cognition, metacognition, and activities. Through four empirical studies employing eye-tracking, knowledge integration frameworks, scripting, and activity analysis, the research demonstrates that coupling processes at all four levels correlate with improved task performance. Scripts and visualizations emerge as effective mechanisms for facilitating collaborative mind-coupling across these distinct information-processing stages.
2018_v13i3_10.1007_s11412-018-9284-z_For.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (eye-tracking, scripts, visualizations), findings (coupling at multiple cognitive levels)
2018_v13i3_10.1007_s11412-018-9284-z_For.coding_notes: The study explicitly uses eye-tracking and multimodal sensors to capture visual attention alongside interaction analysis of collaborative episodes. Scripts and visualizations are core design mechanisms. The theoretical framing emphasizes coupling minds across distributed cognitive levels, aligning with distributed cognition and information-processing perspectives. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09407-y_Ca.title: Can CPS better prepare 8th graders for problem‑solving in electromagnetism and bridging the gap between high‑ and low‑achievers than IPS?
2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09407-y_Ca.authors: Jiun-Wei Guo & Hsiao-Ching She & Meng-Jun Chen & Pei-Yi Tsai
2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09407-y_Ca.summary_haiku: This study compared collaborative problem-solving (CPS) and individual problem-solving (IPS) approaches in an online electromagnetism unit with 109 eighth graders. Using simulation-based instruction across five classes, researchers found CPS significantly enhanced problem-solving performance compared to IPS, while both equally improved conceptual understanding. Critically, CPS more effectively boosted low-achievers' performance and narrowed achievement gaps, as low-achievers received greater peer support during collaboration.
2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09407-y_Ca.evidence_span: methods (design comparing CPS vs IPS conditions) + findings (performance gains, achievement gap narrowing)
2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09407-y_Ca.coding_notes: Study employs a quasi-experimental comparison of two conditions (CPS vs IPS) with inferential statistics to test hypotheses about problem-solving performance and equity. Primary unit is dyadic/small-group collaboration, with secondary focus on individual learner outcomes. Simulation-based instruction suggests shared digital workspace; no AI/LLM involvement detected.

2017_v12i3_10.1007_s11412-017-9265-7_Div.title: Divisive or facilitative: The two faces of technology in CSCL
2017_v12i3_10.1007_s11412-017-9265-7_Div.authors: Carolyn P. Rose & Sten Ludvigsen & Nancy Law & Ulrike Cress & Gerry Stahl
2017_v12i3_10.1007_s11412-017-9265-7_Div.summary_haiku: Technology in computer-supported collaborative learning functions as both divisive and facilitative. This editorial examines four empirical studies across diverse domains using qualitative and quantitative methods. While one study reveals how students may dysfunctionally position themselves around technology to gain power, three studies demonstrate technology's positive potential through script-based scaffolding interventions supporting regulation, argumentation, and peer feedback in collaborative learning contexts.
2017_v12i3_10.1007_s11412-017-9265-7_Div.evidence_span: title, abstract, editorial framing of four empirical studies
2017_v12i3_10.1007_s11412-017-9265-7_Div.coding_notes: This is an editorial synthesizing four empirical studies rather than a single primary study. Coding reflects the dominant patterns across the reviewed work: mixed methods (qualitative and quantitative), small-group collaboration with script-based scaffolding, and sociocultural framing. Confidence is moderate because the editorial's own methodology is synthetic rather than presenting original data collection.

2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9242-6_Fut.title: Future-looking conversations in CSCL
2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9242-6_Fut.authors: Sten Ludvigsen & Ulrike Cress & Nancy Law & Carolyn P. Rose & Gerry Stahl
2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9242-6_Fut.summary_haiku: This editorial surveys emerging research directions in computer-supported collaborative learning, highlighting four key articles addressing socially shared regulation, support for low-achieving students, epistemic games, and script theory. The authors identify future challenges including longer timescale studies, methodological innovations, authentic real-world contexts, semiotic analysis of complex artifacts, and connections to twenty-first-century skills development.
2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9242-6_Fut.evidence_span: editorial abstract and framing of four key research directions
2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9242-6_Fut.coding_notes: This is an editorial survey rather than an empirical study, so methodology and unit assignments reflect the dominant themes across the four highlighted articles (socially shared regulation, support for low-achieving students, epistemic games, script theory). Confidence is moderate because the editorial itself does not conduct original research; coding reflects the research landscape it describes.

2024_v19i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09424-5_Th.title: The perceptions of task cohesion in collaborative learning teams
2024_v19i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09424-5_Th.authors: Andrew Zamecnik & Georg Grossmann & Djazia Ladjal & Abelardo Pardo
2024_v19i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09424-5_Th.summary_haiku: # Summary This mixed-methods study examined task cohesion development in 194 collaborative learning teams using temporal network motif analysis combined with survey data. Teams were classified into four transition groups based on cohesion perception changes across a three-week work-integrated learning program. Findings revealed that teams maintaining aligned perceptions demonstrated higher performance and greater triadic interaction patterns, while teams with divergent perceptions showed lower performance and dyadic interactions. Temporal network motifs proved effective as proxies for task cohesion, validating the approach for understanding team dynamics in collaborative learning environments.
2024_v19i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09424-5_Th.evidence_span: title, summary, methods (temporal network motif analysis + survey), findings (team classification, interaction patterns, performance)
2024_v19i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09424-5_Th.coding_notes: Study combines quantitative network analysis (temporal motifs) with qualitative survey data on team perceptions. Primary unit is collaborative teams (dyads/small groups); secondary cross-level analysis examines individual perception alignment within teams. Technology is learning analytics platform capturing interaction traces; pedagogy emphasizes structured team work and self-regulation of cohesion.

2024_v19i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09419-2_CS.title: CSCL has come of age
2024_v19i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09419-2_CS.summary_haiku: Computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) has matured into normal science after nearly thirty years of development. Baker and Reimann argue that CSCL's foundational triadic object—collaboration, task, and technology—remains established yet constantly evolving. They propose three strategic connections: linking theory with design through design science research methodology, bridging theory and data via computational modeling, and connecting research with educational practice through knowledge brokering. These interconnected approaches aim to advance CSCL's theoretical foundations while enhancing practical utility for educators.
2024_v19i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09419-2_CS.coding_notes: This is a position/review article proposing strategic directions for CSCL research rather than reporting empirical findings. Coding reflects the triadic framework (collaboration, task, technology) and emphasis on design science, computational modeling, and knowledge brokering as methodological bridges. Primary choices reflect the article's focus on design-practice integration and theory-driven intervention; secondary choices capture the multi-level and mixed-method orientation implied by the three strategic connections.

2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-026-09474-x_Co.title: Correction: A temporal network approach to reveal the longitudinal dynamics of CSCL group regulation and productive collaboration
2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-026-09474-x_Co.summary_haiku: This is a correction notice for a research article on temporal network analysis in computer-supported collaborative learning. The original study examined longitudinal dynamics of group regulation and productive collaboration using temporal network methods. The correction addresses a production error where Figure 2 inadvertently duplicated Figure 1, now providing the correct visualization to accurately represent the research findings.
2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-026-09474-x_Co.coding_notes: This is a correction notice rather than a full research article, limiting detail available for coding. The original study's focus on temporal network analysis of group regulation and longitudinal dynamics strongly suggests sequence_process_mining and social_network_analysis as primary methodologies. Group regulation and productive collaboration align with self-peer regulation pedagogy. Sociocultural and activity theory are inferred from the CSCL context and group-level analysis, though full theoretical framing cannot be confirmed from the correction notice alone.

2019_v14i4_10.1007_s11412-019-09312-3_Re.title: Reflections and looking ahead for CSCL: digital infrastructures, digital tools, and collaborative learning
2019_v14i4_10.1007_s11412-019-09312-3_Re.summary_haiku: This editorial examines CSCL's evolution as an interdisciplinary field, arguing that future research must integrate digital infrastructures, digital tools, and human collaboration through expanded units of analysis. The authors advocate for studies addressing intersubjectivity, student agency in complex problem-solving, design for learner variation, and scaling CSCL interventions to influence educational policy and practice across diverse contexts.
2019_v14i4_10.1007_s11412-019-09312-3_Re.coding_notes: This is an editorial/position paper reflecting on CSCL as a field rather than reporting empirical research. No specific methodology, unit of analysis, pedagogy, or technology is studied; instead, the piece synthesizes and advocates for future directions. Sociocultural and dialogic theories are implicit in CSCL's foundational orientation; activity theory is relevant to the call for examining complex systems and infrastructures.

2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09430-7_Co.title: Comparing the effects of a collaboration script and collaborative reflection on promoting knowledge about good collaboration and effective interaction
2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09430-7_Co.authors: Sebastian Strauss & Isis Tunnigkeit & Julia Eberle & Arlind Avdullahu & Nikol Rummel
2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09430-7_Co.doi: Comparing the effects of a collaboration script and collaborative reflection on promoting knowledge about good collaboration and effective interaction
2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09430-7_Co.summary_haiku: This experimental study compared external collaboration scripts and reflection scaffolds for fostering collaboration skills in 150 university students working in groups. Using multilevel modeling, researchers found that learners receiving collaborative reflection gained significantly more knowledge about effective collaboration than those using scripts or no support. However, neither intervention improved subsequent interaction quality. Results suggest reflection-based approaches may offer autonomy-supportive alternatives to directive scripting for knowledge acquisition.
2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09430-7_Co.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (experimental design, multilevel modeling), findings (knowledge gains, interaction quality)
2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09430-7_Co.coding_notes: Study is a controlled experimental comparison of two interventions (collaboration script vs. collaborative reflection) plus control, with multilevel modeling to account for nested group structure. Primary pedagogy is collaboration scripts, but reflection is equally prominent; coded scripts as primary since it is explicitly compared. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09438-z_Di.title: Disagreeing softly: Supporting students in managing disagreement in peer critique
2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09438-z_Di.authors: Jinzhi Zhou & Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver & Zach Ryan & Christina Stiso & Danielle Murphy & Joshua Danish & Clark A. Chinn & Ravit Golan Duncan
2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09438-z_Di.summary_haiku: Fifth-grade students engaged in peer critique within a computer-supported collaborative learning environment predominantly used soft disagreements (64%) rather than direct forms when critiquing groupmates' scientific models. Using conversation analysis, researchers found that students effectively resolved disagreements consensually in 88.6% of episodes, advancing collective knowledge through both direct and soft disagreement forms, while maintaining positive group dynamics.
2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09438-z_Di.evidence_span: methods (conversation analysis) + findings (disagreement patterns, resolution rates)
2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09438-z_Di.coding_notes: Conversation analysis of peer critique episodes is the core methodology. The study examines moment-by-moment interaction patterns (soft vs. direct disagreement) and their resolution within small collaborative groups critiquing scientific models. Dialogic theory is primary because the work centers on how disagreement is negotiated through multi-voiced dialogue; sociocultural framing is secondary given the emphasis on peer interaction and collective knowledge advancement.

2018_v13i2_10.1007_s11412-018-9277-y_Fro.title: From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory
2018_v13i2_10.1007_s11412-018-9277-y_Fro.authors: Paul A. Kirschner & John Sweller & Femke Kirschner & Jimmy Zambrano R
2018_v13i2_10.1007_s11412-018-9277-y_Fro.summary_haiku: Cognitive load theory, traditionally focused on individual learning, is extended to collaborative learning by incorporating the concept of collective working memory and transactive activities. The authors argue that collaboration reduces cognitive load when tasks exceed individual working memory capacity, but transactive costs of communication and coordination can negate benefits. Design principles for effective collaborative learning must consider task complexity, team composition, prior experience, and domain expertise.
2018_v13i2_10.1007_s11412-018-9277-y_Fro.evidence_span: abstract and conceptual framework; no empirical methods or findings reported
2018_v13i2_10.1007_s11412-018-9277-y_Fro.coding_notes: This is a theoretical extension paper synthesizing cognitive load theory for collaborative contexts. No empirical study, controlled experiment, or data analysis is evident; the article presents conceptual principles and design heuristics. Coded as descriptive because it organizes and describes existing theory rather than testing hypotheses or analyzing new data.

2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09330-6_Br.title: Bringing maker practices to school: tracing discursive and materially mediated aspects of student teams’ collaborative making processes
2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09330-6_Br.authors: Pirita Seitamaa-Hakkarainen & Kai Hakkarainen & Sini Riikonen
2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09330-6_Br.summary_haiku: This study examined how seventh-grade student teams engaged in collaborative making projects using digital and traditional fabrication technologies. Researchers developed the Making-Process-Rug video analysis method to trace social-discursive and materially mediated aspects of five teams' co-invention processes. Four successful teams demonstrated iterative cycles integrating model making with focused discussion, while the unsuccessful team lacked substantive prototyping. Shared epistemic objects and well-organized collaboration processes proved essential for successful co-invention.
2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09330-6_Br.evidence_span: methods (Making-Process-Rug video analysis, five teams) + findings (iterative cycles, epistemic objects, collaboration processes)
2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09330-6_Br.coding_notes: The study uses micro-analytic video coding of collaborative making episodes (interaction_analysis) combined with discourse analysis of team talk. The focus on how material artifacts (prototypes, digital/traditional fabrication tools) and discursive practices co-constitute learning aligns with distributed cognition and activity theory. Maker projects are open-ended inquiry-based learning with implicit collaboration structures.

2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09345-7_In.title: Initiating scientific collaborations across career levels and disciplines – a network analysis on behavioral data
2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09345-7_In.authors: Julia Eberle & Karsten Stegmann & Alain Barrat & Frank Fischer & Kristine Lund
2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09345-7_In.summary_haiku: This study examined how researchers initiate scientific collaborations at face-to-face academic events using network analysis of behavioral data. Analyzing 5,736 relations among 287 researchers at two technology-enhanced learning conferences, the researchers employed RFID devices to measure contact duration and social network questionnaires to identify collaboration intentions. Results revealed that longer face-to-face contact, reciprocity, and transitivity significantly predicted new collaboration formation. PhD students were less frequently selected as partners, and Information Technology researchers selected fewer partners overall. Group awareness support reduced disciplinary differences in partner selection, suggesting targeted interventions can facilitate interdisciplinary collaboration.
2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09345-7_In.evidence_span: methods (RFID, network questionnaires, 287 researchers, 5,736 relations) + findings (contact duration, reciprocity, transitivity predicting collaboration; career-level and disciplinary effects; group awareness support)
2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09345-7_In.coding_notes: Primary methodology is social network analysis (graph-based analysis of interaction ties and centrality metrics). RFID sensors and questionnaires capture behavioral and relational data at a large-scale academic community. Group awareness support is the technology intervention, with RFID as a sensor modality. Theory emphasizes distributed cognition across the research community and communities of practice lens on collaboration formation.

2024_v19i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09428-1_Ed.title: Editorial notes: on dialogues and sequences
2024_v19i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09428-1_Ed.summary_haiku: This editorial examines four CSCL papers organized around two themes: dialogues as both collaborative processes and objects of reflection, and temporal sequence analysis methods. The editors discuss how teachers' noticing of collaborative interactions requires interpretative frameworks, explore iterative video-based dialogue reflection, and compare qualitative-narrative versus lag-sequential analysis approaches for understanding collaborative learning dynamics and causation.
2024_v19i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09428-1_Ed.evidence_span: editorial framing and thematic organization of four CSCL papers
2024_v19i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09428-1_Ed.coding_notes: This is an editorial that synthesizes and reflects on four papers rather than reporting original empirical research. The primary focus is on dialogue as both collaborative process and object of reflection, with emphasis on temporal sequence analysis methods and teachers' noticing of interactions. Coded as discourse_analysis with secondary emphasis on interaction_analysis and sequence_process_mining to reflect the editorial's discussion of methodological approaches to studying collaborative dialogue.

2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09395-z_Un.title: Understanding young children’s science learning through embodied communication within an MR environment
2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09395-z_Un.authors: Xintian Tu & Joshua Danish & Megan Humburg & Mengxi Zhou & Nitasha Mathayas & Noel Enyedy
2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09395-z_Un.summary_haiku: This study examines how first and second graders use embodied communication—gestures and body movements—within a mixed-reality environment to learn about particle states of matter. Using interaction analysis and coding schemes, researchers found students developed shared gestures representing challenging concepts during classroom activities and subsequently used these gestures in interviews to clarify understanding. Results reveal embodied communication serves both individual and collective functions, supporting collaborative knowledge construction about microscopic particle behavior and macroscopic state changes.
2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09395-z_Un.evidence_span: methods (interaction analysis, coding schemes) + findings (shared gestures, collaborative knowledge construction)
2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09395-z_Un.coding_notes: Study employs micro-analytic interaction analysis of embodied communication (gestures, body movements) in MR environment. Primary unit is small groups/dyads collaborating on particle-state tasks, situated within classroom context. Sociocultural framing emphasizes socially mediated learning through embodied gesture; distributed cognition captures how meaning is spread across bodies and environment.

2020_v15i4_10.1007_s11412-020-09335-1_Th.title: The richness of CSCL environments
2020_v15i4_10.1007_s11412-020-09335-1_Th.summary_haiku: This editorial examines the richness of computer-supported collaborative learning environments through four empirical studies. Research demonstrates diverse collaboration configurations: knowledge building across classrooms via boundary objects, multimodal practices in makerspaces, professional learning in teacher communities, and technology-mediated dyadic learning. Findings reveal that implicit awareness tools and material artifacts effectively support collaborative processes, while environmental affordances—whether digital or physical—significantly influence interaction and learning outcomes.
2020_v15i4_10.1007_s11412-020-09335-1_Th.evidence_span: editorial framing + four empirical studies across methods and findings
2020_v15i4_10.1007_s11412-020-09335-1_Th.coding_notes: Editorial synthesizes multiple studies with diverse methodologies (knowledge building, makerspaces, teacher communities, dyadic learning); primary coding reflects the overarching focus on boundary objects and material artifacts as analytical units. Confidence moderate due to editorial nature and lack of detailed methodological specifics in excerpt.

2019_v14i4_10.1007_s11412-019-09311-4_Ar.title: Are we together or not? The temporal interplay of monitoring, physiological arousal and physiological synchrony during a collaborative exam
2019_v14i4_10.1007_s11412-019-09311-4_Ar.authors: Jonna Malmberg & Eetu Haataja & Tapio Seppanen & Sanna Jarvela
2019_v14i4_10.1007_s11412-019-09311-4_Ar.summary_haiku: This study examined metacognitive monitoring during collaborative exams using video analysis and physiological sensors measuring electrodermal activity. Results showed all group members contributed to monitoring, with monitoring frequency significantly correlating with physiological arousal peaks. Physiological synchrony occurred in groups experiencing task difficulties, suggesting it may indicate meaningful collaborative learning events requiring intervention.
2019_v14i4_10.1007_s11412-019-09311-4_Ar.evidence_span: methods (video analysis, physiological sensors) + findings (monitoring frequency, arousal peaks, synchrony patterns)
2019_v14i4_10.1007_s11412-019-09311-4_Ar.coding_notes: Study combines micro-analytic video coding of monitoring behaviors with physiological sensor data (electrodermal activity) to examine temporal dynamics in collaborative groups. Primary focus is interaction analysis of moment-by-moment metacognitive monitoring; physiological sensors are secondary methodological tool. Sociocultural framing emphasizes collaborative regulation and shared awareness during joint problem-solving.

2018_v13i2_10.1007_s11412-018-9280-3_Dif.title: Different technologies, methodologies and epistemologies—is CSCL a community or communities?
2018_v13i2_10.1007_s11412-018-9280-3_Dif.authors: Nancy Law & Carolyn P. Rose & Ulrike Cress & Sten Ludvigsen
2018_v13i2_10.1007_s11412-018-9280-3_Dif.summary_haiku: This editorial examines whether CSCL functions as a unified community or fragmented communities by analyzing four papers through eight provocations about the field's future. The papers represent diverse technologies, methodologies, and epistemologies—from location-based mapping to orchestrated math environments to cognitive load theory—revealing fundamental tensions between learner agency and scripting, emerging versus established learning outcomes, and analytical versus interpretive theoretical frameworks. The editors argue that theoretical and methodological diversity strengthens CSCL research.
2018_v13i2_10.1007_s11412-018-9280-3_Dif.coding_notes: This is a meta-analytical editorial examining the CSCL field itself rather than a primary empirical study. It systematically reviews and codes four papers across dimensions (technologies, methodologies, epistemologies), making content_analysis the closest fit. The primary unit is the discourse and artifacts (papers) being analyzed. Pedagogy and theory are not the focus; instead, the editorial examines diversity across the field. No specific technology or AI involvement.

2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09385-1_Th.title: The temporal dynamics of online problem‑based learning: Why and when sequence matters
2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09385-1_Th.summary_haiku: This study analyzed 8,009 qualitatively coded interactions from 204 medical students across four online problem-based learning courses using sequence and process mining. Findings revealed that interaction sequences and their temporal order predicted student achievement better than interaction frequency alone. High-cognitive interactions (argumentation, evaluation) triggered similar high-level responses, while low-cognitive interactions perpetuated low-level engagement. Initiating interactions, regardless of cognitive content, showed strongest association with performance, highlighting the importance of sequential dynamics over simple participation counts.
2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09385-1_Th.evidence_span: methods (sequence and process mining on 8,009 coded interactions), findings (temporal order predicts achievement; interaction sequences and cognitive levels)
2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09385-1_Th.coding_notes: Study explicitly uses sequence and process mining on temporally ordered interaction data from online PBL courses. Qualitative coding of interactions combined with temporal sequence analysis is the core methodology. Secondary methods include learning analytics (trace data from digital platform) and content analysis (the 8,009 interactions were qualitatively coded). Unit of analysis is primarily small-group interactions in PBL, with individual learner outcomes (achievement) as a secondary focus.

2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09356-4_Mo.title: Modelling diffusion in computer-supported collaborative learning: a large scale learning analytics study
2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09356-4_Mo.summary_haiku: This large-scale study of 69 courses (3,277 students) examines whether diffusion-based network centrality measures capture information exchange and predict academic success in computer-supported collaborative learning. Using meta-analysis across all courses, the research demonstrates that diffusion centralities—measuring how ideas spread through networks—show stronger and more consistent correlations with student achievement than traditional network measures. Clustering analysis identified three student roles: influencers, mediators, and isolates, validated through manual coding of interactions.
2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09356-4_Mo.coding_notes: Study employs social network analysis with diffusion-based centrality measures on large-scale CSCL trace data (69 courses, 3,277 students) to model information exchange and predict achievement. Learning analytics and descriptive statistics support the primary SNA methodology. Unit of analysis is the network community with secondary focus on individual learner outcomes.
