Distributed cognition theory aligns with diffusion and information-spread framing; sociocultural perspective implicit in collaborative learning context.

2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09409-w_Co.title: Co‑constructing knowledge with generative AI tools: Reflections from a CSCL perspective
2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09409-w_Co.summary_haiku: # Summary Cress and Kimmerle examine how generative AI tools like ChatGPT can support human knowledge construction from a computer-supported collaborative learning perspective. While AI lacks conceptual understanding, they argue that appropriate prompts enabling argumentative dialogue between humans and AI can facilitate knowledge transformation beyond simple information exchange. The authors propose future CSCL research directions including ethnomethodological studies, experimental investigations of prompting strategies, and exploration of whether genuine collaborative knowledge construction occurs between human-AI dyads.
2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09409-w_Co.evidence_span: abstract, summary, and proposed research directions
2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09409-w_Co.coding_notes: This is a reflective/position paper proposing future CSCL research rather than reporting empirical findings. The primary methodology is conceptual; however, the authors explicitly call for ethnomethodological and experimental studies, and the focus on human-AI dyadic dialogue and knowledge co-construction aligns with interaction analysis and argumentation pedagogy. LLM involvement is central as the paper examines generative AI as a collaborative partner in knowledge construction.

2024_v19i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09426-3_Co.title: Combining Danmaku and Discussion Boards: Toward A Scalable and Sociable Environment for Mass Collaboration in MOOCs
2024_v19i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09426-3_Co.summary_haiku: This study examines how danmaku and discussion boards accommodate mass participation in MOOCs through mixed-method analysis of 2,435 danmaku messages and 739 discussion board posts. Findings reveal danmaku fosters collective indirect interaction emphasizing socio-emotional dimensions, while discussion boards organize learners into threaded small groups supporting direct cognitive discussions. The complementary tools enable scalable, sociable collaborative learning environments addressing both emotional and knowledge-sharing needs.
2024_v19i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09426-3_Co.evidence_span: methods (mixed-method analysis of 2,435 danmaku messages and 739 discussion board posts) + findings (characterization of danmaku vs. discussion board affordances)
2024_v19i3_10.1007_s11412-024-09426-3_Co.coding_notes: Study combines quantitative message counts with qualitative analysis of interaction patterns across two complementary asynchronous/synchronous platforms. Primary unit is the discourse artifacts (messages/posts) analyzed at scale, though findings address classroom-level collaboration dynamics in MOOCs.

2020_v15i2_10.1007_s11412-020-09324-4_Ad.title: Advocating for group interaction in the age of COVID-19
2020_v15i2_10.1007_s11412-020-09324-4_Ad.summary_haiku: During COVID-19, computer-supported collaborative learning becomes essential for maintaining connection and enabling effective teamwork. This editorial synthesizes four empirical studies examining regulation strategies in self-organized groups, meta-level discourse's role in group performance, design-centered research methodology for evaluating collaborative learning alignment, and social network analysis for measuring community-level participation, collectively advancing CSCL research and practice.
2020_v15i2_10.1007_s11412-020-09324-4_Ad.evidence_span: abstract and editorial synthesis of four empirical studies
2020_v15i2_10.1007_s11412-020-09324-4_Ad.coding_notes: This is an editorial synthesizing multiple empirical studies rather than a single primary study. The primary methodology is coded as mixed_methods because the editorial integrates quantitative (social network analysis, regulation strategies) and qualitative (discourse analysis, meta-level discourse) approaches across the four constituent studies. Unit of analysis is cross_level because the synthesis addresses individual regulation, small-group performance, and community-level participation simultaneously.

2024_v19i4_10.1007_s11412-024-09440-5_Ed.title: Editorial Notes: Revitalising foundational concepts
2024_v19i4_10.1007_s11412-024-09440-5_Ed.summary_haiku: This editorial examines whether computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) has emerged as a fully-fledged paradigm by exploring two foundational questions: whether groups are reducible to individuals, and whether technology fundamentally transforms collaborative activity. Through analysis of four papers addressing group understanding, artifact mediation, dialogue creativity, and socially shared regulation, the authors argue that CSCL is consolidating as an autonomous research discipline with deepened conceptual foundations.
2024_v19i4_10.1007_s11412-024-09440-5_Ed.coding_notes: This is an editorial/position paper analyzing foundational CSCL concepts rather than reporting empirical research. It systematically examines four papers' contributions to group-level phenomena, artifact mediation, and regulation—characteristic of content analysis of scholarly discourse. The primary unit is the conceptual and theoretical landscape (artifact/discourse), though it implicitly addresses cross-level questions about individual-group reducibility.

2022_v17i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09370-0_A_.title: A classification of Challenges encountered in Complex Teamwork Settings
2022_v17i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09370-0_A_.authors: Maedeh A. Kazemitabar & Susanne P. Lajoie & Tianshu Li
2022_v17i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09370-0_A_.summary_haiku: This study examined teamwork challenges in a computer-supported collaborative learning environment using a hackathon as the research context. Through multimodal data collection including questionnaires, interviews, and video recordings of 48 participants, researchers employed qualitative theory-driven coding to identify 16 distinct challenges. These challenges were categorized into seven macro-level themes: cognitive, motivational, emotional, behavioral, cognitive/behavioral, general, and external. The analysis revealed which challenges specifically impede mutual trust and shared mental models—key team coordination mechanisms—providing educators with insights for supporting effective collaboration in CSCL settings.
2022_v17i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09370-0_A_.evidence_span: methods (multimodal data collection, qualitative coding) + findings (16 challenges, 7 macro themes)
2022_v17i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09370-0_A_.coding_notes: Study uses systematic qualitative coding of multimodal data (video, interviews, questionnaires) to classify teamwork challenges in a hackathon CSCL context. Primary methodology is content_analysis because the core analytic work involves theory-driven coding of challenges into categorical schemes. Secondary methods include ethnographic elements (naturalistic hackathon setting) and interaction_analysis (video-based observation of collaborative episodes). Unit of analysis is dyad_small_group (teams in hackathon) with secondary focus on discourse/artifacts (video recordings, interview transcripts). Pedagogy reflects structured teamwork in a complex setting; theory is sociocultural (team coordination, shared mental models) with distributed cognition elements (mutual trust, coordination mechanisms).

2022_v17i4_10.1007_s11412-022-09381-x_Th.title: The impact of scripts on blended and online socially shared regulation of learning: A role‑playing game theory perspective
2022_v17i4_10.1007_s11412-022-09381-x_Th.authors: Clyde A. Warden & Chi-Cheng Chang & James O. Stanworth & Judy F. Chen
2022_v17i4_10.1007_s11412-022-09381-x_Th.summary_haiku: Researchers examined how brief "mere exposure prompts" (MEP) affect collaborative learning in role-playing game simulations across online and blended course formats. Using behavioral trace data and social network analysis with 185 students completing business negotiation tasks, they found MEP scripts significantly influenced planning behaviors in fully online learners but not blended learners, despite both groups recalling the prompt message. Results suggest online environments enable script-based interventions more effectively than traditional classroom settings.
2022_v17i4_10.1007_s11412-022-09381-x_Th.evidence_span: methods (behavioral trace data, social network analysis, 185 students) + findings (MEP scripts effect on planning behaviors by course format)
2022_v17i4_10.1007_s11412-022-09381-x_Th.coding_notes: Study uses behavioral trace data and social network analysis to examine script effects on collaborative regulation in role-playing game simulations. Primary methodology is SNA given explicit use of network analysis; secondary methods include learning analytics (trace data from digital platform) and interaction analysis (coding of collaborative episodes). Pedagogy centers on collaboration scripts (MEP prompts) and self/peer regulation of learning. Technology involves shared workspace (game simulation) and likely synchronous interaction in online/blended formats. Sociocultural theory frames socially shared regulation; distributed cognition relevant to role-playing game context.

2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9238-2_Soc.title: Socially shared regulation of learning in CSCL: understanding and prompting individual- and group-level shared regulatory activities
2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9238-2_Soc.authors: Sanna Jarvela & Paul A. Kirschner & Allyson Hadwin & Hanna Jarvenoja & Jonna Malmberg & Mariel Miller & Jari Laru
2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9238-2_Soc.summary_haiku: This review examines socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) in computer-supported collaborative learning. The authors identify gaps in existing CSCL support tools, which focus on knowledge construction and social awareness but neglect regulatory processes. They present conceptual frameworks distinguishing self-regulated, co-regulated, and socially shared regulation, then describe multiple tools (AIRE, SEST, planning tools, VCRI+SSRL, S-REG) designed to prompt metacognitive awareness and support individual and group-level regulation of cognition, motivation, and emotion during collaborative tasks.
2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9238-2_Soc.evidence_span: abstract, introduction, framework sections, tool descriptions
2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9238-2_Soc.coding_notes: This is a review/conceptual paper synthesizing SSRL frameworks and tool designs rather than reporting original empirical research. Primary methodology coded as content_analysis because the paper systematically reviews and categorizes existing tools and regulatory processes. The focus on metacognitive prompts and regulatory scaffolds justifies collaboration_scripting_tools as primary technology. Sociocultural theory is primary given emphasis on socially shared processes; activity theory secondary due to discussion of regulatory contradictions and tool mediation.

2024_v19i4_10.1007_s11412-024-09434-3_Co.title: Comparing the effectiveness of CSCL scripts for shared task perceptions in socially shared regulation of collaborative learning
2024_v19i4_10.1007_s11412-024-09434-3_Co.summary_haiku: High-support group planning scripts significantly improved undergraduate students' accuracy of shared task perceptions and transactive planning discussions compared to low-support scripts, though individual-level support showed no detectable effect. However, enhanced task perceptions did not translate to improved group performance, suggesting groups may struggle to implement shared understanding during task execution.
2024_v19i4_10.1007_s11412-024-09434-3_Co.coding_notes: Study compares high-support vs. low-support CSCL scripts in a controlled design, measuring shared task perceptions and planning discussions at group level. Sociocultural framing emphasizes socially shared regulation; socio-cognitive secondary reflects collaborative conflict/explanation mechanisms. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

2016_v11i2_10.1007_s11412-016-9232-8_Gro.title: Group emotions: the social and cognitive functions of emotions in argumentation
2016_v11i2_10.1007_s11412-016-9232-8_Gro.authors: Claire Polo & Kristine Lund & Christian Plantin & Gerald P. Niccolai
2016_v11i2_10.1007_s11412-016-9232-8_Gro.summary_haiku: Emotions serve dual functions in group argumentation: socially, they signal recognition and engagement in specific talk types (cumulative, disputational, exploratory); cognitively, they frame discourse objects through schematization. Analysis of student debates reveals low-intensity emotional framing correlates with cumulative talk, while high-intensity framing correlates with disputational talk, suggesting optimal emotional engagement supports higher-quality collaborative reasoning.
2016_v11i2_10.1007_s11412-016-9232-8_Gro.evidence_span: methods (interaction analysis of debates) + findings (emotional framing patterns across talk types)
2016_v11i2_10.1007_s11412-016-9232-8_Gro.coding_notes: Study uses micro-analytic coding of student debate episodes to examine how emotions function in argumentation discourse. Primary focus is interaction analysis of moment-by-moment talk; secondary methods include discourse and content analysis. Dialogic theory frames meaning-making through emotional signaling in multi-voiced argumentation.

2017_v12i3_10.1007_s11412-017-9263-9_Inv.title: Investigating the effects of peer to peer prompts on collaborative argumentation, consensus and perceived efficacy in collaborative learning
2017_v12i3_10.1007_s11412-017-9263-9_Inv.authors: Owen M. Harney & Michael J. Hogan & Sarah Quinn
2017_v12i3_10.1007_s11412-017-9263-9_Inv.summary_haiku: Peer-driven prompts in computer-supported collaborative learning using Interactive Management significantly enhanced student outcomes compared to facilitator-driven prompts. With 101 undergraduate students across eight groups, peer-driven conditions produced higher perceived consensus, perceived efficacy, team orientation, and more sophisticated argumentation patterns, while reducing discomfort in group learning. Results demonstrate that structured peer prompting, supported through facilitator modeling and gradual responsibility transfer, effectively supports collaborative learning and critical thinking development.
2017_v12i3_10.1007_s11412-017-9263-9_Inv.coding_notes: Study compares peer-driven vs. facilitator-driven prompts in structured collaborative groups using Interactive Management. Primary focus is on scripted prompting as a pedagogical intervention with measurement of argumentation quality, consensus, and efficacy—classic CSCL experimental design examining collaboration scripts.

2018_v13i2_10.1007_s11412-018-9278-x_Lea.title: Learning through collaborative design of location-based games
2018_v13i2_10.1007_s11412-018-9278-x_Lea.authors: Jo Dugstad Wake & Frode Guribye & Barbara Wasson
2018_v13i2_10.1007_s11412-018-9278-x_Lea.summary_haiku: Students collaboratively designed location-based games to learn history using the SILO authoring tool. Through design-based research and video analysis, the study found that students engaged creatively with historical materials while making design decisions about game difficulty, narrative structure, and location placement. Students explicitly considered peer players' experiences, demonstrating accountability and responsibility in their design process.
2018_v13i2_10.1007_s11412-018-9278-x_Lea.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (design-based research, video analysis), findings (collaborative design, peer accountability)
2018_v13i2_10.1007_s11412-018-9278-x_Lea.coding_notes: Study explicitly frames itself as design-based research iterating on SILO authoring tool in naturalistic classroom setting. Video analysis of moment-by-moment interaction during collaborative design decisions is the primary analytic method. Sociocultural framing evident in emphasis on peer accountability and shared responsibility in design process.

2022_v17i3_10.1007_s11412-022-09376-8_Fo.title: Fostering growth orientations in students’ identities as knowledge builders
2022_v17i3_10.1007_s11412-022-09376-8_Fo.summary_haiku: This study examined how students develop growth orientations in humanistic knowledge building communities (HKBCs). Using grounded analysis of 322 utterances from graduate students' reflective diaries and discussions, researchers identified five dimensions of fixedness-growth orientations: feelings, mindset, personal responsibility, self-constructs, and attitudes toward change. Statistical analysis revealed significant increases in growth orientation across the semester. Case studies illustrated how students transformed from fixed to growth orientations through community support and reflection, with implications for self-regulated learning and emergent roles in collaborative environments.
2022_v17i3_10.1007_s11412-022-09376-8_Fo.evidence_span: methods (grounded analysis of 322 utterances, reflective diaries, discussions) + findings (five dimensions identified, statistical increases, case studies)
2022_v17i3_10.1007_s11412-022-09376-8_Fo.coding_notes: Study uses systematic coding of utterances (content analysis) combined with descriptive statistics and qualitative case studies. Primary unit is graduate students in HKBCs (small collaborative communities), though individual growth orientations are also tracked. Knowledge building theory and self-regulated learning are central; technology is inferred as asynchronous (diaries, discussions) but not explicitly detailed.

2018_v13i3_10.1007_s11412-018-9281-2_Lev.title: Leveraging mobile eye-trackers to capture joint visual attention in co-located collaborative learning groups
2018_v13i3_10.1007_s11412-018-9281-2_Lev.authors: Kshitij Sharma & Bertrand Schneider & Sebastien Cuendet & Guillaume Zufferey & Pierre Dillenbourg & Roy Pea
2018_v13i3_10.1007_s11412-018-9281-2_Lev.summary_haiku: Mobile eye-trackers reveal that joint visual attention correlates with collaborative learning quality in co-located dyads, but high coordination alone doesn't guarantee learning. Qualitative analysis of two high-coordination groups showed that imbalanced participation—where one student dominates initiating joint attention—predicts lower learning gains, suggesting that productive collaboration requires balanced visual leadership between partners.
2018_v13i3_10.1007_s11412-018-9281-2_Lev.evidence_span: methods (eye-tracking protocol), findings (joint visual attention correlation, participation imbalance analysis)
2018_v13i3_10.1007_s11412-018-9281-2_Lev.coding_notes: Study uses mobile eye-trackers as primary sensor to capture embodied joint attention in face-to-face dyads; qualitative interaction analysis of high-coordination episodes reveals that balanced visual leadership (not just coordination) predicts learning. Distributed cognition framing emphasizes how attention is coordinated across partners and artifacts.

2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-026-09465-y_Co.title: Co‑constructing critical data literacy in families: A technology‑mediated learning perspective
2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-026-09465-y_Co.summary_haiku: # Summary This study investigates how families collaboratively develop critical data literacy about smart home technologies through FamiData Hub, a speculative CSCL prototype combining tangible LEGO models with augmented reality. Through workshops with 17 families, researchers found that collaborative learning emerges via material interaction and shared problem-solving, with family roles dynamically shifting. Rather than traditional adult-to-child knowledge transfer, findings reveal multidirectional zones of proximal development where children, parents, and digital artifacts alternately serve as "more knowledgeable others," enabling intergenerational co-construction of understanding about datafication and algorithmic systems.
2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-026-09465-y_Co.evidence_span: methods (workshops, FamiData Hub prototype), findings (family roles, zones of proximal development, co-construction)
2026_v21i2_10.1007_s11412-026-09465-y_Co.coding_notes: Study employs iterative design and testing of a CSCL prototype (FamiData Hub) in naturalistic family settings, characteristic of design-based research. Micro-analytic observation of family interactions with tangible LEGO and AR affordances supports interaction_analysis as secondary. Strong sociocultural framing (ZPD, multidirectional learning) with distributed cognition evident in how artifacts mediate understanding.

2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9250-1_A_m.title: A more reflective form of joint problem solving
2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9250-1_A_m.summary_haiku: This study examines asynchronous online collaboration among university students completing wiki and blog-based writing assignments. Through qualitative analysis of over 7,000 lines of chat transcripts, the research identifies how participants create "venues"—virtual spaces anchoring joint problem-solving across different times and places. The findings reveal a shift toward more reflective, piecemeal collaboration compared to face-to-face interaction, with participants strategically selecting problems for joint attention while leveraging secondary participation through reading and reflection.
2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9250-1_A_m.evidence_span: methods (qualitative analysis of chat transcripts) + findings (venues, reflective collaboration patterns)
2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9250-1_A_m.coding_notes: Primary methodology is discourse_analysis because the study performs qualitative linguistic analysis of 7,000+ lines of chat to identify collaborative patterns and meaning-making. Secondary methods include content_analysis (systematic coding of collaboration types) and interaction_analysis (moment-by-moment joint problem-solving episodes). Unit of analysis is artifact_discourse_trace (chat transcripts, wiki/blog posts) with secondary focus on dyads/small groups engaging in joint work.

2019_v14i2_10.1007_s11412-019-09301-6_To.title: Towards a micro-ecological approach to CSCL
2019_v14i2_10.1007_s11412-019-09301-6_To.summary_haiku: # Summary Current CSCL theories prioritize single-level analysis, limiting understanding of complex orchestration processes. This paper proposes a micro-ecological framework analyzing interactions across individual, group, and classroom levels simultaneously. Through a design club case study, the authors identify "transecological disruptions"—critical moments where actions at one level propagate across levels—demonstrating how this approach reveals orchestration complexity and learning opportunities that traditional single-level analyses miss.
2019_v14i2_10.1007_s11412-019-09301-6_To.coding_notes: The paper proposes a micro-ecological framework analyzing simultaneous interactions across individual, group, and classroom levels, making cross-level multilevel analysis the primary unit. Activity theory and distributed cognition align with the focus on orchestration processes and transecological disruptions propagating across system levels. Ethnographic case study of a design club is the primary methodology, with interaction analysis supporting the micro-level examination of critical moments.

2019_v14i1_10.1007_s11412-019-09294-2_In.title: Instrumental genesis in the design studio
2019_v14i1_10.1007_s11412-019-09294-2_In.authors: Lucila Carvalho & Roberto Martinez-Maldonado & Peter Goodyear
2019_v14i1_10.1007_s11412-019-09294-2_In.summary_haiku: Instrumental Genesis theory explains how artifacts and their uses co-evolve within specific environments. This study applies IG to the neglected "upstream" phase of CSCL design, examining how educational designers use design studio artifacts to create collaborative learning tasks. Through two empirical studies involving design teams using the CoCoDes tool and design patterns, the researchers traced how artifacts move downstream to learners and how designer practices move upstream to inform tool improvements, demonstrating CSCL design as a distributed, dynamic system of instrument-mediated activity.
2019_v14i1_10.1007_s11412-019-09294-2_In.evidence_span: methods, findings, discussion of design studio practices and artifact evolution
2019_v14i1_10.1007_s11412-019-09294-2_In.coding_notes: Study focuses on instrumental genesis of design artifacts (CoCoDes, design patterns) used by educational designers in studio settings. Primary unit is the artifacts and their traces of use; secondary units include designer teams and cross-level analysis of how designer practices inform tool evolution. Activity theory frames the co-evolution of artifacts and practices within the design system.

2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09405-0_Un.title: Understanding the effect of differences in prior knowledge on middle school students’ collaborative interactions and learning
2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09405-0_Un.authors: Sadhana Puntambekar & Dana Gnesdilow & Sinan Yavuz
2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09405-0_Un.summary_haiku: # Summary This study examined how prior knowledge variance within collaborative groups affects middle school students' science learning and interactions. Using hierarchical linear modeling on 102 groups and social network analysis of two contrasting groups, researchers found that students in homogeneous groups achieved significantly greater learning gains than those in heterogeneous groups. Qualitative analysis revealed homogeneous groups exhibited more distributed, reciprocal interactions with mutual scaffolding, while heterogeneous groups showed centralized interactions dominated by the highest-knowledge member, resulting in lower engagement and learning for less-knowledgeable peers.
2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09405-0_Un.evidence_span: methods (HLM, SNA, qualitative coding) + findings (learning gains, interaction patterns)
2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09405-0_Un.coding_notes: Study uses hierarchical linear modeling as primary quantitative method to account for nested group structure, complemented by social network analysis of interaction ties and micro-analytic interaction coding. Sociocultural framing emphasizes scaffolding and distributed cognition within groups; socio-cognitive elements present in conflict/explanation mechanisms.

2022_v17i3_10.1007_s11412-022-09374-w_iT.title: iTalk–iSee: A participatory visual learning analytical tool for productive peer talk
2022_v17i3_10.1007_s11412-022-09374-w_iT.authors: Liru Hu & Jiajun Wu & Gaowei Chen
2022_v17i3_10.1007_s11412-022-09374-w_iT.summary_haiku: iTalk–iSee is a participatory visual learning analytics tool designed to support primary school students' productive peer talk in dialogic collaborative problem-solving. Grounded in Bakhtinian dialogism theory, the tool maps 18 productive talk moves onto three DCPS goals (equality/respect, open-mindedness, convergence) and employs visualization design principles with a three-step macro-script (code→visualize→reflect) to strengthen learner agency. Field study evaluation with 59 fourth-graders demonstrated usability improvements through iterative refinement and positive user experience ratings.
2022_v17i3_10.1007_s11412-022-09374-w_iT.coding_notes: iTalk–iSee is a participatory visual learning analytics tool grounded in Bakhtinian dialogism, employing a macro-script (code→visualize→reflect) to scaffold peer talk. The field study with 59 fourth-graders reflects design-based research with embedded learning analytics (visualization of talk moves) and content analysis (coding of 18 productive talk moves). Primary unit is small-group peer talk; secondary is classroom cohort. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9240-8_Con.title: Contribution to a theory of CSCL scripts: taking into account the appropriation of scripts by learners
2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9240-8_Con.summary_haiku: Tchounikine argues that understanding CSCL script enactment requires examining learner appropriation—how learners perceive, understand, and make scripts their own—rather than assuming direct script implementation. Through theoretical analysis, he demonstrates that appropriation involves complex cognitive processes influenced by technology use, institutional contexts, and domain-specific factors. The paper proposes that appropriation and implementation are intertwined processes requiring holistic analysis, extending the Script Theory of Guidance framework.
2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9240-8_Con.coding_notes: This is primarily a theoretical paper analyzing script appropriation through conceptual and analytical lenses rather than empirical data collection. Coded as ethnographic_case_study as a proxy for qualitative theoretical analysis; could also fit 'other' if strict empirical methodology required. The focus on learner appropriation of scripts and technology-mediated collaboration justifies the primary selections.

2016_v11i1_10.1007_s11412-015-9224-0_Rol.title: Role taking and knowledge building in a blended university course
2016_v11i1_10.1007_s11412-015-9224-0_Rol.authors: Donatella Cesareni & Stefano Cacciamani & Nobuko Fujita
2016_v11i1_10.1007_s11412-015-9224-0_Rol.summary_haiku: Assigning scripted roles aligned with knowledge-building principles significantly enhances student participation in blended university courses. Two studies examined 143 students across three modules, comparing role-takers with non-role-takers using quantitative participation metrics and qualitative content analysis. Results demonstrated that role-takers demonstrated higher reading and writing activity, varied their conversational functions more broadly, and engaged in greater synthesis and metacognitive reflection, supporting collective cognitive responsibility for knowledge advancement.
2016_v11i1_10.1007_s11412-015-9224-0_Rol.coding_notes: Study explicitly examines role-taking (scripted collaboration) within knowledge-building framework in blended (online + face-to-face) university setting. Mixed methods combines quantitative participation metrics with qualitative content analysis of discourse. Primary unit is role-takers vs. non-role-takers within group discussions, though individual learner outcomes also tracked.

2018_v13i3_10.1007_s11412-018-9283-0_Com.title: Comparing effects of two collaboration scripts on learning activities for wiki-based environments
2018_v13i3_10.1007_s11412-018-9283-0_Com.authors: Sven Heimbuch & Lisa Ollesch & Daniel Bodemer
2018_v13i3_10.1007_s11412-018-9283-0_Com.summary_haiku: This experimental study compared two wiki collaboration scripts for educational knowledge construction. The Discuss-Deliberate-Revise (DDR) script, emphasizing upfront discussion before edits, was tested against Wikipedia's Be Bold-Revert-Discuss (BRD) script promoting frequent individual edits. Across a pre-study with dyads and main study with larger groups, DDR encouraged more discussion and produced higher-quality, error-free articles, though direct learning gains were minimal. Individual differences in cognitive closure, metacognitive strategies, and motivation moderated script effectiveness.
2018_v13i3_10.1007_s11412-018-9283-0_Com.coding_notes: Clear experimental design comparing two scripted collaboration conditions (DDR vs. BRD) in wiki environments. Primary focus on scripts regulating discussion and editing sequences; secondary emphasis on knowledge building outcomes. Individual differences (cognitive closure, metacognition, motivation) analyzed as moderators, supporting socio-cognitive framing alongside sociocultural mediation.

2020_v15i1_10.1007_s11412-020-09317-3_Le.title: Learning in embodied activity framework: a sociocultural framework for embodied cognition
2020_v15i1_10.1007_s11412-020-09317-3_Le.authors: Joshua A. Danish & Noel Enyedy & Asmalina Saleh & Megan Humburg
2020_v15i1_10.1007_s11412-020-09317-3_Le.summary_haiku: This paper proposes the Learning in Embodied Activity Framework (LEAF), which synthesizes individual and sociocultural theories to explain how bodies support collaborative learning. Using Cultural Historical Activity Theory, the authors analyze data from the Science through Technology Enhanced Play project, where first and second-grade students used mixed-reality simulations to learn about particle behavior and states of matter. LEAF extends embodied cognition research by explicitly examining how individual and collective embodied actions, mediated by tools, rules, community, and division of labor, jointly shape learning in collaborative contexts.
2020_v15i1_10.1007_s11412-020-09317-3_Le.evidence_span: title, abstract, framework description, methods (mixed-reality simulations with first/second-grade students)
2020_v15i1_10.1007_s11412-020-09317-3_Le.coding_notes: LEAF explicitly grounds analysis in Cultural Historical Activity Theory (Engeström), examining embodied collaborative learning in a naturalistic classroom setting with iterative design of mixed-reality simulations. The focus on how bodies, tools, and social structures jointly mediate learning aligns with activity theory and distributed cognition; interaction analysis of embodied actions is central to the framework.

2017_v12i2_10.1007_s11412-017-9255-9_Lif.title: Life history of a topic in an online discussion: a complex systems theory perspective on how one message attracts class members to create meaning collaboratively
2017_v12i2_10.1007_s11412-017-9255-9_Lif.authors: Jane S. Vogler & Diane L. Schallert & Michelle E. Jordan & Kwangok Song & Anke J. Z. Sanders & Yueh-hui Yan Te Chiang & Ji-Eun Lee & Jeongbin Hannah Park & Li-Tang Yu
2017_v12i2_10.1007_s11412-017-9255-9_Lif.summary_haiku: This qualitative study applied complex adaptive systems theory to analyze how meaning emerges in synchronous online classroom discussions. Researchers tracked one pivotal message (#43) and its resulting topic through multiple data sources including transcripts, screen recordings, and video observations of eight graduate students. Findings revealed that interdependent processes and content co-create understanding, private individual meaning-making mingles with public shared experiences, and topics follow developmental trajectories from inception through decline, demonstrating how collaborative learning emerges through system-level interactions.
2017_v12i2_10.1007_s11412-017-9255-9_Lif.evidence_span: methods (tracking one message, multiple data sources: transcripts, screen recordings, video) + findings (topic trajectories, interdependent processes, meaning co-creation)
2017_v12i2_10.1007_s11412-017-9255-9_Lif.coding_notes: The study's focus on tracking a single message (#43) through its lifecycle and analyzing how meaning emerges through system-level interactions of eight graduate students in synchronous online discussion aligns with interaction analysis and distributed cognition. Complex adaptive systems theory frames cognition as spread across participants and artifacts; the emphasis on transcripts, recordings, and observations supports discourse and interaction coding. Secondary unit includes small group (8 students) dynamics.

2017_v12i3_10.1007_s11412-017-9260-z_How.title: How to combine collaboration scripts and heuristic worked examples to foster mathematical argumentation – when working memory matters
2017_v12i3_10.1007_s11412-017-9260-z_How.authors: Matthias Schwaighofer & Freydis Vogel & Ingo Kollar & Stefan Ufer & Anselm Strohmaier & Ilka Terwedow & Sarah Ottinger & Kristina Reiss
2017_v12i3_10.1007_s11412-017-9260-z_How.summary_haiku: This study examined how sequencing and fading collaboration scripts and heuristic worked examples affect university students' mathematical argumentation skills. Using a 2×2 factorial design with 108 freshmen, researchers found that fading the initially presented scaffold improved dialogic skills regardless of sequence. For dialectic skills, working memory capacity moderated fading effects: low-capacity learners benefited most from fading the collaboration script when presented first, while high-capacity learners benefited from simultaneous scaffold availability.
2017_v12i3_10.1007_s11412-017-9260-z_How.evidence_span: methods (2×2 factorial design, 108 freshmen) + findings (fading effects, working memory moderation)
2017_v12i3_10.1007_s11412-017-9260-z_How.coding_notes: Study uses controlled factorial design comparing script and worked-example sequences with fading manipulations. Primary focus is individual learner outcomes (argumentation skills) analyzed within dyadic collaboration. Working memory capacity as moderator reflects information-processing theory alongside socio-cognitive mechanisms of collaborative scaffolding.

2019_v14i1_10.1007_s11412-019-09295-1_Im.title: Imagining with improvised representations in CSCL environments
2019_v14i1_10.1007_s11412-019-09295-1_Im.authors: Magdalena Kersting & Kenneth Silseth & Rolf Steier
2019_v14i1_10.1007_s11412-019-09295-1_Im.summary_haiku: This study examines how upper secondary physics students collaboratively improvise and introduce representations outside designed learning environments to solve problems. Through video analysis of small groups using an interactive map task comparing two- and three-dimensional spatial representations, researchers identified emergent improvised representations including gestures, physical objects, and digital tools like GoogleEarth. Findings reveal that imagination—conceptualized as a social, embodied, and materially distributed process—enables students to recognize representational needs and discover new possibilities, with multimodal shifts facilitating sophisticated meaning-making across digital, physical, gestural, and dimensional boundaries.
2019_v14i1_10.1007_s11412-019-09295-1_Im.evidence_span: methods (video analysis, interactive map task) + findings (emergent improvised representations, multimodal shifts)
2019_v14i1_10.1007_s11412-019-09295-1_Im.coding_notes: Video analysis of moment-by-moment collaborative episodes with attention to gestures, physical objects, and digital tools (GoogleEarth) indicates interaction analysis as primary. Distributed cognition and sociocultural framing emphasize imagination as socially, embodily, and materially distributed across people and artifacts. Secondary methods include multimodal observation (gestures, objects) and ethnographic case-study design of small-group problem-solving.

2018_v13i3_10.1007_s11412-018-9279-9_Cha.title: Challenges in online collaboration: effects of scripting shared task perceptions
2018_v13i3_10.1007_s11412-018-9279-9_Cha.authors: Allyson F. Hadwin & Aishah Bakhtiar & Mariel Miller
2018_v13i3_10.1007_s11412-018-9279-9_Cha.summary_haiku: This study examined how different types of planning visualizations affect collaborative learning challenges and regulatory strategies. Undergraduate students (N=180) completed collaborative tasks under three conditions: quantified visualization, nominal visualization, or no visualization of group members' planning perceptions. Results showed groups without visualization support reported greater planning challenge severity and experienced cascading difficulties across multiple challenge types. Groups receiving visualization support reported more effective strategy use. Findings support integrating planning awareness tools into computer-supported collaborative learning environments.
2018_v13i3_10.1007_s11412-018-9279-9_Cha.evidence_span: methods (three experimental conditions with N=180), findings (challenge severity, strategy use comparisons across groups)
2018_v13i3_10.1007_s11412-018-9279-9_Cha.coding_notes: Study uses a controlled three-condition design (quantified visualization, nominal visualization, no visualization) comparing group outcomes, making it clearly experimental. The planning visualizations function as awareness tools that scaffold shared task perception and regulatory strategy use, aligning with collaboration scripts and sociocultural theory of mediated learning.

2021_v16i3_10.1007_s11412-021-09349-3_Pr.title: Prompting collaborative and exploratory discourse: An epistemic network analysis study
2021_v16i3_10.1007_s11412-021-09349-3_Pr.authors: Zarifa Zakaria & Jennifer Tsan & Anna Iwanski & Jessica Vandenberg & Collin Lynch & Kristy Elizabeth Boyer & Eric Wiebe
2021_v16i3_10.1007_s11412-021-09349-3_Pr.summary_haiku: This study examined how simple prompting interventions affect elementary students' collaborative discourse during pair programming. Using Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) to analyze coded dialogue from 62 fourth graders, researchers compared intervention students receiving empirically-derived prompts supporting exploratory talk with control students. Results revealed intervention students significantly increased justification, alternative ideas, and simple questions, demonstrating qualitatively different collaboration patterns through network visualizations showing stronger connections between exploratory talk codes.
2021_v16i3_10.1007_s11412-021-09349-3_Pr.evidence_span: methods (ENA coding of dialogue, intervention design) + findings (network visualizations, discourse pattern comparisons)
2021_v16i3_10.1007_s11412-021-09349-3_Pr.coding_notes: Primary methodology is interaction_analysis because the study codes and analyzes moment-by-moment collaborative dialogue; ENA is a secondary social_network_analysis method applied to those coded interactions. Prompting intervention is a collaboration_script that structures exploratory talk. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09396-y_Fa.title: Facilitated model‑based reasoning in immersive virtual reality: Meaning‑making and embodied interactions with dynamic processes
2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09396-y_Fa.authors: Michelle Lui & Kit-Ying Angela Chong & Martha Mullally & Rhonda McEwen
2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09396-y_Fa.summary_haiku: This study examined how 34 undergraduate students engaged with a lac operon VR simulation using head-mounted displays while a facilitator viewed a mirrored display. Using the Structure-Behavior-Function framework to code facilitator-participant interactions, researchers identified four patterns supporting model-based reasoning: spontaneous structural observations, immediate situated feedback, multiple simulated states comparison, and inquiry spanning structural-behavioral-functional levels. Findings demonstrate that facilitated VR simulations effectively support abstract scientific concept understanding through embodied interaction and dialogue.
2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09396-y_Fa.evidence_span: methods (Structure-Behavior-Function coding framework, facilitator-participant interaction analysis) + findings (four patterns of model-based reasoning)
2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09396-y_Fa.coding_notes: Study centers on micro-analytic coding of facilitator-participant dialogue and embodied interaction in VR; immersive VR with head-mounted displays and mirrored facilitator view constitutes multimodal sensor-rich environment. Sociocultural framing emphasizes mediated meaning-making through dialogue and embodied action in shared virtual space.

2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09308-z_A_.title: A handheld classroom dashboard: Teachers’ perspectives on the use of real-time collaborative learning analytics
2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09308-z_A_.summary_haiku: This longitudinal study examined four teachers' perspectives on using a real-time analytics dashboard during 72 classroom sessions over ten weeks in a multi-tabletop collaborative learning environment. The handheld dashboard displayed group participation, task progress, script enactment, and automatically detected misconceptions. Through semi-structured interviews, teachers reported that visualizations enhanced awareness and decision-making, though they identified tensions regarding data incompleteness, immediate versus delayed feedback, orchestration load, and device portability, highlighting critical design considerations for effective CSCL classroom analytics tools.
2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09308-z_A_.evidence_span: methods (longitudinal study, semi-structured interviews, 72 sessions), findings (teacher perspectives on dashboard visualizations, orchestration tensions)
2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09308-z_A_.coding_notes: Study centers on real-time learning analytics dashboard supporting teacher awareness and orchestration in tabletop collaborative environments. Automatic misconception detection suggests ML/AI-based analytics, but no explicit LLM involvement; coded as learning_analytics with awareness_dashboard as primary technology. Teacher facilitation is the primary analytical lens, though classroom cohort is also examined.

2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09398-w_Ge.title: Gesture‑mediated collaboration with augmented reality headsets in a problem‑based astronomy task
2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09398-w_Ge.authors: James Planey & Robin Jephthah Rajarathinam & Emma Mercier & Robb Lindgren
2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09398-w_Ge.summary_haiku: This qualitative study examined 15 undergraduate groups collaborating on an astronomy problem using augmented reality headsets and tablets. Analysis revealed that gesture—particularly spatial pointing and representational gestures—mediated collaborative knowledge construction, especially during complex tasks. Groups with higher AR experience showed greater engagement. Gesture facilitated five key affordances: exploration, orientation, perspective-sharing, synthesizing representations, and symbolic conception. The findings demonstrate how embodied gesture bridges digital and physical spaces, enabling groups to create shared situated conceptual spaces that enhance collaborative problem-solving in extended reality environments.
2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09398-w_Ge.evidence_span: methods (qualitative analysis of 15 groups), findings (gesture affordances and collaborative knowledge construction)
2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09398-w_Ge.coding_notes: Study employs micro-analytic coding of gesture and interaction in small groups solving an astronomy problem with AR headsets. Sociocultural and distributed cognition theories frame how embodied gesture mediates shared conceptual spaces across digital and physical modalities.

2023_v18i3_10.1007_s11412-023-09401-4_Do.title: Does matching peers at finer‑grained levels of prior performance enhance gains in task performance from peer review?
2023_v18i3_10.1007_s11412-023-09401-4_Do.summary_haiku: This study examined whether matching peer reviewers and authors by four performance levels (rather than binary high/low) enhances task performance gains in online peer feedback. Using regression analysis on 766 biology students across multiple assignments, results revealed that providing feedback to same-level peers benefits reviewers, while receiving feedback shows mixed effects. Simulations indicated that performance-based matching algorithms produce better cumulative outcomes than random assignment across all student performance levels.
2023_v18i3_10.1007_s11412-023-09401-4_Do.coding_notes: Study uses regression analysis on trace data (766 students, multiple assignments) to test peer-matching effects on individual learning gains. Peer review is the core pedagogy; matching algorithm design suggests quasi-experimental comparison of conditions. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

2017_v12i3_10.1007_s11412-017-9259-5_Fac.title: Facilitating socio-cognitive and socio-emotional monitoring in collaborative learning with a regulation macro script – an exploratory study
2017_v12i3_10.1007_s11412-017-9259-5_Fac.authors: Jaana Isohatala & Sanna Jarvela & Piia Naykki & Johanna Poysa-Tarhonen & Paivi Hakkinen
2017_v12i3_10.1007_s11412-017-9259-5_Fac.summary_haiku: This exploratory study examined how a regulation macro script supports socio-cognitive and socio-emotional monitoring in collaborative learning among teacher education students. Using video analysis of 20 group sessions, researchers found that groups engaged more actively with orientation phases than intermediate or reflection phases. Active script discussions stimulated significantly more socio-emotional support provision than less active discussions. Importantly, socio-emotional support initiated during scripted phases transferred to subsequent unscripted task work, suggesting scripts can facilitate sustained collaborative regulation.
2017_v12i3_10.1007_s11412-017-9259-5_Fac.evidence_span: methods (video analysis of 20 group sessions) + findings (script engagement patterns, socio-emotional support provision, transfer effects)
2017_v12i3_10.1007_s11412-017-9259-5_Fac.coding_notes: Study uses video analysis with systematic coding of collaborative episodes (interaction_analysis) combined with frequency counts of script engagement and support behaviors (descriptive_statistics). The regulation macro script is the core pedagogical intervention, and socio-cognitive theory (collaborative conflict, explanation) combined with sociocultural framing (monitoring, regulation) guides the analysis.

2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09441-4_Ho.title: How do new ideas come to be adopted during discourse?
2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09441-4_Ho.authors: Deanna Kuhn & Teresa Fraguada & Mariel Halpern
2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09441-4_Ho.summary_haiku: This study examines how adolescents adopt and revise ideas during electronic peer argumentation. Two case studies traced participants' evolving positions across eight successive dialogs on juvenile justice. Results revealed contrasting patterns: one participant readily adopted partners' ideas but struggled defending positions, while the other maintained firm beliefs with strong counterargument skills but limited openness to new ideas. Findings highlight how argumentation skills, epistemological understanding, and metacognitive reflection jointly influence belief change in collaborative discourse.
2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09441-4_Ho.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (case study design, dialog analysis), findings (contrasting patterns of idea adoption and belief change)
2025_v20i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09441-4_Ho.coding_notes: Study uses case-study tracing of idea adoption across successive dialogs, combining micro-level interaction analysis with discourse coding of argumentation moves. Primary focus is dyadic peer argumentation on juvenile justice; secondary attention to individual learner differences in epistemology and metacognition. Electronic platform is asynchronous forum for peer dialogs. Dialogic theory (Bakhtin-lineage uptake and multi-voiced meaning-making) and socio-cognitive conflict mechanisms both evident.

2017_v12i2_10.1007_s11412-017-9254-x_Ada.title: Adaptable scripting to foster regulation processes and skills in
2017_v12i2_10.1007_s11412-017-9254-x_Ada.authors: Ingo Kollar & Karsten Stegmann & Xinghua Wang
2017_v12i2_10.1007_s11412-017-9254-x_Ada.summary_haiku: This study examined how adaptable collaboration scripts—which allow learners to modify script components based on self-perceived needs—affect regulation processes and skill acquisition in computer-supported collaborative learning. Using a three-phase experimental design with 87 university students, results showed adaptable scripts significantly increased metacognitive reflection and monitoring activities compared to fixed scripts, and substantially improved learners' self-regulation skills in subsequent unscripted tasks. Mediation analyses revealed reflection processes during scripted collaboration explained the positive effects on later regulation skill transfer.
2017_v12i2_10.1007_s11412-017-9254-x_Ada.evidence_span: methods (three-phase experimental design, 87 students) + findings (mediation analyses, metacognitive reflection, regulation skill transfer)
2017_v12i2_10.1007_s11412-017-9254-x_Ada.coding_notes: Study uses controlled experimental comparison of adaptable vs. fixed scripts with mediation analysis to test mechanisms. Primary focus is on collaboration scripts and self-regulation; sociocultural framing emphasizes internalization of regulation processes through scaffolded interaction.

2016_v11i2_10.1007_s11412-016-9233-7_Cul.title: Cultural ways of constructing knowledge: the role of identities in online group discussions
2016_v11i2_10.1007_s11412-016-9233-7_Cul.summary_haiku: This study explores how students utilize multiple identification categories—such as gender, profession, ethnicity, and group affinity—during online group discussions to construct knowledge collaboratively. Through case analysis of asynchronous threaded discussions in a graduate education course, the research demonstrates that individuals flexibly enact different identities at various knowledge-construction phases, using personal experiences to negotiate meaning and advance collective understanding. The findings reveal that identification plays a central role in mediating between personal cognition and social learning processes.
2016_v11i2_10.1007_s11412-016-9233-7_Cul.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (case analysis of threaded discussions), findings (identity enactment and knowledge construction)
2016_v11i2_10.1007_s11412-016-9233-7_Cul.coding_notes: The study is fundamentally a discourse analysis of online threaded discussions, examining how identities are linguistically and rhetorically enacted during knowledge construction. It combines case study methodology with systematic coding of discussion posts. Sociocultural and dialogic theories frame how identities mediate learning through collaborative meaning-making in an asynchronous forum.

2025_v20i3_10.1007_s11412-025-09448-5_Co.title: Collaborative science? Formalism and a unified language: Future directions for computer‑supported collaborative learning
2025_v20i3_10.1007_s11412-025-09448-5_Co.authors: Sten Ludvigsen & Hans C. Arnseth & Kenneth Silseth & Rolf Steier
2025_v20i3_10.1007_s11412-025-09448-5_Co.summary_haiku: # Summary This article responds to calls for unified language and formalism in computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL). Rather than endorsing computational modeling approaches, the authors propose a meta-stance centered on learning mechanisms that integrate cognitive, socio-cognitive, and sociocultural perspectives. They advocate for analyzing moment-by-moment meaning-making through dialogue, mediational tools, and meaning potentials, arguing this approach better captures collaborative learning processes than probabilistic models alone. The authors present an exchange structure formalism and emphasize mechanistic causality in qualitative research to build cumulative CSCL knowledge.
2025_v20i3_10.1007_s11412-025-09448-5_Co.evidence_span: abstract, summary, and theoretical framing throughout
2025_v20i3_10.1007_s11412-025-09448-5_Co.coding_notes: This is a theoretical/methodological position paper proposing formalism for CSCL research. Primary methodology is interaction_analysis because the authors emphasize moment-by-moment dialogue analysis and exchange structures; discourse_analysis is secondary because linguistic/rhetorical meaning-making is central. Unit of analysis is artifact_discourse_trace (dialogue and mediational tools as primary objects), with secondary cross-level analysis implied. Theory is dialogic (Bakhtin-lineage emphasis on multi-voiced dialogue) with sociocultural and socio-cognitive perspectives integrated. No technology or AI involvement; the paper critiques computational modeling approaches rather than endorsing them.

2023_v18i3_10.1007_s11412-023-09390-4_Th.title: The mechanism and effect of class-wide peer feedback on conceptual knowledge improvement: Does different feedback type matter?
2023_v18i3_10.1007_s11412-023-09390-4_Th.authors: Jesmine S. H. Tan & Wenli Chen & Junzhu Su & Guo Su
2023_v18i3_10.1007_s11412-023-09390-4_Th.summary_haiku: Class-wide peer feedback in computer-supported collaborative learning significantly improved students' conceptual knowledge about biological adaptations. Using mixed methods with 38 sixth-graders, researchers found that feedback seeking clarity and providing suggestions yielded highest response rates and knowledge improvement. Elaborated comments with moderate depth were most effective, while excessive elaboration proved cognitively demanding. Results demonstrate that intergroup peer feedback supports knowledge advancement when group-level cognitive capacity is maximized.
2023_v18i3_10.1007_s11412-023-09390-4_Th.coding_notes: Study employs mixed methods (quantitative knowledge gains + qualitative feedback analysis) with class-wide peer feedback as the intervention. Primary unit is the classroom cohort receiving feedback; secondary analysis examines group-level dynamics. Sociocultural framing emphasizes peer interaction and knowledge co-construction; socio-cognitive elements address cognitive load and elaboration depth effects.

2020_v15i4_10.1007_s11412-020-09332-4_Gi.title: Give student ideas a larger stage: support cross-community interaction for knowledge building
2020_v15i4_10.1007_s11412-020-09332-4_Gi.authors: Guangji Yuan & Maria Bogouslavsky & Jianwei Zhang
2020_v15i4_10.1007_s11412-020-09332-4_Gi.summary_haiku: Two grade 5/6 science classrooms engaged in knowledge building about human body systems using Knowledge Forum over ten weeks. Students created "super notes"—synthesized summaries of inquiry progress—as epistemic boundary objects shared in a cross-classroom meta-space. Qualitative analysis revealed students conceived super notes as refined, accessible "big ideas" reflecting their learning journey. Super notes facilitated cross-community interaction, enabling students to encounter diverse perspectives, deepen inquiry, and develop integrated system-level understandings, demonstrating how scaling CSCL practices across classrooms fosters high-level epistemic engagement.
2020_v15i4_10.1007_s11412-020-09332-4_Gi.evidence_span: methods, findings, discussion of super notes and cross-classroom interaction
2020_v15i4_10.1007_s11412-020-09332-4_Gi.coding_notes: Study is a qualitative, in-depth examination of two classrooms using Knowledge Forum over ten weeks, analyzing how super notes (artifacts) mediate cross-community knowledge building. Primary focus is knowledge-building theory and epistemic engagement; secondary methods include systematic coding of student conceptions and interaction patterns. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09307-0_It.title: It is not either or: An initial investigation into combining collaborative and individual learning using an ITS
2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09307-0_It.authors: Nikol Rummel & Vincent Aleven & Jennifer K. Olsen
2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09307-0_It.summary_haiku: This study compared combined collaborative-individual learning to either approach alone using an intelligent tutoring system for fractions with 382 elementary students. Results showed the combined condition produced higher learning gains than individual or collaborative-only conditions, particularly for fourth graders. Process data revealed combined-condition students made fewer errors and requested fewer hints, while reporting greater situational interest in the activity.
2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09307-0_It.evidence_span: methods (experimental design, 382 students, three conditions) + findings (learning gains, process data, error rates, hint requests, situational interest)
2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09307-0_It.coding_notes: Study uses a controlled comparison of three conditions (combined collaborative-individual, collaborative-only, individual-only) with an ITS for fractions. Primary unit is individual learner outcomes (learning gains, errors, hints, interest), though dyads are involved in the collaborative conditions. The ITS is a shared workspace supporting both collaborative and individual problem-solving phases.

2021_v16i1_10.1007_s11412-021-09338-6_Th.title: The spiral model of collaborative knowledge improvement: an exploratory study of a networked collaborative classroom
2021_v16i1_10.1007_s11412-021-09338-6_Th.authors: Wenli Chen & Jesmine S. H. Tan & Zhongling Pi
2021_v16i1_10.1007_s11412-021-09338-6_Th.summary_haiku: This exploratory case study introduces the Spiral Model of Collaborative Knowledge Improvement (SMCKI), a five-phase pedagogical framework designed to scaffold multi-layered collaborative learning in networked classrooms. Pre-service teachers collaboratively designed technology-enhanced learning activities through individual ideation, intra-group synergy, inter-group critique, intra-group refinement, and individual achievement phases. Results demonstrate significant quality improvements in technology-enhanced learning designs across all SMCKI phases, with participants progressively advancing from simple to complex knowledge dimensions.
2021_v16i1_10.1007_s11412-021-09338-6_Th.coding_notes: The SMCKI framework is a structured, iterative pedagogical intervention studied in a networked classroom context with phases scaffolding individual and collaborative refinement of designs. The five-phase model with critique and refinement cycles aligns with knowledge-building principles and collaboration scripts. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

2023_v18i3_10.1007_s11412-023-09403-2_Pr.title: Promoting knowledge building through meta‑discourse and epistemic discourse understanding
2023_v18i3_10.1007_s11412-023-09403-2_Pr.authors: Yuyao Tong & Carol K. K. Chan
2023_v18i3_10.1007_s11412-023-09403-2_Pr.summary_haiku: # Summary This quasi-experimental study examined how meta-discourse—students' reflection on and inquiry into their collaborative discourse—promotes epistemic discourse understanding and productive knowledge-building inquiry. Ninth-grade visual arts students (n=63) in two classes used Knowledge Forum for online collaboration. The experimental class engaged in classroom meta-discourse reflecting on discourse processes, principles, and idea development, while the comparison class used regular discussion. Results showed experimental students developed deeper epistemic discourse understanding and domain knowledge, engaged in more sophisticated knowledge-building discourse moves, and demonstrated stronger relationships between epistemic understanding and productive inquiry, suggesting meta-discourse effectively supports collaborative learning.
2023_v18i3_10.1007_s11412-023-09403-2_Pr.coding_notes: Quasi-experimental design with experimental and comparison classes; Knowledge Forum is the primary technology (wiki-based knowledge repository); Scardamalia & Bereiter's knowledge-building theory is central; meta-discourse and epistemic understanding are analyzed through discourse coding of Knowledge Forum posts.

2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09457-4_Un.title: Understanding collaborative programming dynamics: The role of prior knowledge, engagement and ICAP learning modes
2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09457-4_Un.authors: Jihong Ding & Zhihao Fan & Huazhong Liu & James Slotta & Feng Ji & Kefeng Hu
2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09457-4_Un.summary_haiku: This study examined collaborative programming through multimodal learning analytics, integrating four-dimensional engagement (behavioral, cognitive, social, emotional) with the ICAP framework. Analyzing 18 student triads, findings reveal prior knowledge supports individual task execution but requires strong leadership for collaborative engagement. Social and cognitive engagement strongly correlate, while emotional engagement remains largely independent. Interactive discourse modes foster significantly richer engagement and higher achievement than active modes, with social engagement and emotional regulation emerging as primary predictors of learning outcomes.
2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09457-4_Un.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (multimodal learning analytics, ICAP framework, engagement dimensions)
2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09457-4_Un.coding_notes: Study uses multimodal learning analytics to trace engagement and learning outcomes in collaborative programming triads, grounded in ICAP framework. Primary methodology is learning_analytics (trace data from collaborative work); secondary includes multilevel modeling (nested triads within cohort) and interaction_analysis (discourse modes). Pedagogy emphasizes structured collaboration (ICAP modes) and self-regulation. No AI/LLM involvement detected in study design or intervention.

2021_v16i3_10.1007_s11412-021-09353-7_Ag.title: Agency to transform: how did a grade 5 community co‑configure dynamic knowledge building practices in a yearlong science inquiry?
2021_v16i3_10.1007_s11412-021-09353-7_Ag.summary_haiku: This study investigates how a fifth-grade science classroom co-configured dynamic knowledge-building practices through "reflective structuration"—a process where students and teacher collaboratively constructed and adapted shared inquiry structures over a yearlong human body systems investigation. Using qualitative analysis of classroom observations, online discourse, and student artifacts, researchers documented how students co-formulated nine evolving "big questions" that guided inquiry directions. Analysis revealed students' agentic moves expanded, deepened, and reframed collective work, with social network analysis and pre-post testing demonstrating productive knowledge building outcomes and improved scientific understanding.
2021_v16i3_10.1007_s11412-021-09353-7_Ag.coding_notes: Study exemplifies design-based research with iterative co-configuration of inquiry structures over a full school year. Primary methodology is design-based; interaction analysis and social network analysis are secondary analytic methods. Knowledge building theory and sociocultural framing are explicit; activity theory applies to the structuration process. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09386-0_An.title: An automated group learning engagement analysis and feedback approach to promoting collaborative knowledge building, group performance, and socially shared regulation in CSCL
2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09386-0_An.authors: Lanqin Zheng & Miaolang Long & Jiayu Niu & Lu Zhong
2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09386-0_An.summary_haiku: This study examined an automated group learning engagement analysis and feedback approach using deep neural networks in computer-supported collaborative learning. A quasi-experimental design with 120 college students in 40 groups compared the proposed approach to traditional online collaboration. Results showed significant improvements in cognitive, metacognitive, behavioral, emotional, and social engagement; collaborative knowledge building; group performance; and socially shared regulation, without increasing cognitive load.
2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09386-0_An.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (quasi-experimental design, deep neural networks), findings (engagement, knowledge building, group performance, socially shared regulation)
2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09386-0_An.coding_notes: Study uses deep neural networks for automated analysis and feedback on group engagement in CSCL, supporting knowledge building and socially shared regulation. Classified as AI-supported (non-LLM) because deep neural networks are the primary AI mechanism; secondary coding includes LLM-supported analytics if the neural network analysis involved text processing. Quasi-experimental design with 40 groups as primary unit of analysis.

2017_v12i4_10.1007_s11412-017-9262-x_The.title: The value of learning talk: applying a novel dialogue scoring method to inform interaction design in an open-ended, embodied museum exhibit
2017_v12i4_10.1007_s11412-017-9262-x_The.summary_haiku: # Summary Researchers developed SQuILD, a novel dialogue-scoring method for quantifying learning talk in open-ended museum exhibits. Testing this method on 119 visitor groups interacting with an interactive census data map, they compared full-body versus handheld tablet controls and single versus multi-user input configurations. Contrary to theoretical predictions, handheld tablet controls produced significantly higher-quality learning dialogue than full-body interaction, suggesting that intuitive, familiar interfaces may better support collaborative meaning-making than physically immersive designs.
2017_v12i4_10.1007_s11412-017-9262-x_The.evidence_span: methods (SQuILD dialogue-scoring method, experimental design with 119 visitor groups, comparison of interface conditions) + findings (quality of learning dialogue across conditions)
2017_v12i4_10.1007_s11412-017-9262-x_The.coding_notes: The study applies a novel coding scheme (SQuILD) to systematically analyze dialogue quality in visitor interactions, making interaction_analysis the primary methodology. The experimental comparison of full-body versus handheld tablet controls and single versus multi-user configurations supports experimental_quasi_experimental as secondary. The open-ended museum exhibit and focus on collaborative meaning-making align with inquiry-based pedagogy and sociocultural theory.

2024_v19i4_10.1007_s11412-024-09436-1_St.title: Students’ use of technological tools to engage in collective mathematical proof activity
2024_v19i4_10.1007_s11412-024-09436-1_St.summary_haiku: Using instrumental genesis theory, this study examined how students in a remote introduction to proofs course operationalized Google Docs and Zoom to engage in collaborative proof activity. Analysis of six episodes revealed students developed collective utilization schemes coordinating visual mediators with verbal communication to enable collective argumentation and co-construct solutions through iterative text refinement. Google Docs' simultaneous editing and referencing features particularly supported active, process-oriented proof writing.
2024_v19i4_10.1007_s11412-024-09436-1_St.evidence_span: methods (episode analysis, instrumental genesis framework) + findings (collective utilization schemes, iterative refinement)
2024_v19i4_10.1007_s11412-024-09436-1_St.coding_notes: Study uses micro-analytic coding of collaborative proof episodes (interaction_analysis) grounded in instrumental genesis theory (sociocultural). Google Docs and Zoom are the primary technologies; simultaneous editing and visual mediators are central to the analysis. Secondary methods include discourse analysis of argumentation and content analysis of proof artifacts.

2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9269-y_Exp.title: Exploring college English language learners’ self and social regulation of learning during wiki-supported collaborative reading activities
2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9269-y_Exp.authors: You Su & Yanyan Li & Hening Hu & Carolyn P. Rose
2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9269-y_Exp.summary_haiku: This study examined self and social regulation of learning among 60 Chinese college English language learners during wiki-supported collaborative reading activities. Using content analysis and sequential analysis of chat logs, researchers found that high-performing groups demonstrated significantly more content monitoring, evaluation, and emotional regulation than low-performing groups. Sequential analysis revealed high-performing groups exhibited bidirectional patterns between co-regulation and socially shared regulation, while low-performing groups repeated self-regulation patterns.
2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9269-y_Exp.evidence_span: methods (content analysis, sequential analysis of chat logs) + findings (regulation patterns by group performance)
2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9269-y_Exp.coding_notes: Study uses systematic coding of chat logs (content analysis) combined with sequential pattern analysis to examine self and social regulation. Wiki is the primary collaborative technology; chat logs are the primary artifact analyzed. Sociocultural framing of regulation as socially mediated learning process.

2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9270-5_Lea.title: Learning to monitor and regulate collective thinking processes
2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9270-5_Lea.authors: Yann Shiou Ong & Marcela Borge & Carolyn Penstein Rose
2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9270-5_Lea.summary_haiku: Students using a computer-supported framework for monitoring collaborative discussions significantly improved discourse quality over ten weeks. The study examined 37 students across 13 teams engaging in five discussion sessions, comparing two reflective scripting conditions. Results showed teams enhanced collaborative processes through individual assessment of communication patterns followed by collective sense-making, with evidence-based reflection prompts yielding higher-quality discourse than future-thinking prompts.
2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9270-5_Lea.evidence_span: methods (37 students, 13 teams, 5 sessions, two conditions) + findings (discourse quality improvement, reflection prompts comparison)
2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9270-5_Lea.coding_notes: Study compares two reflective scripting conditions (evidence-based vs. future-thinking prompts) in a controlled design. Primary focus is on self and peer regulation through monitoring and collective sense-making of communication patterns. Awareness dashboard displays collaborative discussion data to support reflection.

2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09328-0_Di.title: Dialogic intervisualizing in multimodal inquiry
2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09328-0_Di.authors: Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver & Lap Ki Chan & Judith L. Green & Susan M. Bridges & Asmalina Saleh
2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09328-0_Di.summary_haiku: Medical students collaboratively constructed understanding of cardiovascular physiology through facilitated problem-based learning using multimodal digital texts. Using Interactional Ethnography to analyze one PBL cycle, researchers traced how students iteratively accessed, curated, and generated visual representations—from simple diagrams to complex cardiac cycle charts—within dialogic exchanges with their facilitator. The study proposes "dialogic intervisualizing" as a theoretical construct characterizing dynamic interplay between information problem-solving, textual negotiation, and purposeful dialogue for deep knowledge co-construction in computer-supported inquiry.
2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09328-0_Di.evidence_span: methods (Interactional Ethnography, PBL cycle analysis) + findings (dialogic intervisualizing construct, iterative visual representation use)
2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09328-0_Di.coding_notes: Study employs fine-grained interaction analysis of collaborative medical students' moment-by-moment dialogue and multimodal artifact use within problem-based learning. Interactional Ethnography is a qualitative, discourse-centered methodology aligned with interaction analysis and ethnographic case study. Primary technology is the shared digital workspace where visual representations are co-constructed; multimodal analysis of texts and dialogue is central.

2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9272-3_Con.title: Connecting levels of activity with classroom network technology
2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9272-3_Con.summary_haiku: Classroom network technology enables fluid transitions between individual, small-group, and whole-class mathematics instruction. Through design-based research analyzing two learning environments, this study identifies mechanisms—appropriation, mediation, emergence, and orchestration—that support multilevel activity. Findings reveal that rather than sequential shifts between levels, classroom activity often exhibits simultaneous, overlapping interactions across planes, with shared mathematical objects mediating connections between groups and facilitating dynamic classroom participation.
2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9272-3_Con.coding_notes: Design-based research iteratively studying classroom network technology across individual, small-group, and whole-class levels. Activity theory framework explicitly referenced through mechanisms (appropriation, mediation, emergence, orchestration) and analysis of overlapping activity planes. Classroom network technology enables shared mathematical objects mediating multilevel interactions.

2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09325-3_Fi.title: Finding a place for equity in CSCL: ambitious learning practices as a lever for sustained educational change
2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09325-3_Fi.authors: Suraj Uttamchandani & Ayesha Bhimdiwala & Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver
2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09325-3_Fi.summary_haiku: This conceptual article argues that computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) should prioritize educational equity by implementing ambitious learning practices—pedagogies emphasizing collaboration, dialogue, and disciplinary engagement. The authors contend that centering equity through student agency, shared meaning-making, and disruption of social inequality positions CSCL to meaningfully contribute to sustained educational change. They examine adaptive collaborative learning support as a case study, highlighting tensions between technological structure and learner agency while proposing that CSCL innovations can support equitable educational transformation when equity considerations guide development throughout.
2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09325-3_Fi.evidence_span: abstract, conceptual framing, case study discussion
2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09325-3_Fi.coding_notes: This is a conceptual/position paper rather than an empirical study, so methodology is inferred from the case study of adaptive collaborative learning support and the emphasis on examining tensions between technology and learner agency. The focus on equity, agency, and disruption of inequality aligns with critical pragmatic theory alongside sociocultural foundations.

2018_v13i2_10.1007_s11412-018-9276-z_Orc.title: Orchestrating the emergence of conceptual learning: a case study in a geometry class
2018_v13i2_10.1007_s11412-018-9276-z_Orc.authors: Baruch B. Schwarz & Naomi Prusak & Osama Swidan & Adva Livny & Kobi Gal & Avi Segal
2018_v13i2_10.1007_s11412-018-9276-z_Orc.summary_haiku: # Summary This case study investigates whether teachers can orchestrate conceptual learning across multiple student groups working simultaneously on geometry tasks. Using SAGLET, a system that monitors parallel group work and alerts teachers to critical moments via machine learning, the researchers observed one experienced teacher guiding eight groups through challenging quadrilateral hierarchy problems. Analysis revealed five intervention types—collaboration encouragement, task supervision, justification requests, argumentation scaffolding, and social validation—with scaffolding being most frequent. Results demonstrate successful orchestration: seven of eight groups solved difficult tasks requiring abstract geometric reasoning, suggesting that real-time alerts and visibility tools enable adaptive guidance across multiple groups in classroom settings.
2018_v13i2_10.1007_s11412-018-9276-z_Orc.coding_notes: SAGLET uses machine learning to monitor and alert teachers to critical moments in parallel group work, enabling real-time orchestration. The study is design-based (iterative intervention in naturalistic classroom) with strong interaction analysis of teacher moves and learning analytics components. AI involvement is non-LLM (ML classifiers for moment detection); secondary coding includes potential post-hoc analysis support.

2021_v16i3_10.1007_s11412-021-09350-w_Th.title: The impact of a gamified mobile question‑asking app on museum visitor group interactions: an ICAP framing
2021_v16i3_10.1007_s11412-021-09350-w_Th.authors: Jesse Ha & Luis E. Perez Cortes & Man Su & Brian C. Nelson & Catherine Bowman & Judd D. Bowman
