2021_v16i3_10.1007_s11412-021-09350-w_Th.summary_haiku: This study examined how a gamified mobile question-asking app affects museum visitor group interactions using the ICAP framework. Researchers compared two app modes—Ask Mode (baseline) and Game Mode (gamified)—across 1,539 visitor groups at two museums. Results showed gamified versions significantly increased group discussion frequency and collaborative question-asking, particularly among family groups and when children controlled the device, supporting mobile apps' potential for fostering informal collaborative learning.
2021_v16i3_10.1007_s11412-021-09350-w_Th.evidence_span: methods (comparison of Ask Mode vs. Game Mode), findings (group discussion frequency, collaborative question-asking)
2021_v16i3_10.1007_s11412-021-09350-w_Th.coding_notes: Study compares two app conditions (quasi-experimental design) with large sample of visitor groups (n=1,539). ICAP framework guides analysis of collaborative interaction quality. Technology is a mobile app supporting question-asking; classified as synchronous because real-time group interaction is the focus, though awareness/gamification elements also present. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

2017_v12i4_10.1007_s11412-017-9266-6_I_t.title: I think you just got mixed up: confident peer tutors hedge to support partners’ face needs
2017_v12i4_10.1007_s11412-017-9266-6_I_t.authors: Justine Cassell & Amy Ogan & Michael Madaio
2017_v12i4_10.1007_s11412-017-9266-6_I_t.summary_haiku: Peer tutors with lower social closeness to tutees provide more positive feedback and use indirect language when delivering instructions and comprehension-monitoring, but only when they possess high tutoring self-efficacy. Conversely, tutees benefit from hedged instructions and comprehension-monitoring specifically in low-rapport dyads, suggesting that interpersonal closeness reduces the need for indirectness while self-efficacy enables strategic face-threat mitigation.
2017_v12i4_10.1007_s11412-017-9266-6_I_t.coding_notes: Study analyzes peer tutoring dyads through coded linguistic features (hedging, indirectness) and feedback patterns, examining how tutors strategically mitigate face threats based on self-efficacy and social closeness. Interaction analysis is primary; content analysis of language use is secondary. Sociocultural framing (face needs, interpersonal dynamics) with socio-cognitive elements (self-efficacy, comprehension monitoring).

2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09402-3_Co.title: Common “place” observations about embodiment and CSCL
2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09402-3_Co.summary_haiku: This commentary examines embodied computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) by arguing that shared physical or digital "place" is central to how multiple bodies coordinate learning. Unlike earlier embodied learning research focusing on individual sensorimotor experience, embodied CSCL leverages three key resources: differing relative perspectives, body motion/gesture, and common referents. The author proposes that foregrounding place in future embodied CSCL research and design could advance understanding of how technology mediates collaborative meaning-making among co-located learners.
2023_v18i2_10.1007_s11412-023-09402-3_Co.coding_notes: This is a commentary/position paper rather than an empirical study, so methodology is inferred from its focus on embodied interaction in co-located CSCL contexts. The emphasis on shared place, gesture, and relative perspectives suggests tabletop/tangible interfaces and sociocultural framing, though the article is primarily theoretical rather than reporting original data collection.

2024_v19i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09416-x_Ta.title: Taking a stance in the process of learning: Developing perspectival understandings through knowledge co‑construction during synchronous computer‑mediated classroom discussion
2024_v19i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09416-x_Ta.authors: Hannah Park & Diane L. Schallert & Kyle M. Williams & Rachel E. Gaines & Jeonghyun Lee & van de Sande
2024_v19i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09416-x_Ta.summary_haiku: This study examined how graduate students expressed perspectives through stancetaking during synchronous online classroom discussions. Using Du Bois' discourse framework, researchers analyzed 27 chat transcripts, coding for epistemic, affective, and evaluative stances alongside positioning, evaluation, and alignment acts. Findings revealed students predominantly adopted epistemic stances focused on knowledge acquisition, with shifts in discussion topics marking moments of perspectival understanding development. The analysis demonstrates how collaborative knowledge co-construction occurs through iterative combinations of subsidiary stance acts.
2024_v19i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09416-x_Ta.evidence_span: methods (Du Bois framework, coding scheme for stances) + findings (chat transcript analysis, perspectival understanding development)
2024_v19i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09416-x_Ta.coding_notes: Study is fundamentally a discourse analysis of chat transcripts using Du Bois' stancetaking framework with systematic coding of epistemic, affective, and evaluative stances. Interaction analysis is secondary because moment-by-moment collaborative episodes are examined through stance acts and alignment. Content analysis is tertiary as a coding-based approach. Dialogic theory is primary given the focus on multi-voiced perspective expression and uptake; knowledge-building theory is secondary given the emphasis on co-construction.

2017_v12i3_10.1007_s11412-017-9261-y_Cra.title: Cracking her codes: understanding shared technology resources as positioning artifacts for power and status in CSCL environments
2017_v12i3_10.1007_s11412-017-9261-y_Cra.authors: Amber Simpson & Nicole Bannister & Gretchen Matthews
2017_v12i3_10.1007_s11412-017-9261-y_Cra.summary_haiku: Researchers used positioning theory and interaction analysis to examine how two pairs of female students negotiated power and status around shared technology during cryptography tasks. Analysis revealed that technology control functioned as a positioning artifact reflecting and reinforcing power dynamics: one pair exhibited stark dominance limiting participation, while the other showed subtle status imbalances without apparent learning impact. The study concludes that interactions around technology serve as critical indicators of negotiated power and status in collaborative learning environments.
2017_v12i3_10.1007_s11412-017-9261-y_Cra.evidence_span: methods (positioning theory, interaction analysis) + findings (power/status negotiation around technology control)
2017_v12i3_10.1007_s11412-017-9261-y_Cra.coding_notes: Study employs micro-analytic interaction analysis of moment-by-moment collaborative episodes around shared technology use, grounded in positioning theory (a critical lens on power and status). Secondary unit is the technology artifact itself as a positioning resource. Pedagogy coded as collaboration_scripts because the cryptography task structure implicitly regulates interaction; no explicit scripting mentioned but task design constrains roles.

2024_v19i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09421-8_Re.title: Reflective assessment using analytics and artifacts for scaffolding knowledge building competencies among undergraduate students
2024_v19i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09421-8_Re.authors: Yuqin Yang & Carol K. K. Chan & Gaoxia Zhu & Yuyao Tong & Daner Sun
2024_v19i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09421-8_Re.summary_haiku: # Summary This study develops a comprehensive framework of knowledge building (KB) competencies encompassing conceptual, metacognitive, socio-emotional, and epistemic dimensions. Using qualitative discourse analysis of 1,390 Knowledge Forum notes from 41 undergraduates, the research demonstrates that reflective assessment enriched with super synthesis notes, KB interaction rubrics, and KBDeX learning analytics visualizations significantly fosters development of these competencies. Results show undergraduates engaged in higher-level productive discourse moves across all dimensions, with sequential pattern analysis revealing progressive improvements in socio-emotional interactions and epistemic engagement between pre- and post-intervention stages.
2024_v19i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09421-8_Re.evidence_span: methods (discourse analysis of 1,390 KB notes, sequential pattern analysis) + findings (progressive improvements in competencies across dimensions)
2024_v19i2_10.1007_s11412-024-09421-8_Re.coding_notes: Study centers on qualitative discourse analysis of Knowledge Forum artifacts with learning analytics (KBDeX visualizations) as a secondary analytical tool. Knowledge building theory and Scardamalia & Bereiter framework are explicit. No LLM or advanced AI involvement; analytics are rule-based dashboards for reflection scaffolding.

2016_v11i4_10.1007_s11412-016-9246-2_Con.title: Conversational agents for academically productive talk: a comparison of directed and undirected agent interventions
2016_v11i4_10.1007_s11412-016-9246-2_Con.authors: Stergios Tegos & Stavros Demetriadis & Pantelis M. Papadopoulos & Armin Weinberger
2016_v11i4_10.1007_s11412-016-9246-2_Con.summary_haiku: This study compared directed versus undirected conversational agent interventions promoting academically productive talk in 96 computer science students working in dyads. Using a pre-test/post-test experimental design with discourse analysis, results showed directed interventions—addressing individual students—significantly enhanced individual domain knowledge and explicit reasoning compared to undirected interventions addressing both peers. Explicit reasoning mediated the agent's effect on dyad performance, with directed methods proving more effective at stimulating productive discourse.
2016_v11i4_10.1007_s11412-016-9246-2_Con.coding_notes: Study employs pre-test/post-test experimental design comparing two agent intervention conditions (directed vs. undirected) with discourse analysis of talk and inferential statistics on learning outcomes. Conversational agents function as orchestrators of productive dialogue, aligned with dialogic and sociocultural frameworks. Agents provide feedback/prompts to regulate discussion quality.

2016_v11i4_10.1007_s11412-016-9244-4_Wha.title: What happens when you push the button? Analyzing the functional dynamics of concept development in computer supported science inquiry
2016_v11i4_10.1007_s11412-016-9244-4_Wha.summary_haiku: This study examines how high school students develop scientific concepts through computer-supported collaborative inquiry into energy transformation. Using video ethnography, researchers analyzed students' interactions with material and digital tools while learning to explain how a heat pump works. Results demonstrate that students progressively developed sophisticated use of science concepts as explanatory tools through a functional system comprising teacher guidance, material artifacts, and digital models. Teacher practices—including eliciting understanding, providing strategic hints, and modeling coherent concept use—were crucial for supporting students' conceptual development across multiple representations.
2016_v11i4_10.1007_s11412-016-9244-4_Wha.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (video ethnography), findings (teacher guidance, material artifacts, digital models)
2016_v11i4_10.1007_s11412-016-9244-4_Wha.coding_notes: Video ethnography with micro-analytic focus on student–teacher–tool interactions during inquiry into energy transformation. Primary unit is small groups of students, but teacher facilitation and artifact use are integral to the analysis. Sociocultural framing emphasizes mediation through tools and social guidance; distributed cognition captures the functional system spanning people, materials, and digital representations.

2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09392-2_Co.title: Contesting sociocomputational norms: Computer programming instructors and students’ stancetaking around refactoring
2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09392-2_Co.authors: Morgan M. Fong & David DeLiema & Virginia J. Flood & Oia Walker-van Aalst
2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09392-2_Co.summary_haiku: This interaction analysis study examines how elementary and middle school students and instructors negotiate refactoring—revising working code—in a programming workshop. Using stancetaking, sociocomputational norms, and inequity frameworks, researchers analyzed 20 minutes of classroom discourse. Findings reveal that while students initially debated coding approaches, instructors progressively endorsed loops as superior, amplifying relational inequity by devaluing alternative strategies and limiting discussion of efficiency's multiple interpretations.
2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09392-2_Co.coding_notes: Study explicitly frames itself as interaction analysis examining moment-by-moment classroom discourse around refactoring. Stancetaking and sociocomputational norms are analyzed through a critical lens focused on inequity in participation and knowledge valuation. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

2019_v14i2_10.1007_s11412-019-09302-5_Le.title: Learners’ agency and CSCL technologies: towards an emancipatory perspective
2019_v14i2_10.1007_s11412-019-09302-5_Le.summary_haiku: This conceptual article argues that CSCL should adopt an emancipatory perspective prioritizing learners' agency over technology-imposed constraints. Tchounikine proposes that learners should be empowered to select, adapt, and interoperate software applications while receiving informed feedback. The analysis identifies key challenges: enabling technology choice, supporting customization, and providing transparent information—requiring fundamental reconceptualization of CSCL technologies as services rather than fixed applications.
2019_v14i2_10.1007_s11412-019-09302-5_Le.coding_notes: This is a conceptual/theoretical position paper rather than an empirical study, so methodology and unit of analysis do not apply in traditional sense. The work prioritizes learners' agency and emancipatory perspective (critical_pragmatic lens) within a sociocultural framework, but does not report empirical data collection or analysis. Technology is discussed abstractly as a design principle rather than a specific tool.

2016_v11i4_10.1007_s11412-016-9243-5_Imp.title: Improving collaborative learning in the classroom: Text mining based grouping and representing
2016_v11i4_10.1007_s11412-016-9243-5_Imp.authors: Daniel Bodemer & Melanie Erkens & H. Ulrich Hoppe
2016_v11i4_10.1007_s11412-016-9243-5_Imp.summary_haiku: This study developed and tested the Grouping and Representing Tool (GRT), which uses text mining to automatically form heterogeneous learning groups and visualize students' knowledge. Comparing Latent Dirichlet Allocation and Vector Space Models, researchers found LDA superior for visualizing cognitive information while Euclidean distance-based clustering better identified text differences for grouping. An experimental evaluation with 54 high school students showed GRT-supported dyads achieved twice the knowledge gains compared to unsupported groups, demonstrating text mining's effectiveness for supporting collaborative learning.
2016_v11i4_10.1007_s11412-016-9243-5_Imp.coding_notes: Study uses text mining (LDA, Vector Space Models, clustering) as an AI mechanism to automate group formation and knowledge visualization—not LLM-based. The experimental comparison of GRT-supported vs. unsupported dyads with learning gains as outcome is the primary methodological contribution. Secondary methods include NLP/text mining for analysis and learning analytics via trace data from student texts.

2024_v19i4_10.1007_s11412-024-09437-0_Us.title: Using generative ai as a simulation to support higher‑order thinking
2024_v19i4_10.1007_s11412-024-09437-0_Us.authors: M. Borge & B. K. Smith & T. Aldemir
2024_v19i4_10.1007_s11412-024-09437-0_Us.summary_haiku: # Summary This case study examines whether generative AI can support higher-order thinking through human-computer collaboration. An expert in collaborative learning engaged in extended dialogue with ChatGPT, practicing metacognitive and sociometacognitive skills while reflecting on interaction quality using a framework of six communication patterns. Findings indicate ChatGPT feasibly supports both individual metacognition and collective sensemaking when users actively regulate conversations and employ structured reflection prompts, though limitations like tendency toward definitive unsupported claims require human oversight for effective learning.
2024_v19i4_10.1007_s11412-024-09437-0_Us.evidence_span: methods + findings; case study design with dialogue analysis and reflection framework
2024_v19i4_10.1007_s11412-024-09437-0_Us.coding_notes: Case study of one expert user in extended dialogue with ChatGPT, analyzing interaction patterns and metacognitive reflection. Primary focus is the dyadic human-AI collaboration and discourse analysis of communication patterns. Sociocultural and dialogic theories frame learning as mediated through dialogue and reflection.

2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09355-5_Th.title: The trade‑off between individuals and groups: role interactions under different technology affordance conditions
2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09355-5_Th.summary_haiku: This study examined how technology affordances—specifically device-to-student ratios (1:1 versus 1:m) and external scripts—influence role-based interactions during collaborative scientific inquiry. Using thematic analysis, descriptive statistics, and social network analysis with 130 fifth-grade students across three inquiry experiments, researchers identified eleven emergent roles organized into five categories. Key findings revealed that limited technology resources and external scripts promoted collective awareness, while personal device ownership encouraged individual-focused behavior. Stable group action orientations facilitated better coordination and learning outcomes, though close interaction density did not guarantee collaborative effectiveness.
2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09355-5_Th.evidence_span: methods (thematic analysis, SNA, descriptive statistics) + findings (role interactions, group coordination, learning outcomes)
2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09355-5_Th.coding_notes: Primary methodology is social network analysis of role-based interactions; secondary methods include thematic coding (content analysis) and descriptive statistics. Study examines both individual roles and group-level coordination under different technology affordances, supporting cross-level analysis. External scripts and device ratios are core pedagogical manipulations.

2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9271-4_Usi.title: Using technological functions on a multi-touch table and their affordances to counteract biases and foster collaborative problem solving
2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9271-4_Usi.authors: Inga M. Bause & Irina R. Brich & Ann-Katrin Wesslein & Friedrich W. Hesse
2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9271-4_Usi.summary_haiku: Multi-touch table support functions with affordances for moving, structuring, and merging information significantly enhanced collaborative problem-solving in hidden-profile tasks. University student triads using the collaboration support kit showed greater discussion intensity, more balanced information exchange, stronger mutual understanding indicators, and five times higher correct decision rates compared to standard conditions, demonstrating that intuitive technological affordances can overcome biases from prior preferences.
2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9271-4_Usi.evidence_span: methods (experimental design with triads, multi-touch table conditions) + findings (discussion intensity, information exchange balance, decision accuracy)
2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9271-4_Usi.coding_notes: Study compares multi-touch table with affordances (moving, structuring, merging) against standard conditions in hidden-profile collaborative problem-solving tasks. The technological affordances function as collaboration scripts by structuring how information is manipulated and shared. Distributed cognition is primary because cognition is distributed across the group and the tangible interface; sociocultural is secondary given the emphasis on social interaction and mediation.

2019_v14i4_10.1007_s11412-019-09309-y_Co.title: Cohesion in online environments
2019_v14i4_10.1007_s11412-019-09309-y_Co.summary_haiku: Online group cohesion emerges from students' engagement choices in asynchronous collaboration. This case study analyzed 29 students completing design assignments through a custom platform, measuring cohesion via behavioral engagement, interactivity, and cognitive engagement. Results show students prioritized thoughtful commenting over interactive dialogue, achieving moderate cohesion sufficient for reflective meaning-making but limited direct negotiation of ideas.
2019_v14i4_10.1007_s11412-019-09309-y_Co.evidence_span: methods (case study design, cohesion measurement via behavioral/cognitive engagement coding) + findings (engagement patterns, commenting vs. dialogue)
2019_v14i4_10.1007_s11412-019-09309-y_Co.coding_notes: Study employs systematic coding of student engagement behaviors (behavioral, interactivity, cognitive dimensions) in asynchronous platform interactions, characteristic of content analysis. Secondary methodology includes descriptive statistics on cohesion measures. Peer review/feedback is primary pedagogy given emphasis on commenting; inquiry-based design assignments are secondary. Asynchronous forum is primary technology; shared workspace (custom platform for collaborative design) is secondary.

2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09306-1_Su.title: Supporting classroom orchestration with real-time feedback: A role for teacher dashboards and real-time agents
2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09306-1_Su.summary_haiku: This design-based research study investigates how real-time software agents and teacher dashboards support orchestration of complex collaborative physics inquiry in high school classrooms. Using the Knowledge Community and Inquiry model, researchers developed SAIL Smart Space technology with four agent types to dynamically manage student grouping, material allocation, and teacher notifications. Results demonstrate that the tablet-based orchestration system successfully reduced teacher workload while enabling timely interventions that significantly improved student problem-solving outcomes.
2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09306-1_Su.coding_notes: Design-based research iteratively develops and studies SAIL Smart Space with rule-based software agents (not LLMs) managing grouping and notifications. Teacher dashboards and agents are central to orchestration support in a physics inquiry classroom. Sociocultural framing emphasizes mediation of collaborative learning through technology and teacher awareness.

2022_v17i3_10.1007_s11412-022-09377-7_Im.title: Implementing learning analytics in wiki-supported collaborative learning in secondary education: A framework- motivated empirical study
2022_v17i3_10.1007_s11412-022-09377-7_Im.authors: Xiao Hu & Jeremy T. D. Ng & Samuel K. W. Chu
2022_v17i3_10.1007_s11412-022-09377-7_Im.summary_haiku: This study proposes a learning analytics framework for assessing wiki-supported collaborative learning quality across contribution, participation, transactivity, and social dynamics. Using mixed methods with 440 secondary students and six teachers, regression analyses and interviews revealed that students' and teachers' use of Wikiglass, an LA-enabled group awareness tool, significantly predicted collaboration quality metrics at individual and group levels, particularly when viewing other groups' analytics.
2022_v17i3_10.1007_s11412-022-09377-7_Im.evidence_span: methods (mixed methods, regression, interviews) + findings (individual and group-level analytics predictions)
2022_v17i3_10.1007_s11412-022-09377-7_Im.coding_notes: Study explicitly combines quantitative regression analyses with qualitative interviews across individual and group levels. Wikiglass functions as both a wiki platform and an awareness dashboard displaying group analytics. No LLM or advanced AI involvement detected; focus is on learning analytics framework and group awareness tools.

2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09384-2_Vi.title: Visions of the good in
2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09384-2_Vi.authors: Etan Cohen & Dani Ben-Zvi & Yotam Hod
2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09384-2_Vi.summary_haiku: This article examines ethical dimensions of design-based research in computer-supported collaborative learning. Using a Knowledge Building Community case study, the authors propose three ethical frameworks—aretaic, deontological, and consequentialist—to help CSCL researchers systematically articulate their ideological commitments and visions of the good. They present a seven-question framework for unpacking these ethical foundations across design phases and demonstrate how empirical findings can refine moral principles iteratively.
2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09384-2_Vi.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods, discussion of design phases and ethical frameworks
2023_v18i1_10.1007_s11412-023-09384-2_Vi.coding_notes: The article is a meta-analytical or theoretical examination of design-based research in CSCL using a Knowledge Building Community case study. It focuses on unpacking ethical dimensions through three philosophical frameworks (aretaic, deontological, consequentialist) rather than conducting empirical hypothesis testing. The primary unit of analysis is the design process and its ethical commitments, though discourse and artifacts from the community are examined to illustrate principles.

2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9290-1_Stu.title: Students’ engagement with real-time graphs in CSCL settings: scrutinizing the role of teacher support
2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9290-1_Stu.authors: Line Ingulfsen & Anniken Furberg & Torunn Aanesland Stromme
2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9290-1_Stu.summary_haiku: This study examined student-teacher interactions during collaborative real-time lab work on ocean acidification. Using interaction analysis of 49 student-teacher exchanges, researchers identified challenges students faced interpreting graphs and connecting experimental actions to scientific phenomena. The teacher provided crucial support through eliciting strategies—using gestures, prompts, and cued questions—and elaboration strategies, demonstrating how teacher guidance intersects with digital resources and instructional design to scaffold conceptual understanding in CSCL settings.
2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9290-1_Stu.evidence_span: methods (interaction analysis of 49 exchanges) + findings (teacher eliciting and elaboration strategies)
2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9290-1_Stu.coding_notes: Study uses micro-analytic coding of moment-by-moment student-teacher interactions during collaborative real-time lab work with digital graphs. Teacher support through questioning and demonstration is central; sociocultural framing emphasizes scaffolding and mediation of understanding through dialogue.

2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09400-5_Id.title: Identifying collaborative problem‑solver profiles based on collaborative processing time, actions and skills on a computer‑based task
2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09400-5_Id.authors: Yue Ma & Huilin Zhang & Li Ni & Da Zhou
2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09400-5_Id.summary_haiku: This study employed latent profile analysis on PISA 2015 data from 1,677 Chinese students to identify four distinct collaborative problem-solver profiles based on time-on-task, actions-on-task, and three CPS skills: Disengaged, Struggling, Adaptive, and Excellent. Results revealed that gender, socioeconomic status, and attitudes toward collaboration significantly predicted profile membership, while achievement motivation did not. Profile membership correlated with CPS performance differences.
2023_v18i4_10.1007_s11412-023-09400-5_Id.coding_notes: Latent profile analysis is a descriptive statistical technique identifying subgroups without inferential hypothesis testing; the study uses PISA trace data (learning analytics) to characterize individual problem-solver profiles. Pedagogy is coded 'other' because the study is primarily descriptive/profiling rather than testing a specific pedagogical intervention.

2016_v11i2_10.1007_s11412-016-9234-6_Qua.title: Quantitative approach to collaborative learning: performance prediction, individual assessment, and group composition
2016_v11i2_10.1007_s11412-016-9234-6_Qua.authors: Ling Cen & Dymitr Ruta & Leigh Powell & Benjamin Hirsch & Jason Ng
2016_v11i2_10.1007_s11412-016-9234-6_Qua.summary_haiku: This study applies machine learning techniques to predict group performance in computer-supported collaborative learning using interaction data from 122 students across three assignments. The research develops normalized features capturing collaboration patterns and proposes a comparative model to assess individual student contributions within groups. Results demonstrate 79% classification accuracy and reveal that heterogeneous groups with mixed genders and diverse skill levels achieve significantly greater collaborative synergy than homogeneous groups.
2016_v11i2_10.1007_s11412-016-9234-6_Qua.coding_notes: Study uses machine learning (classification models) on interaction trace data to predict group performance and assess individual contributions; primary focus is learning analytics with group-level outcomes, though individual assessment is also examined. Technology platform not explicitly named but involves CSCL interaction logging. No LLMs involved; classical ML classifiers used.

2022_v17i4_10.1007_s11412-022-09379-5_Em.title: Emotion expression and recognition in written digital discussions on Civic Issues
2022_v17i4_10.1007_s11412-022-09379-5_Em.authors: Benzi Slakmon & Omer Keynan & Orly Shapira
2022_v17i4_10.1007_s11412-022-09379-5_Em.summary_haiku: This study examined emotion expression and recognition in written digital discussions on controversial civic issues among nine undergraduate students. Using mixed methods—analyzing 23 discussion turns through follow-up interviews—researchers compared how participants labeled their own emotions with how peers recognized them. Findings revealed low correlation between composers' emotion labeling and others' recognition, lack of shared emotional vocabulary, and two key recognition strategies: attributing emotions based on perceived closeness/belonging to topics, and using iconized visual imagery. Despite poor alignment, participants successfully communicated emotionally through dialogic engagement.
2022_v17i4_10.1007_s11412-022-09379-5_Em.evidence_span: methods (mixed methods, 23 discussion turns, follow-up interviews), findings (emotion labeling, recognition strategies, dialogic engagement)
2022_v17i4_10.1007_s11412-022-09379-5_Em.coding_notes: Study combines quantitative comparison of emotion labels with qualitative interview data and discourse analysis of written posts. Primary focus is on how emotion is expressed and recognized in peer-to-peer digital discussion; dialogic theory fits the emphasis on multi-voiced meaning-making around emotional content in civic discourse.

2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9251-0_Gro.title: Group practices: a new way of viewing CSCL
2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9251-0_Gro.summary_haiku: Stahl proposes analyzing group practices—observable, routinized behaviors enacted by small collaborative teams—as central to understanding computer-supported collaborative learning. Using design-based research with the Virtual Math Teams project, he demonstrates that groups adopt practices through breakdowns and negotiation, mediating between individual cognition and cultural knowledge. This approach provides systematic methodology for CSCL design, theory, and analysis beyond traditional pre/post comparisons.
2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9251-0_Gro.evidence_span: title, abstract, and conceptual framing of group practices approach
2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9251-0_Gro.coding_notes: Stahl's work is foundational CSCL theory emphasizing group practices as emergent, routinized behaviors. Design-based research with Virtual Math Teams is the primary methodology; interaction analysis of breakdowns and negotiation is secondary. Sociocultural and activity-theoretic framing is evident in the mediation between individual and cultural levels.

2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09453-8_Ho.title: How children blend feedback in a mixed‑reality environment for collective embodied learning
2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09453-8_Ho.authors: Sarah Jaewon Lee & Xintian Tu & Simeon Adebola & D. Teo Keifert & Noel Enyedy & Joshua Danish
2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09453-8_Ho.summary_haiku: # Summary This study examined how young children coordinate multiple feedback sources—self, peers, teachers, and technology—in a mixed-reality learning environment called STEP to understand states of matter. Using interaction analysis of three episodes (making solid, liquid, and gas bonds), researchers found that children progressively blended diverse feedback modalities to collectively construct scientific understanding while exercising agency over their inquiry process. The findings demonstrate that embodied, technology-enhanced environments supporting collective feedback structures enable young children to engage in sophisticated systems thinking earlier than traditionally expected.
2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09453-8_Ho.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (interaction analysis of three episodes), findings (feedback blending and collective construction)
2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09453-8_Ho.coding_notes: Study uses fine-grained interaction analysis of moment-by-moment collaborative episodes in a mixed-reality embodied learning environment (STEP). Primary focus is on how children coordinate multiple feedback sources (self, peer, teacher, technology) in small groups; secondary attention to discourse traces and case-study depth. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

2020_v15i2_10.1007_s11412-020-09320-8_Do.title: Does collaborative learning design align with enactment? An innovative method of evaluating the alignment in the CSCL context
2020_v15i2_10.1007_s11412-020-09320-8_Do.summary_haiku: This study proposes design-centered research (DCR), a novel quantitative methodology for evaluating alignment between collaborative learning designs and their actual enactment. Using three indicators—activated knowledge range, knowledge-building degree, and interactive approach—plus interaction path graphs, researchers analyzed 40 groups across two iterations. Results show significant alignment improvements in round two after design optimization, with corresponding gains in group performance, demonstrating that data-driven design refinement enhances collaborative learning effectiveness.
2020_v15i2_10.1007_s11412-020-09320-8_Do.coding_notes: Study explicitly frames itself as design-centered research with iterative refinement across two rounds. Primary unit is 40 groups analyzed via interaction path graphs and three quantitative indicators (activated knowledge range, knowledge-building degree, interactive approach). Methodology combines design iteration with descriptive statistics and interaction-level analysis of collaborative traces.

2020_v15i1_10.1007_s11412-020-09315-5_Di.title: Distributed spatial Sensemaking on the augmented reality sandbox
2020_v15i1_10.1007_s11412-020-09315-5_Di.summary_haiku: This study uses Interaction Analysis to examine how small collaborative groups engage in distributed spatial sensemaking while using an Augmented Reality Sandbox for topographical learning. Findings reveal that AR features (contour lines, water simulations) coordinated with a 2D monitor representation enable groups to rapidly develop intrinsic-dynamic spatial thinking, facilitate quick trouble-repair sequences, and support divergent-to-convergent turn-taking patterns essential for advancing spatial understanding.
2020_v15i1_10.1007_s11412-020-09315-5_Di.coding_notes: Study explicitly employs Interaction Analysis of moment-by-moment collaborative episodes on an AR tangible interface. Distributed cognition is the primary theoretical lens given emphasis on spatial sensemaking spread across group members, the AR artifact, and the 2D monitor representation. Sociocultural framing is secondary (collaborative learning context).

2019_v14i2_10.1007_s11412-019-09304-3_De.title: Deliberative emotional talk
2019_v14i2_10.1007_s11412-019-09304-3_De.summary_haiku: This study demonstrates that high-quality deliberative discussions about controversial issues can integrate strong emotions with argumentative rigor. Using design-based research, the authors developed the Hot Discussions Platform (HDP), a CSCL tool enabling teachers to design, moderate, and reflect on emotionally-engaged discussions. Through a 30-hour professional development course with 25 teachers, analysis revealed teachers recognize emotions as essential to democratic education and develop sophisticated moderation practices balancing authentic expression with critical thinking standards, establishing proof-of-concept for "deliberative emotional talk."
2019_v14i2_10.1007_s11412-019-09304-3_De.coding_notes: Design-based research iteratively develops and studies the Hot Discussions Platform (HDP) with teachers as primary unit of analysis; focus on teacher moderation practices and deliberative emotional talk reflects dialogic and critical-pragmatic orientations. Secondary methods include content analysis of discussion artifacts and ethnographic observation of teacher learning during PD.

2024_v19i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09418-3_Ef.title: Effects of group awareness support in CSCL on students’ learning performance: A three‑level meta‑analysis
2024_v19i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09418-3_Ef.authors: Dengkang Chen & Yi Zhang & Heng Luo & Zhifang Zhu & Jingsi Ma & Yuru Lin
2024_v19i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09418-3_Ef.summary_haiku: Group awareness support in computer-supported collaborative learning shows moderate positive effects on student learning performance (g = 0.46). A three-level meta-analysis of 46 studies found greatest impact on cognitive development, followed by behavioral participation and social emotion. Combined awareness types outperformed individual types, and larger groups benefited more than smaller groups from awareness support.
2024_v19i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09418-3_Ef.coding_notes: This is a meta-analysis synthesizing 46 primary studies on group awareness support in CSCL. The three-level structure (study, effect size, participant) is characteristic of multilevel modeling. Primary unit is cohort/group because awareness support targets collaborative groups; secondary includes dyad analysis since group size effects are examined. Awareness dashboards are the core technology. Sociocultural framing is implicit in CSCL tradition; distributed cognition captures how awareness distributes information across the group.

2018_v13i3_10.1007_s11412-018-9282-1_Why.title: Why and how do middle school students exchange ideas during science inquiry?
2018_v13i3_10.1007_s11412-018-9282-1_Why.summary_haiku: This study investigates how the Idea Manager tool supports middle school students' peer idea exchange during science inquiry on cancer and cell division. Using the Knowledge Integration framework with 297 grade 7 students, researchers found that students generated more ideas independently than copying peers' ideas, and that collecting redundant self-generated ideas correlated with higher-quality scientific explanations, contrary to expectations favoring diverse ideas. Teachers reported enhanced formative assessment capabilities through monitoring student progress.
2018_v13i3_10.1007_s11412-018-9282-1_Why.evidence_span: methods, findings, discussion of Idea Manager tool and student idea exchange patterns
2018_v13i3_10.1007_s11412-018-9282-1_Why.coding_notes: The study uses trace data from the Idea Manager platform to analyze student idea generation and exchange patterns, fitting learning_analytics as primary methodology. Knowledge Integration framework and focus on collective idea improvement align with knowledge_building_theory. The Idea Manager functions as a shared knowledge repository supporting collaborative inquiry.

2017_v12i2_10.1007_s11412-017-9256-8_Joi.title: Joint interactions in large online knowledge communities: The A3C framework
2017_v12i2_10.1007_s11412-017-9256-8_Joi.authors: Ulrike Cress & Heisawn Jeong & Johannes Moskaliuk & Joachim Kimmerle
2017_v12i2_10.1007_s11412-017-9256-8_Joi.summary_haiku: This conceptual article proposes the A3C framework distinguishing four types of joint interactions in large online knowledge communities: Attendance, Coordination, Cooperation, and Collaboration. These interaction types vary by how members share goals, processes, and outcomes, progressing from individualistic orientations to fully shared endeavors. The framework integrates cognitive and socio-cultural perspectives to explain diverse participation patterns in mass-scale communities like Wikipedia and Scratch.
2017_v12i2_10.1007_s11412-017-9256-8_Joi.coding_notes: This is a conceptual/theoretical article proposing the A3C framework rather than reporting empirical research with a traditional methodology. Coded as 'other' for methodology_primary because it is framework development and theoretical analysis. Primary unit is community_network (Wikipedia, Scratch) with secondary focus on artifacts/traces. Sociocultural theory dominates; communities of practice and distributed cognition are secondary theoretical lenses.

2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09343-9_Ne.title: Net.Create: Network Visualization to Support Collaborative Historical Knowledge Building
2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09343-9_Ne.authors: Kalani Craig & Joshua Danish & Megan Humburg & Cindy Hmelo-Silver & Maksymilian Szostalo & Ann McCranie
2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09343-9_Ne.summary_haiku: # Summary This study examines Net.Create, a collaborative network visualization tool designed to help undergraduate history students analyze complex texts. Using activity theory, researchers analyzed how the tool and accompanying activities help students reconcile contradictions between detail and context, active learning and large lectures, and memorization versus historical reasoning. Analysis of log data, video recordings, and student papers from 76 students reveals that quality of historical significance annotations—not quantity of entries—correlates with stronger final papers. Students successfully moved between local details and aggregate patterns, with high-performing groups engaging in deeper "why" analysis compared to low-performing groups focused on "who" and "what."
2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09343-9_Ne.evidence_span: methods (log data, video, student papers) + findings (annotation quality, group performance patterns)
2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09343-9_Ne.coding_notes: Primary methodology is learning_analytics because trace data (logs) from the digital platform are used to model learning outcomes (paper quality, group performance). Activity theory is the explicit theoretical frame; knowledge_building_theory is secondary because the tool supports collaborative knowledge construction about historical significance. Net.Create is a network visualization and co-editing workspace, classified as shared_workspace_canvas with awareness features.

2017_v12i4_10.1007_s11412-017-9264-8_Dev.title: Developing & using interaction geography in a museum
2017_v12i4_10.1007_s11412-017-9264-8_Dev.authors: Ben Rydal Shapiro & Rogers P. Hall & David A. Owens
2017_v12i4_10.1007_s11412-017-9264-8_Dev.summary_haiku: Researchers developed "interaction geography," an integrative approach combining conversation analysis, movement tracking, and spatial design to study visitor engagement in museum settings. Using Mondrian Transcription and the Interaction Geography Slicer visualization tool, they analyzed 22 visitor groups' complete museum visits. A CSCL environment enabled museum professionals to reframe their understanding of visitor behavior—particularly children's movement—from disruptive to purposeful learning, supporting evidence-based design decisions for equitable learning opportunities.
2017_v12i4_10.1007_s11412-017-9264-8_Dev.evidence_span: methods (Mondrian Transcription, Interaction Geography Slicer, movement tracking) + findings (visitor group analysis, spatial design implications)
2017_v12i4_10.1007_s11412-017-9264-8_Dev.coding_notes: Primary methodology is interaction_analysis because the study uses micro-analytic coding of moment-by-moment collaborative episodes (conversation + movement). Secondary methods include discourse_analysis (conversation analysis) and sequence_process_mining (temporal patterns of visitor movement). Pedagogy is 'other' because the focus is on museum visitor learning design rather than a formal pedagogical model; the study reframes children's movement as purposeful learning. Technology_primary is awareness_dashboard because the Interaction Geography Slicer visualization tool displays group activity and spatial patterns to museum professionals for design decisions.

2019_v14i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9293-y_Pro.title: Providing different types of group awareness information to guide collaborative learning
2019_v14i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9293-y_Pro.summary_haiku: # Summary This experimental study with 260 university students examined how different types of group awareness information guide collaborative learning. Dyads discussed blood-sugar regulation while receiving either cognitive information about peers' assumptions, metacognitive information about peers' confidence levels, both, or neither. Results showed that visualized information strongly influenced task selection strategies—learners focused on conflicting assumptions or uncertain topics based on available information. However, providing awareness information did not significantly improve learning outcomes, suggesting that guiding study behavior alone may be insufficient without additional support for collaborative knowledge construction processes.
2019_v14i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9293-y_Pro.evidence_span: methods (experimental design, dyadic interaction, awareness conditions) + findings (task selection, learning outcomes)
2019_v14i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9293-y_Pro.coding_notes: Clear experimental design with 2×2 factorial manipulation of awareness information types (cognitive vs. metacognitive) delivered via visualization dashboard to guide dyadic collaboration. Primary focus on how awareness tools influence collaborative behavior and learning; sociocultural framing of peer awareness as mediating collaborative knowledge construction.

2022_v17i3_10.1007_s11412-022-09375-9_Sh.title: Shared meaning-making in online intergroup discussions around sensitive topics
2022_v17i3_10.1007_s11412-022-09375-9_Sh.authors: Tugce Aldemir & Marcela Borge & Jose Soto
2022_v17i3_10.1007_s11412-022-09375-9_Sh.summary_haiku: This study identifies four communication patterns associated with multicultural collaborative competence (MCC) in online intergroup discussions about sensitive identity topics: grounding with narratives, exploring differences and commonalities, critical reflection, and emotional support. Through qualitative analysis of four undergraduate teams' discussions, the researchers found that existing general collaborative competence frameworks inadequately capture these socio-political dynamics, though some overlap exists between MCC sophistication and traditional collaboration quality measures.
2022_v17i3_10.1007_s11412-022-09375-9_Sh.evidence_span: methods, findings, discussion of communication patterns and MCC framework
2022_v17i3_10.1007_s11412-022-09375-9_Sh.coding_notes: Study employs qualitative analysis of online discussion transcripts to identify communication patterns in small teams; dialogic and critical-pragmatic lenses fit the focus on meaning-making around sensitive identity topics and socio-political dynamics. Interaction analysis is primary because the work codes moment-by-moment collaborative episodes; content analysis is secondary because systematic coding of communication patterns is applied.

2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09366-w_Su.title: Supporting children’s place-based observations and explanations using collaboration scripts while learning-on- the-move outdoors
2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09366-w_Su.authors: Heather Toomey Zimmerman & Susan M. Land
2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09366-w_Su.summary_haiku: This design-based research study examined how collaboration scripts embedded in a mobile augmented reality app supported children's learning during outdoor activities. Across two iterations with 87 youth participants, researchers found significant gains in tree life cycle knowledge for both groups. Iteration B, which included additional scripts for socially-shared regulation of learning, showed improved collaborative sense-making where children better coordinated observational evidence with explanations, though knowledge gains were comparable between iterations.
2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09366-w_Su.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (design-based iterations), findings (knowledge gains, collaborative sense-making)
2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09366-w_Su.coding_notes: Design-based research with two iterative cycles testing collaboration scripts in a mobile AR app. Primary focus on dyadic/small-group collaboration during outdoor learning; secondary attention to individual knowledge outcomes. Sociocultural framing evident in emphasis on socially-shared regulation and collaborative sense-making.

2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09359-1_Ed.title: Educational dialogues and computer supported collaborative learning: critical analysis and research perspectives
2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09359-1_Ed.authors: Michael J. Baker & Baruch B. Schwarz & Sten R. Ludvigsen
2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09359-1_Ed.summary_haiku: This critical analysis proposes that educational dialogue research in CSCL requires theoretically grounded integration of diverse data types across multiple timescales. The authors argue the object of study should be collective thinking development in dialogue, with the exchange as the basic analytical unit. They introduce digital platforms as an intermediary analytical level between micro-dialogic exchanges and macro-institutional contexts, emphasizing the need for coherent theoretical frameworks connecting automatic and human analyses to avoid fragmentation.
2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09359-1_Ed.evidence_span: abstract, introduction, and theoretical framing sections
2021_v16i4_10.1007_s11412-021-09359-1_Ed.coding_notes: This is a critical analysis and research perspective paper rather than an empirical study. The focus on educational dialogue, exchange as analytical unit, and integration of micro-dialogic and macro-institutional levels strongly indicates discourse and interaction analysis grounded in dialogic theory. The emphasis on digital platforms as intermediary analytical level suggests multi-level analysis across timescales.

2017_v12i2_10.1007_s11412-017-9258-6_All.title: All in good time: knowledge introduction, restructuring, and development of shared opinions as different stages in collaborative writing
2017_v12i2_10.1007_s11412-017-9258-6_All.summary_haiku: This study examined how secondary school student dyads with differing theoretical perspectives on media effects collaborated to write shared texts. Using quantitative and qualitative content analysis of eight text versions, researchers identified three distinct sequential stages: early knowledge introduction, middle restructuring activities, and late shared opinion development. Results demonstrated that collaborative writing progresses through predictable phases, with different activities dominating each stage as participants integrate divergent perspectives into unified conclusions.
2017_v12i2_10.1007_s11412-017-9258-6_All.evidence_span: methods (content analysis of 8 text versions) + findings (three sequential stages identified)
2017_v12i2_10.1007_s11412-017-9258-6_All.coding_notes: Study uses systematic coding of collaborative writing artifacts across multiple versions to identify temporal phases; this is primarily content analysis with strong sequential/process-mining elements. Sociocultural framing emphasizes integration of divergent perspectives through collaborative activity; dialogic secondary reflects multi-voiced perspective negotiation.

2022_v17i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09371-z_Cr.title: Cross-community knowledge building with idea thread mapper
2022_v17i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09371-z_Cr.authors: Guangji Yuan & Jianwei Zhang & Mei-Hwa Chen
2022_v17i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09371-z_Cr.summary_haiku: # Summary This design-based research study investigated how four Grade 5 classrooms collaboratively built knowledge about human body systems using the Idea Thread Mapper (ITM) platform. Students engaged in local classroom inquiry while generating "super notes"—reflective syntheses—shared in a cross-community meta-space. Through cross-classroom "Super Talk" discussions on how people grow, students integrated diverse ideas from multiple classrooms into sophisticated, multifaceted understandings. Results demonstrated that students produced high-quality reflections and that cross-community collaboration created expansive learning contexts enabling knowledge advancement across social levels.
2022_v17i2_10.1007_s11412-022-09371-z_Cr.coding_notes: Design-based research iteratively studying ITM platform for cross-classroom knowledge building aligned with Scardamalia & Bereiter framework. Multi-level analysis spans individual reflections (super notes), small-group discussions, and cross-classroom meta-space interactions. No AI/LLM involvement evident in study design or technology.

2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09429-0_Re.title: Revealing the interplay of cognitive, meta‑cognitive, and social processes in university students’ collaborative problem solving: a three‑stage analytical framework
2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09429-0_Re.authors: Shuowen An & Si Zhang & Zhihui Cai & Wei Pan & Mingwei Li & Mingwen Tong
2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09429-0_Re.summary_haiku: This study proposes a three-stage analytical framework to examine collaborative problem-solving (CPS) patterns among 24 university students completing instructional design and multimedia development tasks. Using dynamic time warping for clustering and process mining analysis, the researchers identified two distinct CPS subgroups: solution-driven groups that effectively transitioned from divergent to convergent thinking through meta-cognitive monitoring, and problem-driven groups that focused on task requirements but lacked comprehensive evaluation processes, resulting in lower performance outcomes.
2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09429-0_Re.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (three-stage framework, dynamic time warping, process mining)
2025_v20i1_10.1007_s11412-024-09429-0_Re.coding_notes: The study's core contribution is temporal sequence analysis using process mining and dynamic time warping to cluster and characterize CPS patterns. Interaction analysis is secondary because the framework examines moment-by-moment cognitive and meta-cognitive transitions. No AI/LLM involvement detected; technology is used for data collection/analysis, not as a learning tool.

2021_v16i1_10.1007_s11412-021-09339-5_Ca.title: Capturing regulatory patterns in online collaborative learning: A network analytic approach
2021_v16i1_10.1007_s11412-021-09339-5_Ca.authors: Si Zhang & Juan Chen & Yun Wen & Hongxian Chen & Qianqian Gao & Qiyun Wang
2021_v16i1_10.1007_s11412-021-09339-5_Ca.summary_haiku: This study examined 45 student teachers' regulatory patterns during online collaborative learning using content analysis and epistemic network analysis (ENA). Findings revealed that high-performing groups demonstrated significantly more content monitoring and emotional regulation behaviors than low-performing groups across different activity stages. The analysis identified distinct regulatory patterns: high-performing groups emphasized planning and evaluation, while low-performing groups relied on routine-level regulatory strategies throughout collaboration.
2021_v16i1_10.1007_s11412-021-09339-5_Ca.evidence_span: title, methods (content analysis and epistemic network analysis), findings (regulatory patterns across groups and stages)
2021_v16i1_10.1007_s11412-021-09339-5_Ca.coding_notes: Epistemic network analysis (ENA) is a graph-based method for visualizing and analyzing connections among concepts in discourse, making social_network_analysis the primary methodology. The study uses content analysis to code regulatory behaviors and ENA to map their relational patterns. Unit of analysis is small groups (45 student teachers in collaborative teams), with cross-level analysis comparing high vs. low-performing groups. Self-regulation and peer regulation are central to the pedagogical focus.

2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9292-z_Whe.title: When coding-and-counting is not enough: using epistemic network analysis (ENA) to analyze verbal data in CSCL research
2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9292-z_Whe.authors: Brendan Eagan & Ingo Kollar & David Williamson Shaffer
2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9292-z_Whe.summary_haiku: Traditional coding-and-counting analyses of collaborative learning discourse ignore temporal relationships between learning actions, potentially missing important patterns. This study compared traditional frequency-based analysis with Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA), which models temporal co-occurrences of coded actions. Analyzing pre-service teachers' problem-solving discourse, ENA revealed that evidence evaluation was central to dyadic reasoning but not individual reasoning—a pattern invisible to traditional methods. Results confirm that temporal structure, not merely code frequency, drives these findings.
2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9292-z_Whe.coding_notes: ENA is a computational method for analyzing temporal co-occurrence patterns in coded discourse; the study compares it to traditional coding-and-counting, making interaction_analysis primary with sequence_process_mining as secondary. Pre-service teachers solving problems in dyads is the core unit, though individual reasoning is also examined comparatively.

2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9249-7_DCL.title: DCLM framework: understanding collaboration in open-ended tabletop learning environments
2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9249-7_DCL.authors: Matthew Berland & Leilah Lyons & Mike Tissenbaum
2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9249-7_DCL.summary_haiku: This paper introduces the Divergent Collaborative Learning Mechanisms (DCLM) framework for analyzing collaboration in open-ended tabletop learning environments where participants pursue divergent goals. Extending the existing Collaborative Learning Mechanisms framework, DCLM adds six mechanisms including boundary spanning actions and perception, goal adaptation, and modeling. Analysis of the Oztoc museum exhibit demonstrates that participants with non-aligned goals can productively collaborate, providing insights unavailable in shared-goal activities.
2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9249-7_DCL.evidence_span: title, abstract, framework description, museum exhibit analysis
2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9249-7_DCL.coding_notes: The paper presents a framework (DCLM) for analyzing moment-by-moment collaborative mechanisms in a tangible tabletop environment. The primary methodology is interaction analysis of dyadic/small-group behavior; secondary methods include systematic coding of collaborative episodes and ethnographic observation of the museum context. Sociocultural theory underpins the analysis of how divergent goals and boundary-spanning actions enable productive collaboration.

2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9241-7_App.title: Appropriation from a script theory of guidance perspective: a response to Pierre Tchounikine
2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9241-7_App.authors: Karsten Stegmann & Ingo Kollar & Armin Weinberger & Frank Fischer
2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9241-7_App.summary_haiku: This response clarifies how Script Theory of Guidance (SToG) addresses learner appropriation of collaboration scripts. The authors argue SToG inherently concerns appropriation through three mechanisms: learners' goals influence internal script configuration, perceived situational characteristics shape script interpretation, and appropriation involves perception, interpretation, and implementation steps. They propose that internalization follows successful appropriation, and acknowledge that institutional and domain-specific factors merit stronger theoretical integration within SToG's framework.
2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9241-7_App.coding_notes: This is a theoretical response paper clarifying Script Theory of Guidance (SToG) rather than an empirical study; no primary methodology is applied. The focus is on conceptual analysis of how learners appropriate collaboration scripts through perception, interpretation, and implementation—grounded in activity-theoretic and sociocultural perspectives on internalization and appropriation.

2016_v11i2_10.1007_s11412-016-9235-5_The.title: The symmetry of partner modelling
2016_v11i2_10.1007_s11412-016-9235-5_The.authors: Pierre Dillenbourg & Mirweis Sangin & Nicolas Nova
2016_v11i2_10.1007_s11412-016-9235-5_The.summary_haiku: This study examines whether collaborative partners' mutual modeling accuracy—their ability to understand each other's knowledge, intentions, and emotions—depends on individual cognitive skills or interaction quality. Analyzing five experiments across different collaborative tasks, the researchers found that partners' modeling accuracy was significantly correlated in four studies, suggesting interaction quality matters more than individual abilities. However, correlations remained moderate, indicating both factors contribute to mutual understanding in collaborative learning.
2016_v11i2_10.1007_s11412-016-9235-5_The.evidence_span: methods (five experiments) + findings (correlation analysis, modeling accuracy)
2016_v11i2_10.1007_s11412-016-9235-5_The.coding_notes: Study uses correlation and statistical inference to test whether interaction quality predicts mutual modeling accuracy across dyads. Primary focus is dyadic interaction and partner modeling; secondary attention to individual cognitive skills. No explicit technology or AI involvement; collaboration appears face-to-face or minimal-tech.

2020_v15i2_10.1007_s11412-020-09321-7_Ta.title: Talking about group (but not individual) process aids group performance
2020_v15i2_10.1007_s11412-020-09321-7_Ta.authors: Noel Capon & Hueiyi Lai & Deanna Kuhn
2020_v15i2_10.1007_s11412-020-09321-7_Ta.summary_haiku: # Summary This study examined how group discourse relates to collaborative problem-solving performance. Graduate business students worked in small groups through a computer-supported marketing simulation over eight sessions. Discourse analysis revealed that groups discussing their collective process (Meta-group talk) achieved superior outcomes, while talk focused on individual perspectives (Meta-self talk) correlated negatively with performance. Meta-group discourse included understanding others, defining group position, planning, and evaluating—functions that facilitate coordinated action essential for effective collaboration.
2020_v15i2_10.1007_s11412-020-09321-7_Ta.evidence_span: methods (discourse analysis coding scheme) + findings (correlation of meta-group vs meta-self talk with performance)
2020_v15i2_10.1007_s11412-020-09321-7_Ta.coding_notes: Study uses systematic discourse coding to categorize group talk (meta-group vs meta-self) and correlates these categories with performance outcomes. Primary focus is on linguistic/rhetorical analysis of collaborative episodes, with secondary quantitative correlation analysis. Sociocultural framing emphasizes how collective reflection on group process mediates collaborative problem-solving.

2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9237-3_You.title: You like it, you learn it: affectivity and learning in competitive social role play gaming
2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9237-3_You.authors: Cyril Brom & Michaela Slussareff & Tereza Selmbacherova
2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9237-3_You.summary_haiku: This study examined whether positive affect mediates learning gains in game-based education using a between-subjects design with 325 high school and college students. Participants learned about EU policy through a debate-based method delivered via computer game, non-computer game, or traditional workshop. Both game conditions induced higher positive affect and flow, and participants learned more with games. Positive affect—but not flow—mediated the relationship between instructional medium and learning outcomes, suggesting that affective engagement is crucial for game-based learning effectiveness.
2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9237-3_You.evidence_span: methods (between-subjects design, 325 participants, three conditions) + findings (mediation analysis, positive affect as mediator)
2016_v11i3_10.1007_s11412-016-9237-3_You.coding_notes: Study uses controlled comparison of three instructional conditions (computer game, non-computer game, traditional workshop) with random assignment, fitting experimental design. Primary unit is individual learner outcomes (learning gains, affect, flow). Debate-based method emphasizes argumentation; technology is secondary to the pedagogical intervention. Mediation analysis of affect on learning aligns with socio-cognitive and information-processing theories linking emotion to cognition.

2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09362-0_In.title: Integrating a collaboration script and group awareness to support group regulation and emotions towards collaborative problem solving
2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09362-0_In.authors: Matias Rojas & Miguel Nussbaum & Orlando Guerrero & Pablo Chiuminatto & Samuel Greiff & Rodrigo Del Rio & Danilo Alvares
2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09362-0_In.summary_haiku: This study examined how a game-based collaboration script with group awareness tools affects elementary students' collaborative problem-solving skills. Using a quasi-experimental design with 223 sixth-graders, researchers compared an experimental group playing a six-level collaborative game to a control group receiving regular instruction. Results showed the intervention significantly improved attitudes toward collaboration and increased shared regulation and co-regulation processes. Qualitative analysis revealed positive emotions like satisfaction emerged through co-regulation, suggesting collaboration scripts combined with group awareness effectively support regulation skills and emotional development during collaborative problem-solving.
2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09362-0_In.evidence_span: methods (quasi-experimental design, 223 sixth-graders, experimental vs. control), findings (attitudes, shared regulation, co-regulation, emotions)
2022_v17i1_10.1007_s11412-022-09362-0_In.coding_notes: Study uses a game-based collaboration script with group awareness tools in a quasi-experimental design. Primary focus is on how structured collaboration scripts and awareness mechanisms support group regulation and emotions. Qualitative analysis of emotions and regulation processes complements quantitative outcome measures.

2020_v15i4_10.1007_s11412-020-09336-0_A_.title: A review of the International Handbook of
2020_v15i4_10.1007_s11412-020-09336-0_A_.summary_haiku: This review examines the International Handbook of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 2020, analyzing its contributions to the thirty-year-old CSCL field. Using Kuhn's paradigm shift framework, the author identifies the handbook as both a consensus document summarizing established theories, designs, and methods, and a source of productive disequilibria—unresolved tensions in diversity/equity, scalability, learning analytics integration, and methodological coherence—that present opportunities for transformative scholarship and paradigm shifts.
2020_v15i4_10.1007_s11412-020-09336-0_A_.coding_notes: This is a meta-analytic review of a handbook rather than an empirical study of CSCL. The primary methodology is systematic coding and analysis of handbook chapters as artifacts. Pedagogy is not directly applicable since the review examines the field itself rather than implementing a specific pedagogical approach; sociocultural and activity theory are inferred as dominant theoretical frameworks within the reviewed handbook.

2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09298-y_Gu.title: Guiding collaborative revision of science explanations
2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09298-y_Gu.summary_haiku: Combining automated explanation scoring with teacher guidance in a computer-supported collaborative learning environment, this study examined how one sixth-grade teacher customized adaptive feedback to guide 98 student pairs in revising science explanations about plate tectonics. Analysis of classroom interactions revealed five distinct teacher guidance strategies that leveraged automated scores to personalize support. Results showed nearly all pairs engaged in meaningful revision, with significant improvements in explanation quality and individual posttest gains, demonstrating how teacher-computer partnerships can effectively promote collaborative knowledge integration.
2019_v14i3_10.1007_s11412-019-09298-y_Gu.coding_notes: Study combines quantitative outcome measures (posttest gains, revision quality) with qualitative interaction analysis of teacher guidance strategies. Automated explanation scoring is rule-based AI (not LLM), but the teacher uses scores to provide adaptive feedback. Primary unit is student pairs revising collaboratively; teacher facilitation is secondary analytical focus.

2020_v15i2_10.1007_s11412-020-09323-5_Re.title: Regulating self-organized collaborative learning: the importance of homogeneous problem perception, immediacy and intensity of strategy use
2020_v15i2_10.1007_s11412-020-09323-5_Re.authors: Martin Greisel & Markus Dresel & Ingo Kollar & Nadine Melzner
2020_v15i2_10.1007_s11412-020-09323-5_Re.summary_haiku: Self-organized study groups achieve greater satisfaction when members develop shared problem perceptions, apply strategies that directly address identified problems, and use regulation strategies frequently. This longitudinal study of 122 university students across 52 groups examined how problem perception homogeneity, strategy immediacy, and strategy intensity predict satisfaction with collaborative learning experiences during exam preparation, confirming all three hypotheses through hierarchical linear modeling.
2020_v15i2_10.1007_s11412-020-09323-5_Re.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (hierarchical linear modeling of 122 students nested in 52 groups)
2020_v15i2_10.1007_s11412-020-09323-5_Re.coding_notes: Study explicitly uses hierarchical linear modeling to analyze nested data (individuals within groups), making multilevel modeling the primary methodology. Focus on self-regulated strategy use and shared problem perception aligns with self/peer regulation pedagogy. No technology platform mentioned; collaboration is self-organized study groups.

2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9273-2_One.title: One framework to rule them all? Carrying forward the conversation started by Wise and Schwarz
2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9273-2_One.summary_haiku: Rather than seeking one unified CSCL framework top-down, this article proposes using a 12-dimension taxonomy of support characteristics as a foundation for collaborative empirical research. Through experimental studies varying dimensions like timing and foundation of instruction, the author demonstrates how systematic investigation across taxonomy dimensions can generate evidence-based design principles for computer-supported collaborative learning environments.
2018_v13i1_10.1007_s11412-018-9273-2_One.coding_notes: The article proposes a 12-dimension taxonomy and uses experimental studies varying instructional dimensions (timing, foundation) to test collaborative learning. Primary methodology is experimental comparison of conditions; secondary is systematic coding of support characteristics. Sociocultural framing emphasizes mediation of learning through structured collaboration; activity theory relevant to systematic design principles across dimensions.

2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9248-8_Thi.title: This is the size of one meter: Children’s bodily-material collaboration
2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9248-8_Thi.summary_haiku: Two nine-year-old children collaborating around a touchscreen demonstrate that bodily-material resources—gestures, movements, and touch—function as primary vehicles for learning about scale and measurement, not merely supplementary to language. Through detailed video analysis, the study reveals children use bodies communicatively to illustrate understanding, cognitively as auxiliary tools scaffolding knowledge, and physically to shepherd each other's learning in the space between themselves and the screen.
2017_v12i1_10.1007_s11412-017-9248-8_Thi.coding_notes: Study employs detailed video analysis of moment-by-moment collaborative episodes between two children, focusing on gestures, movements, and touch as primary analytical objects. Touchscreen interaction is treated as a tangible/embodied interface rather than a traditional digital tool. Sociocultural framing emphasizes mediation through bodily and material resources; distributed cognition captures the spread of cognition across bodies, artifacts, and environment.

2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09327-1_Da.title: Data wrangling practices and collaborative interactions with aggregated data
2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09327-1_Da.summary_haiku: Youth engaged in data wrangling—selecting and managing large datasets to create models and stories—using interactive visualization tools to explore family migration. Analysis of talk-in-interaction identified ten sociotechnical practices and four learning activity categories: addressing missing data, understanding aggregation, exploring historical events, and varying visual encoding. Collaborative interactions with instructors and peers supported critical inquiry and meaning-making about data's social significance.
2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09327-1_Da.evidence_span: methods (talk-in-interaction analysis, coding of practices and activities) + findings (ten sociotechnical practices, four learning categories, collaborative interactions)
2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09327-1_Da.coding_notes: Study uses micro-analytic coding of moment-by-moment collaborative episodes around data visualization tools, grounded in sociocultural theory. Secondary methods include discourse analysis of talk and content analysis of identified practices; secondary units include the artifacts (visualizations, datasets) being jointly manipulated.

2017_v12i4_10.1007_s11412-017-9267-5_Vis.title: Visions of CSCL: eight provocations for the future of the field
2017_v12i4_10.1007_s11412-017-9267-5_Vis.authors: Alyssa Friend Wise & Baruch B. Schwarz
2017_v12i4_10.1007_s11412-017-9267-5_Vis.summary_haiku: CSCL faces critical identity and relevance questions through eight provocations: the field needs unified conceptual frameworks for diverse tools, should prioritize learner agency over scripting, rigorously define collaboration and community, address methodological divides, pursue computational approaches, prioritize learning analytics and adaptive support, expand to social media and large-scale environments, and reconsider its commitment to educational change through research-practice partnerships.
2017_v12i4_10.1007_s11412-017-9267-5_Vis.coding_notes: This is a position/vision paper presenting eight provocations and future directions for CSCL as a field, not an empirical study. It does not employ a specific research methodology, analyze a bounded unit, instantiate a particular pedagogy, deploy technology, or test theory. The paper is meta-analytical and prescriptive rather than descriptive or experimental.

2016_v11i1_10.1007_s11412-016-9227-5_Tra.title: Tracing the change in discourse in a collaborative dynamic geometry environment: From visual to more mathematical
2016_v11i1_10.1007_s11412-016-9227-5_Tra.summary_haiku: This case study examined three middle-school students' mathematical discourse development while solving geometry construction problems in the Virtual Math Teams collaborative environment. Using Sfard's commognitive framework, the researcher traced changes in students' word usage, visual mediators, and problem-solving routines across six episodes. The team progressively shifted from visual, perception-based approaches to more formal mathematical discourse emphasizing geometric dependencies, demonstrating that well-designed collaborative virtual learning environments can support significant mathematical development comparable to expert instruction.
2016_v11i1_10.1007_s11412-016-9227-5_Tra.evidence_span: title, abstract, methods (Sfard's commognitive framework, discourse analysis across episodes)
2016_v11i1_10.1007_s11412-016-9227-5_Tra.coding_notes: Study explicitly uses Sfard's commognitive framework to trace discourse change through word usage, visual mediators, and routines—core discourse analysis. Virtual Math Teams is a synchronous collaborative geometry environment supporting shared workspace interaction. Three-student group is the primary unit; artifact/discourse traces (problem-solving episodes) are secondary. Inquiry-based geometry construction problems with implicit collaboration scripts in the virtual environment.

2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09326-2_En.title: Encouraging collaboration and building Community in Online Asynchronous Professional Development: designing for social capital
2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09326-2_En.authors: Susan A. Yoon & Katherine Miller & Thomas Richman & Daniel Wendel & Ilana Schoenfeld & Emma Anderson & Jooeun Shim
2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09326-2_En.summary_haiku: This study examined how online asynchronous professional development designed around social capital mechanisms supports science teachers' learning. Eight high school biology teachers participated in a six-week course combining discussion prompts, expert videos, and peer facilitation. Satisfaction surveys showed high ratings across all dimensions. Transactivity analysis revealed that collaborative prompts significantly increased peer interaction compared to content or implementation prompts. Interview data indicated positive perceptions of expertise access and interaction depth, though trust-building remained challenging in the asynchronous format.
2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09326-2_En.evidence_span: methods (transactivity analysis, surveys, interviews) + findings (prompt effects, satisfaction, trust challenges)
2020_v15i3_10.1007_s11412-020-09326-2_En.coding_notes: Transactivity analysis is a form of interaction coding applied to asynchronous discussion posts; the study systematically codes peer interactions by prompt type, supporting content_analysis as primary. Social capital and community-of-practice framing is explicit. Asynchronous forum is the primary technology; peer facilitation and discussion prompts function as collaboration scripts.

2016_v11i1_10.1007_s11412-016-9228-4_Exp.title: Exploring the relationship between resistance and perspectival understanding in computer-mediated discussions
