2016_v11i1_10.1007_s11412-016-9228-4_Exp.summary_haiku: This discourse analytic study examined how graduate students expressed resistance while negotiating ideas in computer-mediated discussions. Findings revealed that resistance expressions frequently accompanied perspectival understanding as students elaborated on course readings and peer ideas. Resistance functioned as a constructive discourse tool, facilitating both individual and collaborative knowledge construction. The study demonstrates resistance's integral role in developing sophisticated perspectives within online classroom discussions.
2016_v11i1_10.1007_s11412-016-9228-4_Exp.coding_notes: Study explicitly employs discourse analysis to examine linguistic expressions of resistance in online discussions. Primary unit is the discourse trace (computer-mediated posts); secondary analysis considers dyadic/small-group negotiation. Dialogic theory best captures the multi-voiced negotiation of perspectives; sociocultural and socio-cognitive theories also relevant to knowledge construction through resistance.

2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09458-3_A_.title: A quarter century of advances in collaboration sensing: a comprehensive review of high‑frequency metrics and their connection to collaborative constructs from 2000 to 2025
2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09458-3_A_.authors: Bertrand Schneider & Xiao Fang & Shinyi Kang & Pankaj Chejara & Jiajun Bu
2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09458-3_A_.summary_haiku: This systematic review of 163 studies (2000-2025) examines how multimodal sensing technologies capture collaboration through high-frequency metrics. Using the PRISMA framework and a construct-to-data mapping approach, researchers analyzed connections between sensor-derived metrics (verbal, gaze, body, physiological, head, log data) and collaborative indicators (coordination, performance, learning, engagement, affects). Key findings reveal most studies employed laboratory settings with small samples, relied on simple synchronization metrics, and lacked standardized measurement tools. Critically, less than 9% leveraged sensor data for real-time interventions, identifying major gaps in designing guidance systems beyond mirroring feedback.
2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09458-3_A_.evidence_span: abstract, methods (PRISMA framework, construct-to-data mapping), findings (sensor metrics, collaborative indicators, intervention gaps)
2026_v21i1_10.1007_s11412-025-09458-3_A_.coding_notes: This is a systematic review of 163 empirical studies on collaboration sensing rather than a primary empirical study. The primary methodology is content analysis of published research using structured coding schemes (construct-to-data mapping). Multimodal sensors (verbal, gaze, body, physiological, head) and log data are the core technology examined across reviewed studies. No AI/LLM involvement in the review itself. Pedagogy is not a primary focus of the review; it examines sensing and metrics rather than instructional design.

2020_v15i1_10.1007_s11412-020-09318-2_Un.title: Unpacking the relationship between existing and new measures of physiological synchrony and collaborative learning: a mixed methods study
2020_v15i1_10.1007_s11412-020-09318-2_Un.summary_haiku: This mixed-methods study examined how electrodermal activity (EDA) measures physiological synchrony in collaborative learning. Forty-two dyads programmed robots while wearing EDA sensors. Pearson's correlation and directional agreement showed modest associations with learning gains and collaboration quality. Qualitative analysis of high and low-performing groups revealed that synchrony peaks during external events, oscillates during collaboration, and drops during independent work. A novel measure—cycles between low and high synchrony—strongly correlated with collaboration quality and learning outcomes, suggesting it captures distinct collaborative dynamics.
2020_v15i1_10.1007_s11412-020-09318-2_Un.coding_notes: Study combines quantitative physiological sensor data (EDA) with qualitative interaction analysis of dyadic robot-programming tasks. The novel synchrony measure (cycles between low/high states) represents a methodological contribution bridging quantitative and qualitative understanding of collaborative dynamics.

2018_v13i2_10.1007_s11412-018-9275-0_Com.title: Community technology mapping: inscribing places when everything is on the move
2018_v13i2_10.1007_s11412-018-9275-0_Com.authors: Katie Headrick Taylor & Reed Stevens & Deborah Silvis
2018_v13i2_10.1007_s11412-018-9275-0_Com.summary_haiku: Community Technology Mapping (CTM) combines interactive digital mapping with structured interviews to support children's reflection on spatiotemporal organization of technology use across daily routines. Through ethnographic analysis of twelve children's mapping activities in Google Earth, researchers identified three inscription processes: making places visible through wayfinding, making places coherent through narrative reconciliation, and making places mobile through dynamic interaction. CTM functions as both pedagogical tool for developing locative literacies and methodological innovation for examining children's place-based learning beyond home observations.
2018_v13i2_10.1007_s11412-018-9275-0_Com.evidence_span: methods (ethnographic analysis, twelve children, Google Earth mapping) + findings (three inscription processes identified)
2018_v13i2_10.1007_s11412-018-9275-0_Com.coding_notes: Study is primarily ethnographic case study examining children's digital mapping artifacts and reflective processes. Google Earth functions as shared workspace for co-construction of place knowledge. Sociocultural framing evident in emphasis on spatiotemporal organization and locative literacies as culturally mediated activity.

2019_v14i2_10.1007_s11412-019-09300-7_Co.title: Conceptualizing the designs of authentic
2019_v14i2_10.1007_s11412-019-09300-7_Co.summary_haiku: This study synthesizes 25 years of CSCL research using constant-comparative analysis to clarify authentic learning design. The authors identify three cultures—current, authentic, and intended—operating in authentic learning environments and distinguish between simulation approaches (classroom-based enculturation) and hybrid approaches (direct practitioner interaction). A coding scheme analyzing participants, settings, time, computer support, and collaboration reveals that timeframe most clearly differentiates approaches, offering CSCL designers a refined conceptual framework and visualization tool for understanding authentic learning environment variations.
2019_v14i2_10.1007_s11412-019-09300-7_Co.evidence_span: methods (constant-comparative analysis, coding scheme) + findings (three cultures framework, simulation vs. hybrid distinction)
2019_v14i2_10.1007_s11412-019-09300-7_Co.coding_notes: This is a systematic literature review synthesizing 25 years of CSCL research using constant-comparative analysis and a structured coding scheme to analyze design dimensions (participants, settings, time, computer support, collaboration). Primary methodology is content_analysis because the authors systematically code and categorize existing CSCL studies. Unit of analysis is artifact_discourse_trace because the primary objects analyzed are research publications and their design descriptions. Theory is communities_of_practice because the framework emphasizes authentic participation in practitioner communities; activity_theory is secondary given the focus on contradictions between intended and actual cultures.

2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9287-9_The.title: The opportunities of networks of research-practice partnerships and why CSCL should not give up on large-scale educational change
2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9287-9_The.authors: Ornit Sagy & Yael Kali & Yotam Hod
2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9287-9_The.summary_haiku: This article argues that CSCL should pursue large-scale educational change through networks of design-centric research-practice partnerships (DC-RPPs). The authors counter arguments that the field has abandoned this goal by demonstrating how collaborative networks integrating researchers, practitioners, and policymakers can generate scalable, sustainable innovations. They illustrate this approach through Taking Citizen Science to School, a five-year Israeli research center connecting citizen science with classroom learning.
2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9287-9_The.evidence_span: title, abstract, and article framing on design-centric research-practice partnerships and large-scale change
2018_v13i4_10.1007_s11412-018-9287-9_The.coding_notes: The article is primarily a position/argument piece advocating for networks of research-practice partnerships (DC-RPPs) as a vehicle for large-scale educational change, illustrated through a citizen science case study. Design-based research is the primary methodology because the work iteratively designs and studies an intervention (Taking Citizen Science to School) in naturalistic settings. The unit of analysis is the network itself (community_network) connecting researchers, practitioners, and policymakers, though classroom cohorts are also involved. Activity theory and communities of practice align with the systemic, networked approach to sustainable innovation.

2021_v16i1_10.1007_s11412-021-09341-x_Af.title: Affording embodied cognition through touchscreen and above-the-surface gestures during collaborative tabletop science learning
2021_v16i1_10.1007_s11412-021-09341-x_Af.summary_haiku: This study examined how family groups use touchscreen and above-the-surface gestures during collaborative learning with multi-touch tabletops displaying ocean temperature data. Using a user-centered design approach, researchers analyzed 11 family groups' utterances and gestures to identify embodied cognition instances. Four gesture types emerged: orienting the group, cooperative gestures, individual intentional gestures, and articulating conceptual understanding. Findings reveal specific gestural interactions that facilitate embodied-cognition-supported collaborative meaning-making in science learning.
2021_v16i1_10.1007_s11412-021-09341-x_Af.coding_notes: Study uses micro-analytic coding of moment-by-moment gestures and utterances during collaborative tabletop interaction. Multimodal analysis of touchscreen and above-the-surface gestures captures embodied cognition; design-based approach with family groups as primary analytical unit. No AI/LLM involvement detected.

2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09344-8_So.title: Social sensitivity: a manifesto for CSCL research
2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09344-8_So.authors: Jaana Isohatala & Piia Naykki & Sanna Jarvela & Michael J. Baker & Kristine Lund
2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09344-8_So.summary_haiku: Current educational technologies inadequately support collaborative learning as both cognitive and socio-emotional processes, risking hindered idea exchange and negative interactions. This manifesto argues CSCL research is fragmented across theoretical silos, failing to communicate coherent evidence to practitioners and developers. The authors propose "social sensitivity"—an interdisciplinary framework emphasizing constructively critical, respectful, and cohesive collaboration—and call for concrete actions: crossing theoretical boundaries, conducting multimodal empirical research, and transferring evidence to educational practices and policies.
2021_v16i2_10.1007_s11412-021-09344-8_So.coding_notes: This is a manifesto and position paper rather than an empirical study, so methodology and unit of analysis do not fit standard research designs. The work advocates for social sensitivity in CSCL—emphasizing respectful, cohesive, and constructively critical collaboration—which aligns with collaboration scripts and self-regulation. Theory draws on sociocultural, dialogic, and socio-cognitive traditions to frame the need for integrating cognitive and socio-emotional processes.
